en: Preface to the *Lübo’an Gao* (Drafts from the Traveler’s Hut):
Heaven and earth are a single inn. The coming and going of the sun and moon, and the standing and flowing of mountains and rivers, constitute the world within this inn.

The meditative stillness of the Two Vehicles and the rising and sinking of beings through the four modes of birth are the sentient beings within this inn. All the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time...
The successive patriarchs of past dynasties have been the ships upon which to cross this inn of transmigration.

The Tripiṭaka and twelve divisions of scripture, the three thousand and seven hundred cases of kōan, are the sedan chairs and staffs within this inn. Since the Dharma was transmitted to the East, the dragon-elephants [of great practitioners] have arisen in succession.

Some are born by riding the momentum of destiny; some arise in response to conditions. Although they adorn their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), they regard the objects of perception as always being like flowers in the sky.
Although they sit extensively at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they view this body as equally like a phantom or a temporary lodging.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Traveling and dwelling within the three realms, they demonstrate a single coming and going. This clarifies this very principle.
For the sake of Master Linpai Gong, who bears the Dharma-seal of the Dongshan school and continues the lamp-transmission of Shigong:

since he first established the Dharma on this mountain and proclaimed the Way at Shuangta, he has stripped away the cataracts of worldly dust and shattered the delusive barriers of the path for thirty years.
In the autumn of the Xinhai year, he suddenly relinquished his sickle-shaped couch and took up his staff once more.
Whether at mountain fastnesses or riverbanks, he wandered at ease; whether in the realm of Buddhas or the palaces of Māras, he was sovereign according to conditions.
Yet, wherever his staff and almsbowl reached, a monastic grove was established; whenever his whisk and fly-whisk were casually raised, they became centers for the Dharma.

Thus, as the Master’s traces grew ever more obscure, his Way became ever more manifest. Thereupon, the clergy and laity of the capital city made earnest entreaties, and [he traveled] by boat and carriage to Baofu.

Traveling back and forth like a silkworm cocooning itself in layers, the Master was unable to remain in perpetual seclusion. Consequently, during the summer of that year, he shook his mendicant’s staff and returned to the mountain.

I followed the procession to welcome him and attended upon him for several nights, consulting and studying under him. Thereupon, I was able to read the Master’s recently published *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings), which he himself titled *Lüpo’an Gao* (Drafts from the Traveller’s Hut).
Alas! For over ten years, the great ocean has been the vast abode of the roaming dragon; the void...
He made the clouds and cranes his native home; the Master was truly one who departs without attachment and arrives without destination.

His name, "The Wanderer," was intended to express this very point. This collection of songs adapts to circumstances as they arise, penetrating the vital points of the teachings and reaching the very marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
It explores the sources and currents of the religious traditions; even its various miscellaneous writings are as vast and inclusive as the ocean.

He bears the weight of the sacred mountains; his character is as lustrous as jade and as perfect as a pearl. Among the masters and craftsmen of the Dharma in this age, who else could we turn to but the Great Master?
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "There was a guide who well knew the paths of obstruction and passage, of danger and difficulty;
thus he was able to lead the multitude forward to the place of treasure. From now on, for this vast and boundless sea of suffering, there is a shore where one knows the way home.
The profound and endless heavy gates leave no hidden corner unopened. May those who are travelers on this journey each take heed.
Were it otherwise, there would be few indeed who do not become like the destitute son who fled from his father.

Preface to the *Lupoan Gao* (Drafts from the Lodging Hut), respectfully composed with hands washed by the disciple of Wenzhou, Gong Xi-yuan, during the first ten days of the eleventh lunar month in the year of Jiazi of the Kangxi era.

Originally, all sentient beings of the great earth were lost in their true nature; they took external objects to be themselves and wandered through the cycle of birth and death for countless tens of millions of kalpas.
Consequently, the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world, preaching the Dharma according to what was appropriate to shatter the barrier of delusion and cause them to return to their source.
Throughout this process—whether appearing or remaining, speaking or remaining silent—they acted according to the occasion, never missing the proper time.
It is simply a matter of correctness; how could there be any substantial dharma?
When my teacher, Venerable Master Lin, retired from his duties at Shigong, he lamented the corruption within the Dharma-gate and the daily decline of the world.
He then reflected upon the intent of Zhongfeng’s four residences, wandering by mountains and by waters as circumstances led him. By means of this—

He lived in self-reclusion to cultivate his practice. Taking the words from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, "journeying through the triple world to demonstrate a single coming and going," he named his hermitage "Lupo" (Journeying Lodger), intending to abide in non-abiding. Consequently, the dharma-milk soaked into the earth and spread everywhere;

wherever his staff and almsbowl reached, the fourfold assembly gathered like a ring, flourishing into a great monastic grove. It was as if wind passing over water suddenly forms ripples and patterns. And...

From the beginning, he had no fixed mind. Having attained the state of a traveler without a home, was there any place that was not his home? Yet, his willow-nature remained intensely pungent and his ice-like heart grew ever colder.
Upon first arriving in Puṣpa, he humbly acceded to the requests of the multitude to build a hall and erect a stupa—efforts as easy as planting grass or gathering sand.
Once the great work was completed, he abandoned it and departed. Whenever he encountered fame, reputation, profit, or sustenance, they all crossed before him in a chaotic jumble.
Chen: As it is said in the sutras, one would not dare to let even a single drop of water from a region of *gū* poison touch oneself.
For since his youth, the Master had already scrutinized and seen through the nature of worldly phenomena.

His resolve was to seek the Great Dharma for the sake of benefiting himself and others, rather than being distracted by the illusory fame and profit that flicker like sparks from stones or flashes of lightning. Thus, he has spent nearly thirty years preaching the Dharma beyond this world.
In his later years, he transcended the mundane world and stood out in solitary majesty, inspiring awe in others yet remaining unapproachable.

Throughout his life, he never accumulated superfluous possessions; whatever he acquired, he immediately distributed, bestowing gifts without stinginess. Yet, he alone was cautious regarding the Great Dharma, never giving it away lightly.
Thus, he composed the *Treatise on Not Granting Receptivity* to manifest his resolve. Indeed, his discernment of the Dharma was rigorous and clear.
I cannot bear that those who possess a superficial understanding of the teachings should confuse the true source.

I have often lamented how contemporary students treat the vast sutras and great treatises of the Tathāgata’s holy teaching as mere discarded rags; regarding the records of the ancient masters’ personal awakenings and realizations, they merely mimic their expressions from the very moment they first enter the gate.
Thus, teachers and disciples deceive one another, circulating these matters as mere worldly conventions, even to the point of—

Because he was shameless in his grandiloquence and corrupted the mental faculties [of others], while at Mount Gu, he prohibited formal lectures, informal sermons (*xiaocan*), and the composition of *nian* and *song* verses.
Later, while residing at Lubo, he personally compiled the *Jingang kan ding ji lue* (Abridged Record of the Definitive Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra).
Subsequently, he further compiled two treatises on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. These are great canons of the Dharma, disseminated throughout the world, intended so that they might be attained by all.
Those rare individuals who, from early youth, possessed the spiritual bone [of enlightenment] entered the ocean of the Flower Treasury through the gate of Prajñāpāramitā.

They settled their minds within the Dharma-realm and engaged in universal practice amidst its manifold manifestations, hoping thereby to cure their chronic ailments and stem the surging tide of decline.

Otherwise, what means would there be to grind away [delusions] and bring them to rest? Since the time of Qingliang and Zao-bo, such a person has been seen but once; the merit of their defense of the Way is inconceivable.

(Regarding this,) how could I possibly contribute a single word? However, there are drafts from my travels and stays, including dharma discourses, verses, and various miscellaneous writings such as prefaces, treatises, and biographies.
Their forms are not uniform, and their prose incorporates the strengths of many styles;

yet all of them flow forth from my own wisdom-ocean, none of which fail to elucidate the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, open the eye of wisdom for later students, and rectify the tendencies of the degenerate age.
This work rectifies long-standing corruptions and illuminates the profound darkness of the deluded path; it has been compiled into a massive volume and was not lightly shown to others.

(I, Ben,) have followed [the Master] too late, yet I am moved by the depth of his kindness. One day, while attending the Master in the Dharma Hall of Baofu Monastery, I obtained a copy and read it with ritual purity.
Thereupon, I sighed deeply and said: "Is the Master not one who, riding the wheel of great vows, has manifested in the body of a traveler to preach the Dharma?"

How extraordinary that he should shoulder the Great Dharma and strive toward it with such vigor! Consequently, my fellow student Feiqing and I, together with Master Qiye, requested that this work be carved into woodblocks for circulation, so as to broaden the gift of the Dharma.

In the future, throughout the world, there will surely be those who possess the eye of discernment and can clearly perceive our Master’s conduct—how he entered and withdrew from the world, and how his speech and silence were at all times intended to remedy defects and protect the True Dharma.
For the sake of later students, I have fashioned this golden probe to remove the cataracts [of ignorance]; let it not be regarded as a mere exercise in literary composition.
With due reverence, I burn incense and prepare this blank silk, presumptuously placing this preface at the beginning of the volumes.
On the first day of the sixth month in the twenty-second year of the Kangxi era, Dao Ben,
disciple of Fusha who studies Prajñā, respectfully bathed and prostrated himself to inscribe this in gratitude to Hong Zhong.

Postscripts to Miscellaneous Writings (Twelve pieces), including Prose (Seven pieces) and Calligraphy (Two pieces).
Biographies (4 pieces), Eulogies (46 pieces), Inscriptions (8 pieces),
Verses (102 pieces), Commentaries (11 pieces), Couplets (19 pieces). *Lupoan Gao* (Volume One).
The Record of the Sayings of Master Feijia Sengshuo, Compiled by His Disciple Taiquan,
on the Re-establishment of Baiyun Chongfan Chan Monastery.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the winter of the seventh year of the Kangxi era, the Master entered the monastery.
Three Gates: In the past you left through this gate; now you enter through this gate to come. How laughable is this man from Hanshan!
Walking barefoot to Tiantai. (A shout.)
The Foundation of the Buddha Hall: Who among those in the Palace of the Empty King is a true connoisseur? Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, none can reach it.
Even so, as for manifesting a jeweled land upon the tip of a hair and turning the wheel of Dharma within a speck of dust—how is this?
White clouds are originally mindless things, yet they are drawn forth by the pure wind.
Vaiśravaṇa Shrine: To protect the Dharma and protect people, there is only this single mallet. But tell me, from where does this mallet come?
(He lets out a shout. Gālava Shrine:
Entering fire without being burned—by whose power is this possible? The prophecy given at Vulture Peak is realized right here today.
The Patriarchs’ Hall: If there were a Dharma to transmit, one would deceive oneself; if there is no Dharma to transmit, one deceives others.
Ultimately, how is it? In the azure sky there are no shadows of clouds; from within the fire, a lotus blooms of its own accord.
Ascending the hall at the Precious Hall of the Buddha of Enlightenment, after the incense has been offered to pray for the Emperor, he said:
"In the Zen cave of Baiyun, the ancestral style is arrayed; this Way remains ever-present, as if the past thousand ages were but yesterday."
Today, this mountain monk plants another blade of grass right here. Although it is a pavilion in the void, it is constructed from solid ground.
You must know that this expanse of solid ground is inherently possessed by every person; it has never been lacking.
Since immeasurable kalpas past, one has always walked, stood, sat, and lain within it, yet has simply never stepped upon it. Since it is ever-present...
Among these, why is it that one has never trodden upon them? It is not that the Way is unknown in daily life;

if you were to know it, you would be free to traverse the heavens and weave the earth, turn the celestial pole and rotate the earth, and open up a world of cool clarity within the field of burning affliction.
Within the midst of the red dust, he establishes a water-moon Dharma-hall.

May he universally cause all beings throughout the entire earth—whether possessing nature or lacking it—to together illuminate this matter, together realize this Dharma, together cross the river of birth and death, and together reach the shore of nirvana.
Thus may he repay the unrepayable kindness and respectfully assist the effortless transformation. Right now, he stands upright as a jade pillar supporting the heavens.
The Pillar: High-rising it supports the ridgepole and the painted beams. How can one speak a single phrase of this very ground? Ultimately, one has never been apart from beneath one's feet;
you must know that with every step, one naturally soars. Again, he raised the case:
A monk asked Master Kaishan Yuezu, "If a person does not sit in the hall of biased emptiness, nor dwell in the stage of no-learning, where should they be placed? Yuezu said:
The blue sky has no shadows. The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, am not like that. Suppose someone were to ask today:
'If one does not sit in the hall of biased emptiness, nor dwell in the stage of no-learning, where should such a person be placed? Simply tell them: [The blue sky has no shadows]."
He acts as rain and dew within the sea of afflictions; he serves as clouds and thunder upon the mountain of ignorance.
Tell me, is this the same as or different from the Patriarch Yue? If anyone can discern this, I grant that they possess the true eye.
Ascending the hall upon the completion of the Precious Hall of the Buddha of Enlightenment, the Master held up his staff and said: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
'All the dust motes within the Flower Treasury World—within each and every mote, one perceives the Dharma-realm; jewel-radiance and transformation Buddhas gather like clouds.

This is the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata’s lands. Therefore, throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, there is not a single land or a single mote of dust that is not [thus]."
There is the Tathāgata Śākyamuni seated within a precious palace, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings, continuing without interruption until the end of the future.

Today, this mountain monk extracts a single world-system from the tip of a single hair and causes it to mutually illuminate and interpenetrate with those myriad world-systems. This is where the assembly of officials present before me now resides.
The virtuous men, faithful women, and all kinsmen of the Dharma have each renounced their possessions to provide mutual support and encouragement.
This, too, flows forth from the ocean of merit and wisdom adorned by our Śākyamuni Tathāgata; it is ultimately pure, non-dual, and without distinction.

How much more so, for the merit of the Tathāgata flows through ten thousand generations and remains ever-present, while his Way penetrates a hundred kalpas and becomes ever more firm. It is without...
Not a single person fails to be moistened by the grace of his Dharma; not a single thing remains untouched by the radiance of his compassion.
Those who see or hear it and rejoice shall together reach the site of enlightenment; with palms joined and heads bowed, they shall all equally attain the Buddha-way.

Just as today this entire set of merit has been completed and brought to fulfillment, where ultimately does this merit reside? Its subtle and profound roots of goodness spread throughout the nature of the earth, and its vast ocean of blessings flows forth endlessly.
The spiritual source surges forth. [The Master] planted his staff and descended from the seat.
When the Master arrived at Ruyi Hermitage, he invited Chan Master Yinhan to take charge of Baoyun Monastery. He ascended the hall and said: "This is the Lotus Source, the blessed ground of the Duke;
these are the Yunshan Mountains, the ancestral site of the patriarchs. Then he planted his staff and said: "Everything is established right here. This...
What kind of place is this? I dare say that no one in the world can fathom it. Only Chan Master Yingo received his training in this very land and attained the Dharma at Longtang.
A practitioner of the true school who dwelt among the mountains, his Way long circulated throughout the two provinces of Zhejiang;

with a sincere heart for all beings, his virtue has already permeated the eight regions of Fujian. He may truly be called a bridge and raft for the final age, a stabilizing pillar against the wild waves. Therefore...
One who is able to shoulder this burden here nakedly, without borrowing the power of another, has today personally arrived at the mountain peak.
When host and guest meet in accord, how do you express it in a single phrase? "Splitting open the Hua-yue Mountains, their beauty reaches the heavens;

releasing the Yellow River, its clarity flows to the sea. He spoke again: "Climbing the ridges of Pan-shan, one arrives at such a state; I earnestly invite Master Yin to dwell at Baiyun. And so it was.
With joy, he took up his entire body as a burden. Before the steps, a rain of flowers already fell in profusion. He planted his staff and descended from the seat.
When the Master arrived at Dongyan, the brothers Fu Gongxian and his younger brother, together with their mother Lady Lu, requested him to ascend the hall.
"The entire earth is this Land of Ultimate Bliss; where else could there be a Sahā world? The entire earth is this Amitābha; where else could there be another?"
In this state, there are no further sentient beings; since there are no sentient beings, there are likewise no Buddhas.
Since there is neither the Sahā world nor the Pure Land, it is starkly bare, vividly clear, and utterly beyond grasp.

Suddenly, if there is a person who does not seek after the sages and does not prize their own spiritual essence, they will directly take responsibility for it—casting both hands wide open at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff and throwing their entire body down.
Downward, when the breaths no longer remain, one then awakens and rises. Where there is no Buddha, one acts as a Buddha; where there is no Dharma, one preaches the Dharma;
where there are no sentient beings, one delivers sentient beings. Thus, one looks upward to repay the four debts of gratitude and universally supports those in the three realms of existence.
Only then can one truly be called a descendant under the feet of the Elder Śākyamuni. This mountain was first opened by Master Yunyang; [it has been maintained by] Shouchang and Bo...
The three elders—Shan, Zhen, and Ji—passed through here and transformed the world; to this day, the assembly of dragons and elephants remains vast, and their true spirit has not declined.
Today, I, this mountain monk, have come here to reveal a bit of my heart, yet I have already cast filth upon the pure ground.
Is there anyone who will sweep it away for me? If such a person comes forward, I shall give them thirty solid blows of the staff.
When the Master arrived at Shoushan, Layman Li Gongbai invited him to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "I do not ask about Linji; what is the Cao-Dong school?
The Master said, "Killing people without seeing blood. The monk pressed further, "The World-Honored One held up a flower;
Kāśyapa smiled. What was the meaning of this? The Master said, "The assembly laughs at you. The monk said, "Please let the Master certify me."

The Master said, "How do you understand this? The monk was speechless. The Master struck him and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are nothing other than sentient beings who have awakened.
All sentient beings are nothing other than Buddhas who are deluded. To be deluded is to pluck empty flowers from eyes afflicted by cataracts;
to awaken is to shatter the dream-world across many lifetimes. Therefore, when a sentient being awakens, they are a Buddha. Buddha...
Delusion is precisely the sentient being. Suppose a man were suddenly to come forth and ask, "When did the Buddhas fall into delusion?

One cannot help but reply to him, "When did you, O Venerable Sir, attain enlightenment? At this point, even if one could utter a turning phrase that causes both delusion and enlightenment to be forgotten and both the living and the Buddha to be exhausted, it would still be the right time to buy straw sandals and travel under the gate of Gushan. Why is this?
"To be on the road from another land is not yet to have arrived home. For now, what is the phrase for having arrived home? He then planted his staff upright and said:
"Having traveled throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have never left my door. He spoke again:
"The ancient Chan grove atop the pond of Mount Shouyan deeply relies upon the power of the donors' vows; it does not fail the personal entrustment of Vulture Peak. [He added: "A golden fortress."
The Great Dharma ferries those lost at the ford.
[The Master] descended from his seat. The Master arrived at Baoshen Hermitage. Layman Wang Shi-yu led the assembly in preparing a vegetarian feast and requested him to ascend the hall.
"My parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my Way; who is the ultimate Way? In days of old, the Ancients...
The old man has established this shop here to provide for his parents’ incense offerings and perform Buddhist rites.

He wishes to cause all people to know that there are true parents. Just as Prince Nanda split his bones to return to his father and his flesh to return to his mother, and only then manifested his original body to preach the Dharma for his parents—only then was he able to repay his parents' kindness. Thus it is with the mountain.
The Sangha has arrived here today. We rejoice that the monastic grove remains unharmed and that the lineage of robes and bowls continues to be transmitted.
We venture to borrow the majestic light of the host to deliberate with the great assembly on this very point:

having already severed one's flesh and bones to return them to one’s parents, what, after all, is the true self of each person? After a long silence, he said: "Do not ask Zeng Xi while facing Zeng Shen. From of old...
A filial son avoids pronouncing his father’s name.
Master Dongyan Wu invited the assembly to receive his instruction. The Master said: "Since the time Venerable Yunyang founded Mount Dongyan, more than one hundred years have passed.
There have been the Great Ancestor Shouchang, as well as the great virtuous masters Boshan and Zhenji."
All knowledge and the opening of the Dharma originate here; it may truly be called a rare Dharma-cave in all the world.
The monastic community residing here has cast aside both body and mind, remaining for three or four decades at a time; they may truly be called a rare assembly of monks in all the world.
From the original donor, the elder lay devotee Zhao Yuzhai, down to the present Mr. Ai Gong and his descendants, they have provided protection and support for four generations.

One might say that such a donor is rare indeed in all the world. This mountain monk, having been summoned to this mountain, has spent the entire day eating vegetarian food and drinking tea, not daring to easily open my mouth.

Tonight, because the three venerable elders Wusi, Shishi, and Shisong have requested me to expound for the assembly, I cannot help but "blow the fire with the wind" and prattle on a bit for the sake of the community. Within the three realms and six paths, only...
A human body is difficult to obtain; yet, to encounter the Buddha-dharma and leave the household life is even more difficult.

If one does not understand for what purpose one has left the household life, then though one may be busy all day long, one will fail to return to the source. Is this not to bring one’s entire life to naught?

Tell me, after all, for what purpose does one leave the household life? Have you not heard the World-Honored One say: "To leave kin and leave the household life is to realize the mind and reach the source"?
One who understands unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is called a śramaṇa. Why must one recognize the mind? It is because sentient beings do not recognize the true mind;
instead, they cling to deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), creating karma and receiving retribution. Thus, they sink into birth and death with no prospect of escape.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings, because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the nature of pure clarity."
One employs various deluded thoughts; because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic existence. Therefore, the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya must value and recognize their own true mind.
If a person recognizes the mind, there is not even an inch of earth in the great earth—how could there be further birth and death?
Why must one penetrate the source? All phenomena in the world have a fundamental root; why should it be otherwise for man alone?
Yet, what is their fundamental basis? In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are two kinds of roots:
first, the root of beginningless birth and death, which refers to sentient beings who mistake the攀緣心 (the mind that clings to objects) for their own self-nature;

second, the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa, which refers to the original luminosity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*) that can give rise to all conditions, yet is itself lost amidst those conditions. If one can discern these clearly...
[The disciple] said: "One who is able to personally turn back from delusion to return to the truth, and who realizes that all things are one with oneself, may first be called a śramaṇa.
Why, then, must one necessarily understand the dharma of non-action (asaṃskṛta-dharma)? It is because sentient beings are greedily attached to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).

They do not realize that conditioned dharmas are born of causes and conditions; they appear to exist but are not real. Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: 'All conditioned dharmas are like dreams and illusions.'"
Like bubbles and shadows, these unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are not produced by causes of birth; they are only realized through the cause of realization (*vyañjanahetu*).
Therefore, it is only upon attaining the understanding of unconditioned dharmas that one is first named a śramaṇa. Today, someone asked this mountain monk, "What is the mind?
To him, I said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. He asked, "What is the fundamental? To him, I said, "Before mountains, rivers, and the great earth existed."
At that time, take it up. If asked what the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is, tell him: "Carrying water and hauling firewood.
If you can directly grasp and carry this away right here, then cast it off and go; without passing through the City of Transformation, you will arrive straight at the Treasure Place.
Is this not most wonderful? If it is otherwise, then for now set aside body and mind, and sit quietly for a short while during the twelve periods of the day.

Only through retrospective observation can one truly attain it. An ancient master said: "If you do not practice *dhyāna* and tranquil contemplation, you will be utterly bewildered when you reach this point.
Therefore, you must collect your thoughts and sit in meditation, applying your mind to investigate the truth and refining it over years and months; there is nothing that will not correspond to this.
Furthermore, the practice of reciting scriptures during the six periods of the day originated with Master Huiyuan at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu. At that time, the monastics of his community...
One hundred and ten people in total were all reborn in the Pure Land. Dong Yan recited the scriptures during the six periods of the day—a practice not found elsewhere.

Indeed, if one can, with a sincere heart, a profound heart, and a heart of dedication and aspiration, diligently perform prostrations and recitations without fail during the six periods, this serves as the provision for the Pure Land;
such is the fundamental practice of us śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya when facing the end of life.
At the time of death, one shall not be dragged away by karmic conditions to fall into the three evil realms, but shall instead be reborn in the Pure Land, where the flower opens to behold the Buddha.

One’s consciousness will penetrate the fundamental source and understand the unconditioned Dharma, reaching a state of certainty free from doubt. Furthermore, the fortnightly recitation of the precepts is the ritual of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
the confession of past transgressions and the cultivation for the future both depend entirely upon this practice, which must never be neglected.

Regarding the three matters cited above, if the assembly does not discard these words because of the person who spoke them, and if everyone encourages one another to resolve to practice with determination, then naturally the monastic community will flourish, eminent "dragon-elephants" will emerge, and future generations will be transformed.
Thus, we shall repay the Buddha’s kindness, and the meaning of being a *śramaṇa* will be free from shame. After a long silence, he said: "The night is deep; the assembly has stood for a long time."
Let us set aside this entanglement.
Yang Biao, a filial son, requests instruction from the assembly for a Blood Basin Repentance Rite (*xiěpén zhāi*). The Master said:
"All who possess a body have parents; all who possess a mind know how to repay their parents. Yet the grace of these two parents is as high as heaven."
It is as bright as the heavens, as vast and profound as the earth, and as illuminating as the sun and moon. How could one possibly repay such kindness?

If one lies upon ice and carp leap forth, or weeps by the bamboo and shoots sprout—these are the outward manifestations of filial piety toward one's parents. To bite one’s finger and feel pain in the heart is likewise a sign of it.
When wood was carved and blood flowed, this was the divine manifestation of filial piety toward one’s parents. Indeed, the resonance between form and spirit can reach such a state.
However, this can only bring forth filial devotion toward one's parents in the present life; it is not yet the "Great Filial Piety. Why is this?
Because since beginningless time, all sentient beings have undergone countless millions of births and deaths within the six realms of existence.
[The number] is one hundred million. The Sūtra says: "The bones accumulated from one's bodies would equal Mount Vipula; the breast milk one has drunk would equal the waters of the four great oceans.

Therefore, all sentient beings of the six realms have been one's own parents. To be able to practice filial piety toward all sentient beings is precisely to practice filial piety toward the parents of many lifetimes. In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni alone is able to cultivate the Great [Vehicle].
Filial piety! Thus, the Honored One Śākyamuni is called the Greatly Filial One. Through countless kalpas he repaid his parents' kindness; by accumulating causes, he attained Perfect Enlightenment.
This was achieved through the cultivation of filial conduct, leading to Buddhahood—how much more so, then, for the blessings and retributions of humans and devas!

The filial son Yang Biao was able to embody the Buddha’s mind and cultivate the Buddha’s practice; he specifically observed the fast for three years on behalf of his deceased father, Lord Ruo Yu, and his mother, Lady Zhang.

Having completed the recitation of the entire Tripitaka, he prostrated before the Compassionate Honored One of the Three Times atop the Golden Hall and made offerings to the Sangha of the ten directions within the Ullambana vessel.
Thus he looked upward to repay his boundless debt and manifested his filial devotion, gradually attaining Buddhahood and never again regressing.
All are based upon this single thought of supreme filial piety. Now tell me: from where does this single thought ultimately arise?
He then planted his staff upright and said: "The numinous root spreads beyond the kalpas; its leaves cover the present moment. Be careful."
The Buddha’s work is of singular purity. We respectfully address the Three Holy Bodhisattvas—Ye, Ji, and Lü—at Chongfan Chan Temple on Mount Baiyun, who once attended the Vulture Peak assembly.

We pray for the consecration of the newly sculpted image of the Temple Guardian commissioned by Layman Xie. We reverently contemplate you, O Three Holy Bodhisattvas. You once [partook] at the Vulture Peak...

Having personally received the prophecy, his emanations protect the world in every place. Amidst a single sheet of white clouds over the land of the *kāṣāya*, we rely all the more upon the divine mind for secret protection and sustenance.

Just as today the precious hall is restored and the sacred image is re-carved, he takes up a brush made of tortoise hair and brings forth the light of the eternal night. How is this one phrase? He then applied the "eye" and said: "Countless eons."
The source from which it comes is never obscured. Its brilliance illuminates heaven and its discernment surveys the earth;

how could this be due to another? This ceremony for the founding patriarch, Master Yuezu, is of the lineage of Cuiwei and the school of Baiyun. Without traversing the waters or lands, he has arrived directly at the center. As for the matter within that center—act!
How so? A single stupa with its tiered roofs honors the ancestors; a thousand peaks arrayed pay homage to the descendants.

This ceremonial offering was made at the stupa of Zen Master Zu, where the holy arrow of the transmission of the lamp reached this place. The Dharma-transformation of Fusha arose amidst the clouds and mountains. Throughout antiquity and today, there has been no gap—truly extinguished.
Breath. A single stream of clear brook winds around the space between the seats.

I pay my respects at the stupa of the late Master Hang, who for many years piloted his iron boat upon the pond; even now, his lingering resonance remains vividly clear. My coming here to gaze upon it was originally without [intention].
In an instant, a single thread of sandalwood incense clouds swirls before the stupa.
Before the spirit tablets of the Abbot, my original teacher, and my parents, I offer this incense.
The teacher’s Way is my Way; the teacher’s kin are my kin. As soon as this fragrant offering is raised, the entire Dharma-realm manifests its full body.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time bestow light;
the Tathāgatas of the three periods are one Dharma-body. When the true light is applied, their majestic spirit is revealed.
Does the assembly see me yet? My spiraling blue-black hair is as green as a thousand peaks; my full-moon compassionate countenance is like spring in ten thousand lands. (He then prostrates.)

Master Yinhen has passed away, razing the hollow pit of birth and death to the ground and toppling Mount Nirvana. Having severed both ends completely, he has cast off his hands and emerged from the heavy barrier.
I reverently contemplate Venerable Master Yinpung of Baiyun Hall, who continues the lineage of the Ye River and upholds the mandate of the Dragon and Tang dynasties.
Standing upon the further shore, he extends his hand into this present age. He has grandly opened the profound gates of the five ranks and directly pointed to the shortcut of the one mind.

Skillfully expounding the essential teachings, he causes demons and outsiders to vanish in an instant. Habitually threading the golden needle, even the most seasoned monks are left at a loss. He is diligent and tireless.
He bore the Way with a simple and honest character. Having attained truth because of his genuine nature, he was upright from beginning to end.

We had hoped for the long-lasting drenching of the rain of Dharma; who would have expected that the moon of wisdom would sink in the west? The great earth is now without light, and the monastic groves have lost their luster.
Alas! How lamentable! Nevertheless, the appointed time for his departure was fixed for this very day. His full manifestation of the authentic command remains most profound and subtle.
Pushed into the void, the door is shut; even the Buddha-eye cannot peer within. *Ei!* Thus it is sealed. (Sealing the coffin) The countenance of Master Yin has never been hidden.
The mountains are azure and the waters are vast. Whether he was born or dead, let not be measured in vain.
For ten thousand autumns and ten thousand springs, there is but one incense burner. (Hanging the portrait)
It has been three years since Lord Yin departed. A white pagoda stands loftily beside the monastery.
Today I come to sweep away the withered leaves; a single bright moon reflects upon the river ahead.
(Sweeping the Pagoda) Chan Master Hengpu passes away.
The transformative rain from the clouds and mountains falls in profusion. Suddenly, the report of his return to the West is heard—unbearable to hear.

It is surely because the merit and power of all living beings are thin that the Eye of Humanity and Heaven has been extinguished; how could one’s grief surpass this? Just now, as we offer this cup of fragrant tea, would Master Monk Heng grant us his assent?
After a long silence, he said: "Beyond the night-bright curtain, the golden wind is cold; the myriad phenomena stand in solemn array."
All nodded their heads. (The upper offering:
With the fire of the emptiness of nature, one burns this body that is like foam and bubbles. Outside the body there is no fire; fire is itself the body.
Outside the fire there is no body; the body is itself the fire. Fire does not burn fire; the body does not incinerate the body. Even if one were to forget both body and fire, [it would still be so].
This was still not the place where Master Heng finally found his rest. "O Great Assembly, do you know where Master Heng has gone?

Before the gate of the "Gate of Victory" (Shenghuo), the wind blows chillingly; upon the mountain of blades and the mass of fire, he remains as he is. Thereupon, he threw himself into the torches (cremation).
[Poem]
County Magistrate Mr. Yu prepared offerings following the rhyme of Layman Pan Mingfu Shiyun; all these gentlemen were men of national caliber.
Riding side by side toward the east, they discussed governance to understand the ailments of the people, and conversed on Chan to manifest the light of wisdom.

Only by inhaling the fragrance does one perceive the flavor; only upon entering the Buddha-dharma does one become free from partiality. How warm and harmonious it is this winter day! I have utterly forgotten that my hair has turned white with frost.
Xie Jian, the Guangwen teacher, visited me; following the rhyme of his fan-poem, I offer this reply:

For a thousand years, the Buddha and the Confucian have shared the same heart. Today, our meeting is especially profound. The mountains and rivers of the "Not-Aging" (Bulao) have long been known to us.
A new set of bells and drums awaits its sound; he emerges to welcome us, his sandals not yet removed from the Bear Peak. To save all beings, he precedes the time with a rain like that of Fu Yue.
A full hand of pure wind comes forth, never ceasing; he further leaves behind jade-like spittle within the Pearl Forest.
Offering at Fuxian Temple to the True Bodies of the Two Great Masters Ciji and Cijie, in the Rhyme of He Baiyuanchan (The True Bodies:
One Looking Up, One Looking Down) The Great Way permeates both past and present;
Of these true bodies, which comes first and which last? If one only knows that the mind is the Buddha, What need is there to seek immortals elsewhere?

Looking down, I see many people shrouded in ignorance; looking up, I observe that all things are *dhyāna*. Out of compassion, you remain to deliver the world; how many years have passed since the incense and lamps were first lit?

**Preface to the Fourteen Poems on Scenic Views** In my youth, I left the secular world for this mountain, yet I did not know its true face. Wandering beyond the mundane for over thirty years, I have finally come to understand it.
This year, I have come once more to tour the site in its entirety and have gained a considerable appreciation for its essence.
Consequently, I have compiled the names of the various scenic sites—both past and present—that can be verified, arranging them as fourteen views.

To each, I have appended a seven-character quatrain, seeking to invite the fine compositions of renowned gentlemen to shed light upon these waters and rocks, lest I be ridiculed for "throwing a brick" [in place of a gem]. How could I...?
I venture to decline.

[The Peak of] Crane Dance in the Vermilion Sky (located to the northeast of the temple; its shape resembles a crane, hence its name. According to the local gazetteer, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, a diviner remarked that the mountain possessed an extraordinary aura. He ordered artisans to excavate it;
though they dug in the morning, it closed up by evening).
In what year did you take flight and descend from between the clouds? At a single glance, you stand loftily above all other mountains. With one clear cry, heaven and earth are awakened;
auspicious vapors swirl and fill the mundane world.
The Imperial Pheasant Carriage at the Ancient Ferry (located to the left of the temple; it was here that Han Mei Fu rode a phoenix to ascend to heaven).
The affairs of the House of Han have long since collapsed. He hung his official cap and returned home to study the art of longevity. Where is the Daoist who rode the phoenix now?
Only at the ferry crossing does the name of the immortal still remain renowned.
The Immortal Elder Casts His Net (this refers to the rear screen of the temple; its mountain is rounded, circular above and broad below, shaped like a cast net).
The rocks crumble and the pines wither as the game ends; he returns to cast his net to capture the golden dragon.
Lofty and solitary, it stands behind the clouds and mountains, bringing forth the radiant palace of Śakra and Brahmā.
**Two Boys Discussing the Classics** (Located to the southwest of the temple; two peaks stand facing each other, shaped like two boys.
The two boys discuss the texts until they forget their age, wishing to exhaust the meaning before even a single stroke was drawn by Fuxi.
When they reach the deepest point where words are forgotten, they laugh as they watch the bright moon fall into the river ahead.
At the morning assembly on Plum Peak (the main hall of the monastery; its five peaks are shaped like the petals of a plum blossom), the five-leaf flower blooms as an offering before the seat.
Its ice-like skin and snow-like bones shine with exquisite beauty upon those who behold it. When it is casually brought forth, who can entrust themselves to it?
Yet I recall the Venerable Dhūta’s smile.

The Li Peak towers into the clouds (located to the southeast of the temple; its extraordinary beauty and steep prominence are like a screen or curtain, making it the foremost among all mountains near the city).

To the southeast, a screen-like curtain rises as a lofty peak; brushing the Milky Way and rubbing the clouds, its momentum is naturally majestic. There is no need to toil with climbing shoes to ascend it;
every morning, its refreshing air enters the curtains and windows.

The Fierce Tiger Leaping over the Wall (This mountain lies on the opposite shore from the temple; its shape is like that of a tiger. It is blocked in front by a square mountain, so it appears as though it wishes to leap out but cannot.
Formed when the chaotic void first divided, it crouches upon the mountain’s slope as if listening to the sutras.
It wishes to leap over the heavy wall to pass beyond the distant peaks, yet fears startling the Lion (referring to Tieshi Peak) beneath the cloud-screens.
A white heron holds a loach in its beak (located on the sunny side of the fierce tiger; this refers to the mountain directly ahead, whose shape resembles it).
From where has it flown to perch by the water’s edge? The loach, held in its mouth, quivers alive in the shimmering waves. With spring wind and spring rain, [the heron] is as green as dark pigment;
having lost its whiteness, its entire body appears like silver.

A pair of elephants lie prostrate before [the temple] (situated across the river from the front of the monastery; two rounded hills lie low like elephants, complete with tusks and trunks, known as the "Great" and "Small" Elephants).

Their docile nature has been so from the beginning that they require no tethers. Extending their long trunks, they coil them by the lakeside. Hooked staffs and the labor of barbarian herdsmen are utterly useless;
they are permitted only to sleep facing the mountain flowers in solitude.
A solitary swallow descends from its nest (located to the right of Yong’an Temple; this is the Sand of Descending White Clouds).
A purple swallow flies alone, descending and circling about. It builds its nest here—how could it have been pre-arranged? To nourish its young, it need not exert the strength of carrying insects;
there are naturally celestial flowers to dot upon the green moss.
The clear stream winds like a sash (flowing from Songjeong, its form like a belt as it meanders across before the temple). A single length of silk is dragged across, circling the temple;
the green mountains turn back the water, which swirls and eddies. When the wind ceases and the waves grow still, the surface is as level as the palm of a hand;
halls and pavilions, peaks and ridges, all open out like a single mirror.

The Azure Isle is spread like a felt rug (this isle stretches long before the temple, measuring about two li in length and breadth; the mention of "spreading a felt rug" follows the terminology of geomancers).
The Azure Isle is level and vast as if covered by a felt rug. Old gardeners bustle about, competing to water their plots. Leaning on my staff at the gate, I gaze out idly;
startled sand-gulls fly up from the edge of the emerald stream.
The fish swim up and down; (the two mountains stand on opposite banks by the stream, one above and one below, their shapes resembling fish, hence the name).

Up and down the solitary mountains look like a pair of fish, swimming and gliding as if toward the abode of white clouds. Even if the Master of Angling did not cast his line lightly, the winds and clouds would remain just as they are for ten thousand ages.
The precious canopy flutters aloft (the mountain lies across the river in front of the temple; its rounded summit and soaring ridges are shaped like a precious canopy, hence its name).

A lofty precious canopy hangs down from heaven, its trailing band flying afar to the river’s edge. Intending to offer it to the Buddha within the Brahma palace, the single stream cuts it off, leaving it standing majestic and solitary.
Drafts from the Lupo-an (Traveler’s Hut).
Recorded by the disciples (Deng et al. together with the various records of Kaiyuan Guangfu, as dictated by the Elder of Feijia.
Ascending the hall upon the ridgepole of the Great Hero Treasure Hall of Kaiyuan Temple, a monk asked: "I do not ask about the magnificent splendor of this Buddhist temple;
what is the phrase for receiving beings and benefiting life? The Master said: "Writing Sanskrit characters in the air. The monk pressed further:
"If that is so, then the layered jeweled pavilions appear amidst the clouds, and the myriad phenomena all nod their heads. The Master said: "The ancient hall is precisely..."
The temple was restored. The monks prostrated, and the Master said: "Planting a marker to establish a monastery fills the ten directions;
cleaving open a speck of dust to reveal the sutras uncovers a treasure trove. To act as a Buddha where there is no Buddha is to paint the void with five colors;

to preach the Dharma where there is no Dharma is for the myriad apertures to sound the celestial pipes. The mud ox at the bottom of the sea rides the waves; the wooden horse in the clouds neighs in the wind."

At night, brightness shines beyond the curtains, shaking the family’s reputation; atop the shadowless tree, spring colors are spread. At this very moment, the ancient halls of Kaiyuan are magnificent and renewed;
the old traces of forest and spring, and its illustrious legacy, remain undiminished. With valor, he shattered the four māras and attained Buddhahood, named the Great Hero (Mahāvīra).
He broadly opened the profound gate of the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha), where all who come enter directly, like a thousand forests intermingling.
Illumination is like two mirrors containing light; they interpenetrate in infinite layers, neither destroyed nor confused.
Adorning the Buddha-lands for billions of kalpas, they support the imperial destiny for eternal years. They entice and lead all children, pushing them out through the gate of the burning house;
they rescue the drowning masses, causing them to leap joyfully onto the shore of Bodhi. But tell me, ultimately from what place is this established? Truly...
Jiuyun said: "Taking up a single speck of snow from the red furnace, it shall forever serve as ice in the human world during the sixth month.
He then cited the words of Chan Master Kaiyuan Ying upon ascending the hall: "There is a mirror hung everywhere; neither ordinary nor holy beings come before it. Who is above? Who is below?
He took up his staff and said, "This is the staff. Which one is the mirror? After a long silence, he said: "Ten thousand..."
The ancient emerald pool, the empty realm of the moon—only after thrice stirring and scooping can one truly know it. The Master said: "Throughout kalpas it has been nameless;
it is manifested as the 'ancient mirror. It is simply that you people must know it exists, so as not to be deluded by its shadows.
Master Ying had a great way of benefiting others. Today I, too, have a verse; I cannot help but present it to the assembly. There is one..."
The Face-Mirror. Hung everywhere, it manifests universally for both the ordinary and the sagely. It is neither internal nor external. Holding up the whisk, he says:
"This is the mirror; what do you call this whisk? Do you understand clearly? Clearly facing each other, there is nothing else that is real;
do not further lose your head by still recognizing the reflection. He descends from his seat.
The spire of the Prabhūtaratna Buddha Stupa was joined, and the Master ascended the seat. He said: "The stupa has been reconstructed;

Prabhūtaratna reveals his entire body. The śarīra relics are enshrined; Śākyamuni has already shared half his seat. This altar, solemn and pure, is itself the threefold transformation of the Pure Land."

The gathering of the ordained and the laity like clouds—how is this different from the emanations of the ten directions? The wind whistling through ten thousand apertures is the Tathāgata personally preaching the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The birds chirping in a thousand forests are the precious stūpa emitting sounds to praise what is good. Past and present are one boundary; the ordinary and the sage are one source.
Essence and function are one suchness; cause and effect are one dharma. The single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly undispersed. Behold further this majestic treasure!
Atop the summit of the seven-tiered [pagoda], a brilliant golden light blazes forth, illuminating all beneath heaven, so that those with eyes may see,
those with ears may hear, those with hearts may know, and those with mouths may speak; even children playing and reciting the Buddha’s name with distracted minds,
as well as the officials, commoners, gentry, men, women, old, and young of the entire district, are provided with food and sustenance.

Whether contributing wealth, carrying bricks, or transporting earth—whosoever raises a single thought toward this stupa, donates a single coin, or exerts a single effort, shall all be included within the Tathāgata’s prophecy;
it is not merely for the sake of superior merit among humans and devas. Do you all believe this yourselves?
After a long silence, he said: "I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. He then descended from his seat.
At the time of raising the ridgepole for the construction of the hall at Chiryeongsa Temple, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Upon the tip of a single hair, the Jewel King’s realm appears;

adorned with a hundred blessings, joy pervades all under heaven. The beams, pillars, rafters, and purlins—lords and attendants in infinite layers—jointly establish this through the merit of non-action.
At such a moment as this, tell me, what is the Lord among lords? He then said: "As soon as the precious ridgepole..."
The Buddha-sun is raised high; may it shine forever bright.
On the occasion of the seventy-year birthday of the lay devotee Wu Rugu, the Master was requested to ascend the seat. The Master said:
"Before emerging from the womb, ten thousand kalpas are but a single kṣaṇa; after emerging from the womb, a single kṣaṇa is ten thousand kalpas. Does the assembly know this?"
In a single *kṣaṇa*: Śākyamuni descended from Tuṣita Heaven in that very instant;

he was born into the royal palace, pointed to heaven and earth to proclaim his supremacy, attained Buddhahood by awakening himself and awakening others, delivered sentient beings across the sands of worlds, and turned the Wheel of Dharma throughout the great trichiliocosm.
The ancestral masters of successive generations, within that same *kṣaṇa*, did not rely on written words but pointed directly at the human mind.

When the mind perceives its own nature, one attains Buddhahood. Just as you, Layman Gong, have studied Confucianism and Buddhism, composed writings, and established your teachings within a single kṣaṇa;

and as you have reached your seventies while roaming freely through the subtle mysteries of the Way—extending even to the three teachings, the nine schools, the four classes of people, the myriad commoners, and down to all wriggling and flying creatures—you have all, within that very kṣaṇa, emitted light and shaken the earth, each attaining [enlightenment].
One enjoys it as appropriate, without lack or remainder. It must be understood that this single kṣaṇa is like the heavens universally covering all and the earth universally supporting all.
One exhausts the primordial heaven (xiantian) and does not see its beginning; one investigates the subsequent heaven (houtian) and does not see its trace.
What more need be said of the cyclical recurrence of the Xuanyuan jiazi era? Even if one were to count through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one would still remain ignorant of it.
"The limit lies within him. Now tell me, at this very moment, who exactly is it that establishes this?
Do you know? After a long silence, he said: "The river is viewed unchanged from one's first year; Calculations of worldly time are like flowers in the sky.
If you ask about the lifespan of a layman such as Gong, Just look at this vision—where could its boundaries end?"
At Baoshan Monastery, the stupa was opened to invite the śarīra.
By the Tathāgata’s power of vows, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; the radiance of the śarīra flows forth everywhere without obstruction.

Once again the precious stupa was opened to manifest its presence to devas and humans; Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna both revealed their true bodies. In the city south of Puṣkaravatī, the stūpa stands majestic and lofty.
May this be divided into three parts and seven portions to pacify posterity for a thousand ages. May light be emitted and auspicious omens manifest to awaken those with karmic affinity.
May it forever serve as a vast field of merit for all sentient beings. Thus is the stupa sealed.
Deep within the Jewel Mountain lies the Śāriputra Treasury, indestructible throughout kalpas and radiating its light through all eternity.
Disciple Zhao Benzhen has hung this Dharma discourse upon a banner of ancient brocade;
its colors are brilliantly radiant. As the wind moves, the banner moves; its merit transcends that of humans and devas. All phenomena are fundamentally empty.
The One True Reality is primordially present, pure, eternally blissful, and indestructible throughout kalpas. This fundamental wondrous wisdom penetrates the source of nature;

it is utterly devoid of a single thing and is completely liberated from the entanglements of the defilements. Among the six perfections and myriad practices, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is foremost; it is the merit of formlessness.

Like the sun illuminating the sky, may he, in birth after birth and life after life, never obscure the true cause, fully cultivate merit and wisdom, and broadly deliver those lost in the perilous straits.
*The Drafts from the Floating Hermitage* (Volume Two),
spoken by the Elder Without Home, recorded by the disciple Xinliang.

From the *Recorded Sayings of Baofu*, at the request of the lay practitioner Wu Shangqing of Zhapu, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are merely ordinary people without a mind;
the sentient beings of the great earth are merely Buddhas with many affairs. You must know that sentient beings..."
Originally there is no affair; that is not a sentient being. The Buddhas originally have no mind, nor are they Buddhas.
Today, this old monk brings forth a string of scales upon the tip of his whisk: one is eight *liang*, the other is half a *jin*. There is neither deficiency nor surplus;
neither heavy nor light. Water does not wash water; gold does not trade with gold. If there is a man who can directly confront this point—
If you can attain true faith, see through to the bottom, and take up this burden, you will know that from time immemorial all matters have been perfectly luminous in their very essence;
all Buddhas and all sentient beings of the great earth have already attained Buddhahood simultaneously prior to the time of King of Dignified Sound (Vaiśvānara).
Since this cannot be calculated by the kalpa-stone, how could it possibly be measured by the mind-consciousness?
At such a time, when neither sentient beings nor Buddhas have yet taken form—what of the ten days prior? After a long silence, he said:
"Layman Wu Shangqing, you father and sons, brothers and sisters, have come up the mountain to request the Dharma; it is no small matter to travel so far from home. He then descended from his seat.

Addressing the assembly, he cited Master Zhongfeng’s instruction to his Zen students: "Do you wish to study the Buddha? Do you wish to study the Patriarchs? Do you wish to study the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)?

The entire Tripitaka, the records of various lamps, the bequeathed words, and the past deeds of the patriarchs are all the foundational basis for studying the Buddha, studying the Patriarchs, and studying the spiritual friends.
It is not inappropriate to take this as a foundation and put it into authentic practice once."

Simply practice without wavering and maintain it without alteration. After a long time, you will become thoroughly proficient; this is what is meant by the Buddhas, Patriarchs, and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) being realized without needing to be learned.
Some say that a man of spirit naturally possesses the ambition to soar through the clouds and does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked.
To attain the status of a Buddha or Patriarch and reach the level of a spiritual friend, one must first take the entire Great Canon...
He casts the recorded sayings, last instructions, and past deeds of all the patriarchs beyond the worlds of the ten directions.
Holding aloft a single blade of sharp, hair-cutting sword, he kills the Buddhas upon encountering them and kills the Patriarchs upon encountering them.
He ensures that not a single thing can stand before him, nor can a single dharma follow behind him. After a long while, even the handle in his hand is cast away all at once.
Set it aside. Casting yourself beyond all things, you walk alone upon the Great Path; naturally, at every turn you follow the same track, and in every place you encounter the source.

Nevertheless, you should know that these two explanations are both merely the words of old nests. If you give rise to even a single thought toward them as a point of reliance, you have fallen into the nest.
If you wish to become a Buddha, a Patriarch, or a true spiritual friend, you do not yet know this.
"That is acceptable. Furthermore, setting aside these two paths, ultimately by what standard does one reach the ground of the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)?
Upon reaching this point, even I, Huanzhu, am rendered speechless. There are many venerable elders throughout the various quarters;
you should not hesitate to take each of these topics and go to question them. The Master said, "The three points mentioned above were spoken by the Elder Zhongfeng."
This great highway has already been traversed throughout one’s entire life; coming and going with complete mastery, one returns home to sit in peace—what more need be said?
Therefore, I have had you take up this saying to inquire of all quarters:
upon which of these three great highways do you actually tread? Everyone, try to examine this for yourselves. Nevertheless, even so...
One must not skip levels; one must pass through each stage one by one before attaining realization.
If it were otherwise, one would merely be a person who plunders empty air—what common ground for conversation could there be?
On the Great Snow of the New Year’s Eve of the Gengshen year, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"This old monk, amidst the mountains of Baofu, has swept away the ashes of the kalpa and cleared away the thorns and brambles to erect several thatched huts.

A few brothers who aspire to the Way have followed me, and for many years we have chattered incessantly about the Patriarchal School and the Teachings, leaving a trail of entanglements covering the ground. Look at this—it is like chewing up food to feed an infant."
Child, as we have lingered until this day, we have not realized that the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month has arrived. It is freezing cold;
the rain falls and the snow comes. We sit together in a circle, eating coarse grain and biting into the roots of vegetables, yet we are full of joy.
We exchange a few simple words to mark the end of the year. Such is the flavor of poverty—a state that pervades the entire Great Qing Empire.
It is feared that such instances will not be seen often. I recall that in the past, when Chan Master Guanshan Ning resided on his mountain, he composed a verse which said:
"The earthen stove has no fire, and the traveler’s bag is empty; The snow falls like willow blossoms as the year draws to its end. I gather stray hemp to sew together my tattered robe."
One does not realize that one’s own body is within such profound stillness. One can well imagine the pure conditions of the ancient worthies who dwelt in the mountains.

This old monk, imitating them, has also composed a verse; I cannot help but present it to the assembly: Without firewood and without charcoal, we pass through the three winters; Snow and rain fall thickly and without end.
The Dharma-body is frozen stiff, bare and skeletal, Yet fortunately at the third watch, the sun rises red. And so it is.
"How far apart are the Way and the ancients? Try to discern this for yourselves. After a long silence, he said, "Venerable assembly, it is well to return to the hall and rest. Take care."

On the first day of the new year in the Xin-you year, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The New Year is originally the person of the Old Year; though one changes garments, the body remains unchanged.
