rather, it is by these words that you are said to live for eighty, ninety, a hundred years, a thousand years, or even for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Until the end of the future, it shall not go beyond this. For my words are not false, and Gongshou’s [life] is not in vain;
the conditions for Prajñā have coincided by chance, and thus I have specially brought this forth to inform all who possess discernment.
The assembly all responded with unanimous acclaim, and I immediately arranged these words in sequence as a congratulatory message for Master Gongda. This serves as the preface.
Preface for the Sixtieth Birthday Celebration of Senior Commandant Shanseng Zheng Gong.
On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the summer of the Guihai year, we reverently celebrated the auspicious occasion of Senior Master Shanseng’s sixtieth birthday.
Among the spiritual friends from all mountains and the monastic community of various Chan temples, there was not one who did not rejoice with boundless exultation.
Each, before the Triple Gem’s throne in their respective dwellings, recited the scriptures, chanted hymns, burned incense, and scattered flowers to offer prayers for the Nine Auspicious Events.
Subsequently, you further commissioned me with this preface. Although I have not yet had the honor of meeting you in person, our spiritual paths have long been in accord;
thus, my thoughts toward you have remained constant. For many years, correspondence has passed between us without ceasing. It is only fitting that I compose this for you.
It would be improper not to employ refined language here; therefore, I shall venture to offer this brief discourse:

When the Supreme Person is born into the world of humanity, it is surely not for naught. They receive the orthodox vital energy of Heaven and Earth and are endowed with the quintessence of the five elements.
Riding upon a fortunate destiny, he was born among them as the glory of the nation and the auspicious omen of the people.
Whatever benefits the state and the world, it is solely upon such a person as this that they rely.

For this reason, everyone regards him no less than a celestial star or a phoenix, gazing up at him with unceasing love and admiration. In you, sir, I have seen such a man. You, sir, in your early years...
He passed the highest civil service examination. Before long, he was tested in the administration of Jingzhou, where for over a decade his virtuous governance was as swift and pervasive as a tempest.
When the present Emperor heard of his reputation, he summoned him to the capital. As a Minister of Personnel, he ensured the public integrity of the official ranks;

as a Grand Chancellor, he cleared away both the treacherous and the corrupt. His moral character and literary brilliance were admired by both the court and the common people. In the midst of these achievements—

Externally humble and compliant, his loyalty and affection flow forth spontaneously. He points toward the day he shall ascend the imperial steps and grasp the pivot of governance, thereby fulfilling the hopes of the myriad beings of the world for a rain of grace.
All without exception wipe their eyes in anticipation of this completion. Furthermore, you, sir, possess profound knowledge of the Great Way of our Awakened Sage appearing in the world;
you dwell your mind in vastness, wisdom, merit, virtue, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
All these qualities converge within his single person. Thus, he exerted every effort to provide external protection for the various Dharma gates;

with the monastics beyond the mundane world, he shared the same Way and was of one spirit, exchanging the joy of the Dharma. Compared to Páng and Péi of the Táng dynasty, or Yáng and Lǐ of the Sòng dynasty, how could he be considered inferior?
This is because the Master’s mind is the very mind of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the mind of Heaven, Earth, the sun, and the moon. It is rooted in...
The leaves are deep and luxuriant; the source is distant and the stream is long. His noble form illuminates the world; his station is high and his rank is exalted.

His fame is lofty and his longevity is great—such is the magnitude of his radiance. How much more so when the orchids and cassias before his courtyard stand in dense rows and the ocean of his blessings surges boundlessly;
its excellence is yet far from exhausted. What, then, is not the manifestation and propagation of the measure of his lifespan and his radiant light? This is what we mean.
May the Master’s longevity be as enduring and luminous as that of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Heaven and Earth, and the Sun and Moon;
it is fitting that it should descend upon us as something imperishable. Thus, I have carefully arranged these humble words as a prayer for the Master’s great and inexhaustible years.
Preface to the Fiftieth Birthday Celebration of Layman Li Weiwu.

When I came to Fusha to construct the two halls of Baiyun and Kaiyuan, I was honored by the elder, Master Li Weiwu, who practiced the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) until his meritorious deeds were accomplished.
Furthermore, he frequently rode his horse to visit me, discussing the Way and conversing on the mind with tireless diligence.
His tireless diligence reveals that he was endowed with the causal conditions for *prajñā* from an early age; thus, our meeting this once was no mere coincidence.

On the nineteenth day of the tenth month of the winter of the Xinhai year, coinciding with the moment when the *Dayan* (Great Expansion) reaches the number nine, I reflected that there was nothing else I could offer for the Master’s longevity.
I have therefore composed these crude words and present them to express my sincere devotion in offering this tribute. I have heard this from the ancients...
De said: "In fortune, one observes a person's capacity; in longevity, one observes a person's application of mind.

This means that the presence or absence of fortune is seen in the magnitude of one's capacity, while the abundance or deficiency of longevity is seen in the depth or shallowness of one's mental application.

Your Excellency’s capacity encompasses both enmity and gratitude, harmonizing those above and below; it is vast and expansive like ten thousand acres of ponds, which remain undisturbed even when churned."

One pours into it without it overflowing; it receives the hundred streams and gathers the myriad waters. How could its capacity ever be measured by the size of a mountain brook, a gully, a basin, or a bowl?
Since the Master’s capacity is such, how can the depth and breadth of his merit and virtue be fathomed?
In his application of mind, though his body dwells amidst the toil of the mundane world, his heart roams beyond all phenomena. He sought the Way from various...
His bridges and ferry crossings throughout the mountains were widely established, truly embodying the spirit of Vimalakīrti and Lao Pang.
His creation of Buddha-statues, his provision of meals for the Sangha, and his printing of scriptures for the benefit of the masses were all the public, effortless, and wondrous deeds of a noble man.

Since his dedication of heart has been so persistent in these matters, how could his lifespan be measured? Now, as you stand at the age of fifty—the year one comes to know their fate—you are like the blazing sun.

Throughout the four quarters, the heavens were universally illuminated. I and you, sir, traveled together within the Tathāgata’s Great Treasury of Radiance, acting as host and guest to one another and engaging in mutual exhortation and inspiration.
Whether in a single word or silence, a single movement or stillness, there was nothing that was not overshadowed by the light of your longevity.
How could the worldly calculations of a tortoise's age or a crane's count, or discourses on the rising sun and the waxing moon, ever be compared to this?

And yet, as for the Dharma-body being formless and its lifespan being immeasurable—its roots spreading before heaven and earth, its radiance surpassing the sun and moon—you, sir, have already attained silent realization beyond words. How could it be fully exhausted by mere brush and tongue?
For now, I shall briefly describe your noble magnanimity and vastness, and how you employ your mind to bring blessings to the good, as a great blessing for you.
Regarding the divination for this year:
I, [Name], have composed this preface for the eightieth birthday of Master Wugu Chunyi of Gushan.
I consider that while the mark of longevity is transcended by Prajñā, it is nevertheless the foremost blessing among the "Nine Categories" of the *Hongfan*. As for this blessing—
Thus, one’s innate nature is blessed by Heaven; yet that which is "dispatched" is the dispatching of attachment to signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, it is only those who do not cling to signs who can merge mysteriously with true nature and naturally attain infinite blessings and longevity.

When Master Wugong, being over forty years of age, ascended Mount Gu to pay his respects at the seat of his former teacher, the Venerable Yong, he immediately made a vow to remain there for the rest of his life.
He served in various offices—whether as a *huashì*, a *zhikè*, a *weina*, or a *jiānsì*—in all of which he exhausted his mind and strength without ever showing the slightest laxity.
After our late master passed away, I was honored to succeed him on the seat. When I retired from my duties, Master Jìng succeeded me.
In holding office and managing affairs, Master Jìng acted exactly as the late master had when he was still hale and hearty; he never allowed his conduct to differ according to the change in time.
At that time, whether his will was tested by ease or difficulty, there were none—whether monastics or laypeople—who did not hold him in high esteem.

Their praise resounded like a drum, extolling the Elder Abbot of Gushan. Now, on the twentieth day of the first month of autumn in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, coinciding with the Master’s eightieth birthday, his disciples Zixing and Qinxing have brought white silk and incense to prostrate themselves before me, requesting a word from me.
To offer a blessing for Your Excellency’s great longevity, I reflect that for over forty years you have applied yourself with diligence to meditation and recitation, practicing without ceasing;
your words and deeds have been sincere, and your understanding of cause and effect has been true. By these very qualities alone, Your Excellency’s merit and lifespan are already immeasurable.
What need is there to wait for my own words to be redundant? I simply intend to commemorate Your Excellency’s life by establishing [this monument] through the power of Prajñā.

Wondrous conduct! Unattached to all marks, you are in profound harmony with the emptiness of nature. That you may enjoy your own merit and longevity for eternity—this is my prayer for your great longevity.
Preface for the Seventieth Birthday of Master Yuan of the Gushan Lineage.

In the spring of the Wuxu year of the Shunzhi era, I assumed my duties at this mountain. Having resided here for fourteen years, I have, together with others, established the Triple Gem and propagated the Great Dharma.
Those who have assisted me by turning left and right in mutual support are none other than two venerable elders; one is said to be...
As for Master Chunei Wo (Pure Unity Awakening): one style of name is Yimae Won (Single Lineage Source). Last autumn, on the twentieth day of the seventh month, Master Wo reached his eightieth year;

I have already composed a text to celebrate his longevity. Now, this autumn, on the third day of the ninth month, it is the auspicious occasion of Master Won’s seventieth birthday, the day he hangs the bow.
On this day, disciples from Bokcheong, including He Chengjiao, Tao, and others, have prepared this memorial service.
Zuo Chen, Xingjin, Xue Xingdong, and others all presented a written request for me to compose a text to celebrate the Master’s longevity.

I said: "The Master’s sublime virtue and flourishing conduct are precisely what I ought to celebrate. Why wait for such a request? Nevertheless, since the gentlemen have made this earnest entreaty, how could I afford to delay?
Thereupon, I ventured to offer this brief discourse: "The true body is without form; the true lifespan is immeasurable."
The momentary is fundamentally unborn; where arising and ceasing occur, there is profound stillness. Thus, though the kalpa-fire burns the void, the entire body remains refreshingly cool;
though the great flood submerges the heavens, the whole person remains unmoistened. Worldly phenomena are eternally abiding; the Dharma dwells in its own station.
Because one possesses such a true body, there is such a true life. It is common to all living beings, yet they do not realize it in their daily lives.
With a single thought of turning the light back upon itself, it is once attained and forever attained. Master Yuan was one who realized this; therefore, I venture to present this to him.
Master Gong was a man from San-shan. He descended from the He clan, a lineage that has produced many eminent scholars; yet the Master took no pleasure in the worldly dust.

In his youth, he entered the monastic order and received the tonsure under Master Zhiguang. He received the full precepts from the Elder Wuyi of Boshan. At the age of over thirty, he ascended Mount Gu and came into the presence of my late teacher.
Upon seeing him once, the teacher granted him permission to enter the hall for formal study. He shared a single meditation seat with me.
Our neighbor [Master] polished his skills day and night. At that time, the monastic forests were just beginning to flourish, and a hundred tasks were gathered like a swarm of insects.
The community appointed him to manage labor and affairs; having no other choice, he took up the post. Since our late master had passed away, I have humbly assumed his place.

Regarding all matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as the unfinished undertakings of this mountain gate, I have diligently applied myself to their restoration and repair. There was nothing—*mo*—that I did not attend to.
He did not act with you in a spirit of shared purpose and cooperation. You did not allow your mind to be divided by ease or difficulty, nor did you let weariness and toil shift your resolve.
There are countless instances of which I am unaware where you braved frost and snow and encountered wind and waves, achieving safety only after having been in peril.
"Bending the body to the utmost and exhausting one's strength and heart, hoping for success—this was the Master’s resolve.

In the autumn of the Xinhai year, I retired from my duties and departed the mountain, appointing Master Jing to succeed me on the seat. The Master remained no different from when I was in the mountains;

he exerted his full effort in assisting and managing affairs, never wavering in his virtue. Although ten other individuals were established to take turns attending to the monastery's business, the Master [continued to] preside over them.
This was his retirement; yet, regarding the great principles and essential pillars of the mountain gate, he never failed to guide and sustain them from both left and right.
Furthermore, with his remaining strength, he constructed the Wanshou Stone Bridge at Shangdui and paved a stone road from outside the Suimuemun Gate straight to Baegun Hermitage.
He also carved and printed Buddhist scriptures, including the Brahmajāla Sūtra, the Forty-two Sections Sūtra, and the Śāriputra-prakaraṇa-śikṣāpada-sūtra.
He had the scriptures bound in fine cloth and decorated with ornaments to distribute throughout the monasteries.

Previously, he had already cast images of the Three Holy Ones of the West in iron behind the main hall, and later he had a copper mold for an image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara at the Xi Jiang Hermitage;

both were coated in gold and were so dignified and exquisite that they stood preeminent within Min Province. The Master performed prostrations and repentance morning and evening with such profound sincerity.
In the winter of the Ding-si year, the Master visited the stupas at Shouchang, Boshan, Yunqi, and Pingtao to perform memorial rites.
He then traveled to Jinling to pay homage at the Śarīra Stupa of Baoguan Temple, where he lit lamps as an offering to express his sincerity and reverence.

In the spring of the following year, he returned to the mountains and retired from external affairs, secluding himself in the Xi Jiang Aranya (Absorbing the River Hermitage) for over two years to refine himself in meditation. Previously, I...

Having completed the compilation of the commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Master made a vow to oversee the production and distribution of the woodblocks, intending to plant the seeds of the Vajra for all sentient beings throughout the great earth.
I then transcribed the texts myself and commissioned a craftsman to carve the blocks; however, as the Master was then in seclusion, I did not dare inform him.
After some time, the Master became aware of this and, breaking through his retreat, boarded a boat with Master Chunyi to travel upstream against the current.
Upon seeing me at Baofu Mountain during the Zhenghe era, he was filled with a mixture of grief and joy.
He remarked, "Throughout our lives, we have established meritorious deeds together like shadow following form; there has not been the slightest discrepancy between us.
How could I suddenly consume my own previous words and sever my connection to the Great Dharma? Thereupon, he took the remaining scrolls back to the assembly hall and raised a subscription for them.
Fellow practitioners, these engraved woodblocks are now being circulated. This is because the Master’s resolve to propagate the Dharma has remained steadfast from beginning to end.

Previously, the Great Hall within the mountain had undergone major repairs during the Gengzi year of the Shunzhi era; yet, barely twenty years later, it was once again leaking due to the wind and rain that batter the mountain’s coastal location.
Undeterred by his advanced age or physical exhaustion, the Master nevertheless applied himself to the task of supporting the bridge across the stream of the teachings. Thus, he...
He resolutely took upon himself the responsibility of restoration; from this, one knows that the Master’s vow regarding the mountain gate was firm and deep, ultimately never regressing.

Now, as his great birthday approaches, I, being aged and infirm, am recuperating my health in a deep valley and cannot go in person to the mountain peak to offer a single incense stick for his long life. Furthermore, due to poverty, I have not a single thing to offer.

One may pay homage [to this]. I shall set forth Master Gong’s lifelong service as a minister and advisor, his bearing of responsibility for the monastic community, and his various bodhisattva practices and great vows, so as to illuminate them for future generations.
This will cause those of later times who possess great aspirations to see the worthy and desire to emulate him, springing forward with inspired resolve.
In this way, the mountain gate shall not fall into desolation, and the Way of the Dharma shall likewise be sustained thereby.
This is indeed to be relied upon. Thus, the longevity of the Master is the longevity of the great assembly of the mountain; it is also the longevity of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity.
Since his true body shares its formlessness with theirs, and his true longevity shares its immeasurability with theirs, how could he be considered unworthy?
This serves as the preface.
Preface for the Seventieth Birthday of Chan Master Zhanna of Longkong:
I consider that Longkong in Jianxi stands preeminent among all mountains not merely because of its striking topographical excellence,
nor its vast and grand foundations, nor the profound, expansive, and fertile expanse of its forests, mountains, fields, and gardens, but because of its flourishing lineage of descendants...
This flourishing and expansive prosperity is truly due to the presence of those possessing great fortune, great virtue, and great longevity, who provide guidance and maintain order within it.

Consequently, it enables the scenic landscapes to become ever more marvelous and beautiful, the architectural foundations ever more magnificent, the mountains, forests, fields, and gardens ever more extensive, and the virtuous descendants ever more numerous. As an ancient saying goes: "The mountain does not need to be high."
The existence of sages bestows a name upon a place; how could it not be that the land gains great weight because of its people?
This is precisely the case with the contemporary mountain-dwelling Chan master Zhàn-ān. From the age of his topknot, he entered the quarters of the Great Ancestor Dúfēng as a *chū'wū* novice.
He attended to sweeping, responding to commands, and performing manual labor without fail from dawn until dusk. The Ancestor held him in deep esteem.
He was granted the meaning of the scriptures. Furthermore, he was commanded to attend upon the late Master Yong at Mount He.
When the late Master appeared in the world at Mount Gu, the Master visited him without interruption for over thirty years, deeply experiencing the joy of the Dharma.

He also established a "square friendship" (a formal bond between scholars) with Mr. Xie Chunyi of Guilin; their hearts and aspirations were identical. For forty or fifty years, during wind and dawn...
On moonlit evenings, as we sat close together in conversation, we never failed to pledge one another to the great principles of the Buddha-dharma.
His sons and nephews—such as Jianzi, Qinzi, Yuzhi, and Qian—were all influenced by their uncle’s conduct.
Although the Xie family had transmitted its lineage through Confucian arts, they were in truth cultivating the mind and practice of the Buddha. Thus, they sought [enlightenment] alongside the Master.
On the shores of this secluded and desolate wilderness, several decades have passed as if they were but a single day.
I recall that even in his youth, you were already able to cast a bronze image of the Holy Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and enshrine it in your private chamber.

Day and night, you prostrated yourself and knelt in recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the "Chapter on the Practice of Entering the Inconceivable Realm of Liberation of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra."
In the "Chapter on Vows," one may know that his spirit abides within the Dharma-realm and that his great vows flourish extensively.
Thus, it is said in the sutra: "This person has well obtained a supreme lifespan; this person has come well to birth among humans;
before long, this person shall achieve accomplishment, just like the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Judging by today’s circumstances, the Duke’s merit and longevity are vast and great.

Cause and effect correspond; indeed, there is no error here. However, since the time of Zen Master Tienchen Daojue, it was due to the merit of a single stroke from the First Patriarch Dufeng Gong that the mountain was revitalized, its foundations established, and its legacy secured. He passed away at over eighty years of age.
He was succeeded by Monk Benkong Cheng, who expanded his mind to encompass all the hundred affairs of the monastery. Following him...

Master Chenggong served as the liaison officer for Master Xijigong. At over fifty years of age, he passed away. This was during a period following a dynastic transition, when various crises arose like swarming bees.
It was only through the concerted efforts and mutual cooperation of Master Chenggong and Master Ruixiang that internal and external affairs were harmonized and managed;

they not only resolved conflicts and warded off calamities, but further magnified the legacy of their predecessors. As the saying goes: "To establish an enterprise is difficult; to preserve what has been achieved is no less so."
Master Xiang and Master Gong were of similar age; having both reached their seventies, they were truly what the Dharma-gate calls "brothers in dharma.

In this age of the final five hundred years, when strife and contention are rampant, these two brothers maintain such harmony that they are like water and milk mingling, together shouldering the affairs of the Dharma-gate—how rare is such a sight!
Master Gong was skilled in poetry; whenever he encountered an object that stirred his sentiments, he would often compose verses.

His excellent verses are as famous as minced meat and roasted meat, yet he excels particularly in the five-character regulated verse (wuyan jinti), possessing a style reminiscent of Wang Wei and Meng Haoran.
I have previously selected several of his finest pieces from his collected works, prefaces them, and had them carved for printing.

Recently, I have also compiled his Tang-style couplets into a hundred-verse poem on mountain life; they appear as if written by a single hand, being so perfectly integrated that no seams whatsoever can be detected.

There is no doubt that you have ascended the platform of the great masters. On the ninth day of the middle autumn month, coinciding with your seventieth birthday, it was as if a *buddha-uṣṇīṣa* flower had manifested.
Among all your friends and relatives, there were none who did not join in mutual celebration and devise ways to offer their felicitations to you.

Master Chun then entrusted me with these words on longevity. I have the honor of having been a fellow student under our former teacher for the longest time, and we have engaged most intimately in refining one another through this Way.
Not daring to refuse on account of my dullness and lack of literary skill, I have ventured to offer a tentative discussion, saying:
From the Son of Heaven above down to the common people, there is none who does not possess a household; though they may be noble...
Though there are vast differences in status between the noble and the lowly, all alike rely upon the power of merit and virtue. This is like water having its source or a tree having its root;
if the source or the root should fail, their withering and exhaustion can be anticipated at once.

The *I Ching* speaks of the "overflowing blessings" that result from accumulating goodness, and the *Shi Jing* sings of "seeking blessings without turning back. These are all means for establishing one's source and root. Such is the case within the precincts of the monastic grounds.

This is truly the household of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King. If one who possesses merit, virtue, longevity, and maturity were to dwell therein as its presiding master, they would be able to provide shelter and protection for the great assembly, cause the Three Jewels to flourish, transmit the sacred torch without end, and propagate the practice of the Way inexhaustibly.
In my observation of Master Zhan’s tenure at Longkong, he was indeed such a person. Therefore, I have compiled his [account].
These words serve as a blessing for his great fortune, great virtue, and great longevity;
he should rightly be expected to reach seven hundred years of age, modeled after Zhaozhou, rather than merely reaching the age of ninety. This is the preface.

Preface for the Sixtieth Birthday of Master Bishouzhu Master Bishouzhu has resided in the secluded depths of Songyuan at Yongqing Hermitage for over twenty years. By nature, he is pure, magnanimous, and steadfast;
both monastics and laypeople alike admire his character. Furthermore, he has renovated the hermitage buildings and established a collection of scriptures.
Regarding his ritual implements and requisites, everything necessary for making offerings to the Triple Gem—including mountain forests, fields, and gardens—was fully provided.
As for his own spiritual cultivation, although he did not strictly adhere to formal constraints, his disciples occasionally sought precepts from various quarters.
Some dwell in seclusion within mountain valleys, diligently pursuing the Way and remaining untainted by worldly entanglements; all of this is due to the Master’s instruction and exhortation.

Now, on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of autumn, marking the Master’s sixtieth birthday, his disciples Jiji and his grand-disciples Zhao and Ding have requested a few words as a blessing for him.
I reflect that the five blessings, the nine auspicious phrases, the longevity of a tortoise, and the lifespan of a crane—these are all...

Worldly auspicious greetings are but conventional clichés; they cannot serve as a standard for weighing public affairs. You ought to advance them through my Way, so that they may perhaps provide you with some inspiration.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the World-Honored One personally posed this question to King Prasenajit:
"Is this body of yours of the same nature as a diamond, eternally abiding and indestructible, or is it subject to change and decay? The King replied: "World-Honored One..."
"Venerable One, this body of mine perishes from moment to moment; ever-new, it does not abide, but ultimately undergoes transformation and extinction.
The Buddha said, "Do you know of anything within the body that is imperishable? The King said, "I truly do not know. The Buddha said, "At what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?
The King said, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother led me to visit the deity Jīva, and we passed by this stream."
At that time, he immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges. The Buddha said, "In your sixty-second year, you observed the Ganges;
compared to the vision you had when you were three years old, is there any difference in its youthfulness or decrepitude? The King replied, "There is no difference.
The Buddha said, "Though your face is wrinkled, this nature of your seeing has never truly wrinkled. That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change."

"That which changes is subject to cessation; that which does not change is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Upon hearing these words of the Buddha, the King leaped for joy, experiencing a state he had never known before.

Since the King has now realized that this body shifts imperceptibly from moment to moment and ultimately undergoes dissolution and transformation, he has transcended the deluded recognition of the four elements as a self and the passing of years and months as a lifespan—a distinction between them that is no less than that between heaven and earth.

How much more so when, through the words of the Buddha, one realizes within this body of birth and death that there exists a nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, which cannot be altered by cold or heat, nor changed by youth or old age—how can the leaping joy and rapture be measured?
Thus, a poem by an ancient virtuous master dwelling in the mountains says: "Beholding the river, it is not different from the sight of my first years; the seeds..."
The chrysanthemum is prized for its fragrance in its late season. One must awaken to this truth before one can be fragrant in the latter years of life.
This is what is called true longevity and a true standard of excellence. Who would not hear of this and rejoice in it with admiration?
I ask that you take this very thing as a blessing for you, my lord. May you strive toward it. This serves as the preface.

The discourse on "the tree rooted in the trunk and the water originating in the source" has long been established. When the root is nourished, the branches flourish; when the source is deep and clear, the current flows far.
It is the same for the source and root of human beings: one's grandparents are the very source and root of one’s person. Virtue, morality, and benevolence...
This is the very source and foundation of the righteous mind. How could one fail to nourish it generously and deepen its roots?

I have observed throughout history that those families whose descendants have multiplied and whose generational influence has endured for long periods all attained this through generous nourishment and deep cultivation;
it did not arrive by chance or without cause. As Mencius said: "One does not level things without first measuring their foundation."
"Trifling matters. A piece of wood only a cubit square can be made higher than a tall tower. No warning against abandoning the fundamental and pursuing the trivial exceeds these words.
It further says: "What did Zhongni take from water? Its source springs forth in abundance, flowing on without ceasing day or night;
it fills every hollow before advancing, until it reaches the four seas. That which has a root is like this—this is what he took from it. This is an exhortation to apply oneself to the fundamental.

Could there indeed be anything further than this? From this perspective, it is evident that for a human being born between heaven and earth, it is fundamental that one’s roots must be firm and one’s source must be deepened.
The Xie clan of Guilin are descendants of the great Song Confucian scholar, the Prince Consort (Fu Ma Gong);
they constitute a prominent lineage of Jian River, renowned for the flourishing of poetry and the classics, and for their abundant population.
Jia is located to the east of the commandery. Master Chunyi and I were fellow disciples. Our spiritual friendship has endured for over forty years as if it were but a single day.

He was one who studied Buddhism and thereby came to understand Confucianism. Tracing back from Master Yanggu and Master Xianke to the Master himself and his two sons, Jianzi and Qinzi, the lineage has been transmitted through four generations.
His family has venerated the Buddha for generations; although he pursued the civil service examinations, [he remained devoted to the Dharma].
He established a system for classifying karmic actions, yet both his cultivation of the mind and his conduct were fundamentally rooted in the Buddha-dharma.

At a time when military incursions and rebellions were in turmoil, the Master and his son served as a bulwark against calamities and harms for their clan and all the monasteries, performing meritorious deeds for the people that are beyond counting.
Consequently, his family lineage has flourished ever more widely; his descendants have multiplied and increased, flowing forth in an unending stream that shows no sign of ceasing.

Furthermore, when one wears the *kāṣāya*, wields the mendicant’s staff, drinks from clear streams, and chants the *Prajñāpāramitā*, even the robes of a prince, the delicacies of the eight treasures, resonant music, or brilliant splendors cannot compare to this.
Viewed in this light, that which is held most precious lies herein, and not elsewhere.
[The Master] was there. The guest was suddenly enlightened and said, "I have been mired in names and forms.
Had I not encountered you, I would have nearly spent my entire life in vain. How could I have known that the temple of the Buddha’s Dharma is so vast and profound?
From this day forward, I shall never again dare to speak lightly of the Buddha. He then prostrated himself twice and departed. After a long while, he asked an attendant monk:
"What did you just say in your dreamy rambling? The attendant monk had no reply, and the Master likewise fell silent, forgetting his words.

(When the Jingyang Bell is struck with a blade of grass, its sound cannot pass beyond the threshold; yet when asked by a guest about this, it is said that one strikes it with something large. However, were it not for an elder who has reached the very source of the Dharma and possesses unimpeded eloquence, how could he speak with such freedom and mastery?)

He opens up and bestows or withholds as he pleases; he has revealed the secret that the thousand sages had not yet disclosed! A true person is difficult to encounter, and the True Dharma is difficult to hear. I venture to share this with gentlemen of discernment. (Respectfully inscribed by the dharma-grandson Xinglin).

On the third day after the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year of Yi-mao (1835), I sat with the abbot Gu Yue on the eastern tower of Guangfu Temple. At that time, the moon rose over the high ridges, turning the forest trees entirely white; the cold crickets chirped, and the human world was silent. The abbot then stepped forward and said: [The text continues with the title: *A Discourse on Not Despising the Transmission of the Dharma* (Bu qing shou shou lun).

[The date: The third day after the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year of Yi-mao. [The setting: I and the abbot Gu Yue sat at night upon the Eastern Tower of Guangfu. At that moment, the moon emerged from the high ridges, and the forest trees were all turned white. Cold crickets chirped incessantly, while the human realm was profoundly still. The abbot then advanced and...

Question: When the virtuous masters of antiquity appeared in the world, their intention was to seek out those to whom they could transmit the teachings one to another, thereby continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
In the past, the Elder Wuyi of Boshan propagated the Dharma for over thirty years and revitalized the tradition of Dongshan.

The reach of his realization was like a thunderclap shaking the ears, and the rush of the dragon-elephants toward him was like water flowing into a ravine. Yet, in the end, he never bestowed the transmission.

He entrusted this to one person, saying: "Now it has been nearly twenty years since the Master entered the world. His merit and wisdom are perfectly complete, and he is revered by both humans and devas;
he is no less than when Boshan was in good health. Yet, he firmly guards the ancestral barrier and does not easily grant approval.
All quarters discuss how the Master refuses to take on disciples, merely following in Boshan’s old footsteps, which contradicts the purpose of his appearing in the world."
[The student] said, "I do not know for certain whether these words are truly so. I replied, "Alas! This is difficult to speak of. Sit, and I shall tell you.

Indeed, there are times of decline and flourishing, yet the mind has no high or low. Nevertheless, once one has entered this gate of practice, if one does not seek out others, what benefit is there in seeking transcendence?
As for 'seeking out others,' it means that the master’s household possesses the eye that discerns the Dharma, used to examine and test those who come."

He scrutinized them with meticulous detail, striving to penetrate to the very source and bottom of the Dharma. With a subtle and profound forge, he refined them through manifold means, examining their virtuous deeds and verifying their words and conduct.

His intent was to preserve the direct lineage of the thousand sages as a single thread. Those who could serve as teachers for humans and devas in this age of the Dharma’s decline were such that, as it is said:
"If one's view equals that of the teacher, one lacks half the teacher's virtue; if one's wisdom exceeds that of the teacher..."

Only then is one fit to receive the transmission. Therefore, for several decades, as the karmic conditions had not yet met, I have kept this matter secret. I have endured until death waiting for the right person;

such has been my expectation. If one merely seeks to create a bustling reputation for their school, seeking to recruit both the worthy and the unworthy to sit beneath them under the pretext of "gaining disciples," this is nothing less than inviting a thief to ruin one's own house—a case of error begetting error, spreading further and further.
To commit such errors would not only be futile, but would instead destroy the original tradition, cause the loss of faith among the laity, and blind the wisdom-eye of future students.
Fearing this, I have treated the matter with great care and deliberation, not daring to recklessly imitate others or engage in indiscriminate transmission.
Truly, I await those of great resolve—ordinary beings capable of bearing the burden upon one shoulder. Therefore:

The "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātuparivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma await their time before being transformed. It further states:
"To bestow the subtle and wondrous Dharma upon one who is not a worthy recipient is the work of Māra. Judging by this, how could [the transmission of the Dharma] possibly be taken lightly?
That the Elder Boshan was so cautious throughout his life and refused to allow the Great Dharma to circulate easily—was it not for this reason?
Is it because of what has been seen? Mount [Shan] once said to me, the layman Zhongcheng Jisheng:

"In the matters of the Chan school, what is valued is the mutual correspondence of heart and marrow, not the mere succession of the lineage. If one truly finds such a person, whether through direct perception or hearsay, it is sufficient."
The beginning and the end are of one principle; [the lineage] has never truly been severed. If the right person is not found, it is like adding water to milk—the flavor becomes thin;

or as the character for "crow" (烏) is mistakenly written three times as "horse" (馬)—how could such things truly exist? Therefore, my intention is that it would be better not to find the right person than to transmit the Dharma to one who is not a worthy vessel.

If the right person is not found, although the succession may be interrupted, the Eye of the Way remains unharmed. However, regarding the Great Dharma, to transmit it to one who is not a worthy vessel is a grave error. Regarding the succession...
Though it persists, its false doctrines naturally collapse. Wise men among his former followers should know how to choose between them. Alas!
These words of blood and tears from Boshan are a sincere plea; may the Buddhas and devas clearly witness them.

Although at that time there was no formal transmission and it seemed as though the lineage were deficient, now his Way prevails throughout the world like the bright sun in the sky for all who possess eyes.

Who would not look up to his radiant glory and receive its illuminating reflection? Yet throughout all quarters, people have indiscriminately transmitted [these teachings] regardless of their merits or flaws.
Among the deluded and ignorant later scholars, there are no instances where they do not engage in self-destruction;

they are currently wearying themselves with such disdain that they have no leisure even for it—how much more so will this be the case in the future? As the ancient masters said: "Where others dwell, I do not dwell; where others walk, I..."
It cannot be done. It is not that it is difficult to dwell together with others; rather, it is simply that the distinction between the monastic and the lay must be clear.

This verse exhausts the matter. What more need be said? The Master thereupon bowed twice and received the instruction, requesting that these words be immediately arranged in order to illuminate them for future generations. I could not decline.
A Warning Against Burning Beehives:
In the four districts of Jianning, during the summer and autumn, there are those who set fire to beehives to seize the larvae, either consuming them themselves or selling them to others.
Furthermore, their flavor is extremely poisonous, their profit is very meager, their conduct is most cruel, and their transgression is grave.
The karma is truly grave; do not fail to reflect upon it. However, because he harbored malice toward others during his lifetime, he has fallen into the class of bees.
A sting is at the tail of a scorpion, and it pierces anyone who offends it; this is caused by the force of his former habits.

Furthermore, those creatures dwell in burrows in the earth, gathering their own food and sustaining themselves through their own kind; what harm do they pose to humans? To have needlessly seized grass-insects and crushed them against bamboo—how can this be justified?
He drew it toward him with a pole. He tied a tuft of light feathers to the creature’s waist as a signal; once the creature had caught the insect, he followed its trail.
Upon reaching the entrance of its burrow, he set fire to it and crushed its nest, exterminating the entire species—counting in the tens of millions—with not a single survivor left.
Thereafter, he dug up the burrow and took its wheel-like chambers; within each chamber were eggs, their forms [as follows].
The details are fully set forth: he takes the flesh of his own child, places it into a cauldron of oil, cooks it, and eats it, considering himself to have attained his desire.
Try to reflect for a moment upon the state of its suffering and the depth of its resentment; can this be endured? Can this be done?
If one thinks it can be endured or done, then the human heart has already been utterly extinguished. When the human heart is extinguished, even...
How can they be called human? Furthermore, the one who saw a donkey being killed manifested himself as a donkey; the butcher of oxen, upon death, saw an ox come to gore him;

the slaughterer of pigs, at the moment of his end, let out a pig’s cry; and the crab-catcher, after death, entered the Crab Mountain Hell and saw a swarm of crabs coming to clamp and devour his flesh.
How do we know that those who roast bees or eat bees will not become bees themselves in another life?
Is it not they who burn and they who eat? One life for one retribution—when will there ever be an end?
Cause and effect are manifest, not failing by even a hair’s breadth. Therefore, I urge you all with bitter words: you ought to quickly reform your karma.
What is there that cannot be done? What is there that cannot be eaten? Why do you persist in committing such extremely evil and cruel great karmic offenses? [The human body...]
It is difficult to encounter. The Buddha-dharma is hard to meet. A single thought of turning the light back upon itself allows one to immediately ascend to the other shore.
May all wise ones exhort and admonish one another; there is no greater merit than this.
A Warning on the Capture of the *huánggé* (Yellow Shell) at Mount Bǎizhàng: The *huánggé* is, in fact, a species of frog.

Every time the spring season arrives, males and females come forth in great numbers, filling the fields and blocking the roads. They do so solely with the intent of producing sons and daughters, unaware that they must avoid death and seek life.
As soon as it was born, the local villagers, unaware of its nature, vied with one another to seize and eat it; they did so with an ease no greater than picking up pebbles.
They severed its head and flayed its skin; they cut open its entrails and butchered its flesh until blood flowed across the ground, indistinguishable from human blood.
Heads piled up in heaps—how do they differ from human heads? The killer cannot endure the suffering [of the victim], yet remains unaware;
the eater’s resentment pierces the heavens, yet he feels no compassion. It is said that in the past, Huang Chao once gathered his troops here to plunder and slaughter the lives of the people;
such is the retribution he received. Indeed, when one kills a person, one will be killed by another; the law of cause and effect is never mistaken. As for eating clams...
They then transform themselves into frogs; the retribution is exacted without fail.

This extends to oxen, sheep, dogs, pigs, chickens, geese, ducks, pigeons, fish, turtles, eels, loach, shrimp, clams, crabs, snails, and so forth—indeed, for all living beings that are slaughtered and eaten.
Their confession and reporting were no different from those of Huang Chao regarding the yellow snails;

life after life they remain in the cycle of transmigration, and birth after birth there is no means for liberation. Without relying on the power of the Triple Gem, how could the offenses accumulated over kalpas be released?

In the winter of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era, while I was practicing seclusion on this mountain, I once gathered my fellow practitioners to perform repentance on their behalf for more than twenty [days].

In former times, such creatures had vanished from sight; yet in recent years, they have once again become numerous. The younger generation, following these old customs, vie with one another to capture and eat them.
They do not consider the suffering of death that their victims endure, caring only for the sweet taste that satisfies their own tongues.

This is entirely because they have not encountered the Buddha-dharma, do not believe in cause and effect, and are ignorant of sin and merit; thus they create this karmic act of killing, which will bring retribution in both the present life and future births.
This is endless suffering. Now, in the autumn of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era, I traveled once more to Zhicheng.
Thereupon, I specially invited various virtuous friends to emulate the events of the Guiwei year, so that both those who catch clams and those who eat them might together perform repentance.

It is my hope that the Buddha’s light will shine through clearly and the power of the Dharma will provide secret assistance, causing the malevolent intent of those who catch clams to cease instantly, so that they shall no longer consume clam meat.

May they be spared from falling into the body of a clam. Those who have become clams may their wisdom-nature increase and brighten; without harboring resentment or seeking retribution, may they forever transcend the realm of clams.

May they gaze upon one another with eyes of compassion, free from any intent to harm. May they ascend together to the Dharma assembly, where both people and things enjoy the joy of kinship and affection.
May they aspire to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) and ultimately realize Bodhi—this is my aspiration. I pray only that those of lofty wisdom will propagate this.
Exhorting one another toward transformation, no merit could be greater than this.
A Memorial Text for the Layman Pan Shige: Alas, Master Ge!
You were a dragon in the ocean of learning; early on you were selected for the imperial classics, and in middle age you bathed in the winds of our school for over thirty years.
The Dharma alone is joy. Exhausting our vigor in study and reflection, we discussed intricate and knotty points until our spirits met and our paths harmonized, without the slightest discrepancy.

Over time, our mutual respect deepened; everything emerged from the divine. We exchanged letters back and forth, our brushstrokes flowing profusely as we critiqued one another’s work like physicians administering acupuncture and moxibustion.
I pledged myself to the Way and its Virtue. In the second month of spring, we parted; already knowing your exhaustion, I spoke words of comfort, yet my heart truly finds it difficult to let you go.
My longing for you, Elder, is as your longing for me; who else knows this? Only the Buddha can bear witness. Several months have passed since then.

The cries of the wild geese have not yet ceased; I pray to the Buddhas and maintain my mantras, still hoping for no further misfortune. Yet, how could I have expected that in the Central Kingdom, news of his passing would finally be heard?

Unconsciously moved by grief, tears fall like a torrential rain. When the old man drew his last breath, he was entirely without lingering attachment; even upon reading my handwritten letter, he remained detached.

His two eyes immediately closed. As for the principle of birth and death, the Elder had long since discerned it with clarity; he met his transformation with serene composure. The waves settled upon the vast river.
Though the Elder’s physical form has departed, his spirit does not perish; it shall eternally endure through all ages without interruption. May he, by virtue of his compassion and wisdom, [guide us].

You have long since set forth your compassionate vessel to widely spread the bridge and raft across these final kalpas. With this incense offering, I reverently pay tribute at your venerable spirit-tablet and pen this chapter of my heart’s dew.
You must surely smile with joy; I pray that you take heed of it, responding without moving and beholding my humble sincerity.
I inhale the fragrance of these chrysanthemums and mugwort. Alas! May you still partake of this offering.
This is the text for the memorial dedication to the Elder Layman Chunyi.
Alas! Has the Master departed? Or is there that which does not depart? For that which departs is but a phantom trace within the human world.
Furthermore, although this six-foot frame stands upright between heaven and earth, it is like foam and like a flash of lightning;

its momentary transformation and inability to be grasped can well be understood. As for that which does not pass away—the public’s spiritual luminosity—it is equal to all Buddhas, equal to all sentient beings, and equal to the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe, pervading and filling the ten directions.
The Void encompasses all phenomena, spanning from antiquity to the present, neither changing nor altering. This is precisely what Mr.
Gong studied throughout his life as a Buddhist and what he and I have discussed at length, attaining deep personal realization and clarity regarding it.

To seek therein the marks of birth and death or the traces of coming and going—how is this any different from trying to grasp bubbles from a raging flame or plucking flowers from the sky at the bottom of the water?
Indeed. Nevertheless, if one traces his legacy according to these illusory traces: at the age of twenty, you were already renowned in the garden of arts;

your literary works and moral character were held in high esteem by the world. Although you rose to prominence through the study of Confucianism, at the mere age of thirty, you turned your heart toward the Great Awakening (Mahābodhi).
You severed all consumption of pungent and aromatic meats, received the Bodhisattva precepts, and in both your mental abiding and your conduct—there was no [fault].
He did not seek merit through the mere accumulation of good deeds; rather, he cultivated both his own and others' benefit with perfect diligence until old age without weariness.

His vow to construct the Great Hall of Baiyun Kaiyuan and the construction of the Many-Jeweled Stūpa (Prabhūtaratna) south of the city—undertaken by exerting all his mental and physical strength and relinquishing all that he possessed—are examples of this public man’s actions.
Furthermore, it was he alone who took responsibility for composing the commentaries (*vyākhyā*) and treatises (*śāstra*) on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He compiled this essential work and further donated his own funds to lead the effort in publishing it for the world.

This was because his mind was set upon the Great Dharma and he possessed the vast wisdom of the practices of Samantabhadra’s Vows. Moreover, his fortune, longevity, health, and peace were all fully perfected.
His worthy sons and excellent grandsons gathered in great numbers, vying with one another to attend at his knees. Having reached the age of seventy-six, he suffered from a slight ailment;

yet his right mindfulness remained vivid and clear, and his mental faculties were undisturbed. Upon reading my letter, he became serene and passed away in accordance with his natural destiny in his main chamber.
Observing this, it is evident that the Master’s merit, virtue, and wisdom were consistent from beginning to end in such a manner. And...
The world is vast and boundless; where could one like you be easily found?

Nevertheless, whether "real" or "illusory" are but relative concepts, whereas your footing was originally not confined by such distinctions. Thus, I wished to weep for you through your illusory traces, yet I did not dare;
yet I could not help but remember those illusory traces. Therefore, upon hearing the news of your passing—

For five days my inner organs felt as if they were being torn apart. I then devised a means to establish a memorial for you, Master. Subsequently, as I reflected upon your life from beginning to end, I could not sleep throughout the long night.
I rose, called for a lamp, and, braving the cold, composed this text to offer a solemn announcement to you, Master, that all these are but illusory traces.
Alas! Master, will you not look upon me with compassion? May you accept this offering. *Shāngxiǎng*.

Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Homage to our original teacher, the Honored Śākyamuni. Homage to the immeasurable and wondrous Dharma-gates of the One Vehicle.
Homage to Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all the great Bodhisattvas. Homage to Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, and all the great Śrāvakas and sages.
Venerable Sangha, I pray that the Triple Gem, the assembly of dragons and devas, will not forsake their compassion but graciously accept me with pity.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from beginningless time until this present life, have sunk and wallowed within the three realms and transmigrated through the five paths.
We have failed to clarify the nature of the single truth and have instead vainly identified with the body composed of the four elements.
Within the Dharma of equality, they falsely give rise to views of self and other; upon the illusory scene, they perversely produce a mind of attachment.

They indulge in greed, hatred, and delusion, manifesting them through body, speech, and mind, committing every possible karma and performing every kind of evil. Thus, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, birth and death have remained unceasing.
Fortunately, having cultivated the seeds of wisdom in past lives, this present retribution has brought them into human form; born within the land of Zhendan, they possess a stature of one zhang.

Now, as for his marks: his six sense faculties were complete and his three karmas were harmonious. He left the household life by riding upon right faith and entered the Way by meeting an enlightened teacher.

He diligently cultivated the Three Studies and attained perfect realization of the One Vehicle. He understood the fundamental truth of all phenomena and reached an understanding of the eternal abiding of the single mind.
Yet, because the Way did not overcome his habitual tendencies and consciousness was unaware of the subtle, the eight winds frequently stirred the source of his mind. The four...
The serpent constantly invades the illusory shell; the fruits of the Way have no cause for maturation. On what day shall the Bodhi tree flourish?
Relying upon the power of repentance, may I truly ascend the path of cultivation and realization. I pray only that the true compassion of the Triple Gem will graciously bestow its protection.

May I (so-and-so) and all sentient beings forever exhaust the conditions of hindrances, deeply realize the Great Dharma, possess great merit and wisdom, manifest great functional power, perform great Buddha-works, establish the Triple Gem, and propagate the Mahāyāna.

May the True Dharma circulate throughout the heavens, and may the true wind endure through the final kalpa. May they demonstrate the Eightfold Noble Path and open the gates of the Four Means of Integration. Broadly...
They transform sentient beings so that they all return together to perfect enlightenment. On the day they relinquish their retributive existence, their wisdom of emptiness remains unclouded;

the realm of the Buddha manifests before them, and they are directly reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. There, they personally behold Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of great sages, receiving their offerings and teachings in person.
Hearing the wondrous Dharma, they enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attain *dhāraṇī*, becoming fully endowed with [these qualities].

Possessing the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they open the three secret treasuries and dwell in the highest grade of the lotus assembly. Their fruit is recorded as being attained in one lifetime;

thereafter, they accord with the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and give rise to the function of the *dharmadhātu*. Without leaving the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), their bodies pervade the ten directions;

while constantly attending Amitābha, they personally bask in the presence of all Buddhas. In every atom and every land where there is a dwelling place of a Buddha, their bodies appear before him. Thus, they become the eldest sons of the Buddhas.
I pray that you turn the fundamental wheel of Dharma. Wherever sentient beings look up with longing and compassion, may you go there in person to respond to their needs.
Be a compassionate vessel for the multitudes, guiding them back to Nirvana. Manifesting forms among diverse species, you uplift those in the four modes of birth.

Moment by moment, the six *pāramitās* are perfectly fulfilled; thought after thought, you realize entry into all the gates of *dhāraṇī*. Where there is no Buddha, you act as a Buddha—like the cassia tree.

The reflection of the wheel appears upon a thousand rivers; preaching the Dharma where there is no place for the Dharma. Like the resonance of an empty valley echoing through ten thousand mouths, there is a response to every invocation and no wish that is not granted.

Possessing the great compassion of Avalokiteśvara and the wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra, from this day until the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings in the future, my vows shall only then be fulfilled. I pray only that the Triple Gem may likewise [grant their protection].
Grant me your compassionate pity; behold my humble sincerity and fulfill my aspiration.
This letter is addressed to the Reverend Master Bian from Zhue.
Last year, a Chan practitioner came from Baoshan and presented me with his venerable commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Upon unfolding and reading it, I saw only that his analytical acumen was fiercely brilliant and his ocean of wisdom vast and deep; he did not fall into conventional paths but produced a distinct hand and eye.
Only then did I realize that Yishan, an ancient Buddha, had appeared long ago and been radiating great light. My private admiration for him has not been a matter of a single day.
In the evening, constrained by mountains and rivers, I have often felt regret at not being able to attend upon you in person.

At the end of autumn in the year Xinhai, while traveling to Baiyun on the Jian River, I was unexpectedly visited by your sons, Chao Ming and Pan Shi. I received their gracious letter along with your esteemed record.
It was as if I were beholding the compassionate countenance in person and hearing his coughing and laughter directly; my joy and exultation were beyond description.

I reflect that our school of the One Cave (Dongshan) flourished during the Tang dynasty but declined during the Song. Thus, at that time, Master Mingjiao employed the metaphor of "drawing a solitary spring from a great drought.
Although such individuals were few and far between, each one was a dragon or elephant of the Dharma-gate, having attained realization.

Since the Gate was thus established, the Way and its Virtue were fully perfected. From Touzi downward, masters such as Furong, Dahong, Zhenxie, and Hongzhi were all capable of shouldering the great Dharma to transmit and transform it for future generations. As for today’s Ji lineage, it does not prioritize words;
rather, it is the school itself that often disregards whether a person is capable or not, valuing only the attainment [of realization] as supreme. This has become pervasive.
The faith of recluses in the villages and lanes truly fears that this single thread will be severed.
It is not a matter of having too few people, but rather that it is to be lamented when there are too many. Since what you have realized is authentic, its application is vast and great;

you bear the burden of the Dharma with vigor, and your noble resolve is so intense and fervent that you truly possess the hearts of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu. Only I do not know when this wind will spread far and wide.

As for my current dwelling: I am solitary in my path and thin in my strength. Witnessing the ills of the times, I have no skillful means to remedy them, nor would I ever be willing to merely follow along with them.
Therefore, I have recently retired from the monastery and left the assembly, wishing urgently to establish my own "Self-Realized Hermitage" in a place where there are no people.
I have spent my days according to circumstances. Furthermore, why should I take the trouble to circulate my names and titles throughout the world, vying with my contemporaries?
Years ago, someone came to request my recorded sayings and life story; the reason I did not dare grant them was precisely for this reason.
That person failed to understand, harboring thoughts of birth and extinction in secret, and was consequently scrutinized by those under me, which could not help but cause me weariness.

That I have once again stirred up such divine activity is, in truth, my own transgression. Having no longer dared to stubbornly cling to my former views, I have respectfully recorded a few points for your perusal, so that you may revise them as you see fit.
As the distance is great, there is no way to convey my intentions in person; I can only gaze longingly toward the peak of Mount Bun, hoping for your compassionate understanding.
[Seal] I pray that you will grant me your full compassion and forbearance. [End]
Reply to Master Tanyuan (with attached letter):
I humbly reflect that the late Master Boshan was a towering peak and his vision was as vast as space.
Had it not been for Dongyuan and the late Master Gushan—who were the men capable of spreading the net of Heaven—how could there be anything of the present day?
I imagine that the Master’s years are most ripe, your virtue most profound, your transformative influence most flourishing, and your school most honored.
Thus, those who look toward you with devotion and longing—such as I am—already harbor a sense of being separated from heaven by an entire age;
how much more so for those who enter your gate, step into your chamber, receive your Dharma, and enjoy your bounty? May it not be that in days to come there will be others like me.
"That person was indeed resentful toward Boshaqiao.
Fortunately," the Master replied, "the Elder of Boshan did not fail to seek someone; it was simply that at that time, there was no one to be found."
Therefore, it is better to sever ties with such a person and preserve the Way to await those who come later;
how could this be compared to the current practice where people indiscriminately transmit and receive [the Dharma], claiming they have "attained the person"? Boshan once said to me, Layman Jisheng:
"In the matters of the Zen school, what is valued is that the heart-essence corresponds, not that the formal lineage is inherited. If one has truly attained such a person, upon seeing them..."
One knows that what is heard and what is known are fundamentally one and the same; they are severed, yet not truly severed.

If one does not encounter the right person, it is like adding water to milk, which thins its flavor, or as when "wu" was written three times and became "ma"—how could that which exists be truly existent? Therefore, my intention is better served by simply not encountering such a person.
Do not bestow [the Dharma] upon those who are not suitable vessels. If the right person is not found, though the lineage may be severed, the Way remains true;

thus, it does no harm to the Great Dharma. To bestow it upon one who is not a vessel, though the lineage may persist, the Way itself becomes false, and one instead destroys the ancestral tradition of one's predecessors.
A wise person should know how to exercise discernment. Viewed in this light, it is clear that at that time, Boshan was not without insight.

I would rather willingly become one who cuts off the seed of the Buddha; my own deluded view is likewise. Thus, for more than ten years, I have sought even a single person with a sincere heart, yet none could be found.
Furthermore, how could anyone be willing to follow the current and drift with the waves, treating the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as a mere worldly convention?

Among those seated here, there are those with the will to shoulder this burden, and it is vital that you uphold and transmit it. While such resolve is truly praiseworthy, it must be firmly established.
Nevertheless, one must also know what to select and abandon; one must not, in a desire for haste, fall into the practices of the present age.
Recorded in the *Record of the Patriarchal Hall of Imje Mountain*.

Now, when Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world, their primary concern is to discern the Dharma with strict clarity and to find authentic successors, so that the seeds of the Buddha may never be severed and the True Dharma may endure forever.
During the Jia-long era, the spirit of the school declined and its name was no longer heard throughout the land.
Our Patriarch Linshan rose up in the West River region, and Shouchang inherited his legacy; thus, his Way eventually overflowed across the world. It is, for example, like...

The Yangtze River originates at Mount Min; its beginning is but a mere trickle, a small stream. Yet as it spreads and flows on until it reaches Chu, it becomes a vast expanse of billowing waves that touch the heavens.
This is precisely what happens when one has a source. His ancestral name was Changzhong, his style name Yunkong, and he belonged to the Huang family of Yihuang.
At the age of twenty, he left home to become a monk at Caoshan in his native district.
Traveling alone, he sought the ultimate Way, relying upon Master Shushan of Xiaoshan for over ten years, after which he received the seal of transmission.

Later, he returned to seclusion at Lingshan in Xincheng, where he practiced the dhūta austerities and expounded the Dharma according to the needs of others, remaining unknown to the public. At that time, the venerable master Shouchang...
When Master Ming was twenty-one years of age, he resolved to leave the household life. Thinking there was no one fit to be his teacher, he traveled to Ling Shan to pay his respects.
Upon seeing him, [the Master] was struck with admiration and said, "This is my teacher. He then followed him to receive the tonsure and ordination.

The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, forged and refined him with the furnace of the fundamental nature. One day, the Master’s father-in-law [the Patriarch] addressed the assembly of brothers.
The Master remarked, "Your discourse on the meaning of the *Vajra* is indeed quite eloquent. The Patriarch said, "If the eye of the school is not clear, it cannot be considered ultimate.

The Master’s father then asked, "What is the eye of the school? The Patriarch shook his robe and rose. His father was deeply perplexed by this. Thereafter, whenever he requested further instruction, the Patriarch would simply say, "I do not know;
you must look for yourself. This only increased his confusion and distress. Later, while casually reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*, he saw a monk ask Master Xing...

Shen asked, "What is the Way? Shen replied, "A magnificent mountain. At these words, his state of doubt was suddenly aroused. One day, while moving stones during the clearing of a field, he attained great enlightenment as if waking from a dream.
He then composed a verse and presented it to the Patriarch. The Patriarch said, "Your awakening is indeed not without merit."
"It must be put into practice; otherwise, it is merely 'quicksilver Zen. The Master bowed twice to receive this instruction and then took his leave.

He settled in a thatched hut on Mount E, where he was accompanied only by his own shadow. He practiced with rigorous austerity. One night, the mountain surroundings became exceedingly noisy, and before he realized it, his mind was stirred.
Recalling his Patriarch’s admonition, he thought: "If even a minor circumstance can move me, how much more so the matter of life and death? Thereupon, he grasped...
Taking up the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) at hand, he opened it to read. It happened that Chan Master Gui was there bestowing the precepts upon a mountain deity, saying:
"If you can harm emptiness, I shall grant them to you. Thereupon, the deity became vast and open, free from fear; the mountain region also became tranquil.

He then remarked: "The Sage has no ground of death. Today, this is indeed so. He subsequently composed a verse and sent it to the Patriarch. The Patriarch said: "This man’s realization is transcendent and expansive."

"In the widespread propagation of the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I am not his equal. My late master remained in seclusion on Mount E’feng for twenty-eight years without setting foot upon the mountain.
When he reached over fifty years of age, the Patriarch had already passed away and the coffinwood for his stupa was already growing tall.
Thereupon, my master came forth from the mountains to respond to the invitation of Baofang; he first went to Lingshan to sweep the stupa."
Thereupon, he entered the monastery. Suddenly, it was as if thirty years had passed since he had forgotten the words of the Way spoken at his arrival.

Before long, because he had resided on the mountain for so long, he felt regret that he had not yet completed his universal pilgrimage (*panshan*). He then traveled north to the Central Plains to visit Master Wuyan at Shaoshi Mountain.
Upon hearing his introductory discourse, the Master recognized his great potential and praised him before the assembly. Later, he traveled to Mount Tai to visit [Master Xuefeng].
The Elder of Rui Feng asked several ancient kōans. Rui Feng answered each one in detail and further requested that the Master offer verses for them.

The Master produced a verse for each. Their spiritual resonance was so harmonious that host and guest were filled with joy, like water and milk blending together. Rui Feng then took his leave and returned to Baofang to open a Dharma hall.
The assembly said that the Master would surely succeed to the lineage of Mount Tai or Shaolin, yet he had only picked up a single pinch of incense.
Upon his emergence, he succeeded to his patriarchal lineage, and the multitude were greatly pleased and submitted to him.
Indeed, the Master’s relationship to his patriarch lay in the mutual accord of their mind-to-mind Dharma, rather than in the exchange of witty repartees.

Later, he moved to Shouchang, from which Boshan, Gushan, and Tianjie arose in succession; thus his Way became greatly renowned throughout the world, and his lineages proliferated, each transforming a particular region.
The source is distant and the stream is long; its origins are ancient. Since the passing of the Patriarch, more than a hundred years have elapsed.
The assembly deliberated upon establishing a Patriarchal Hall beneath the Patriarch’s stupa to enshrine his sacred remains, thereby facilitating the offering of incense and lamps.

Furthermore, they established fields to provide for the incense and lamps, and purchased land to support the gathering of firewood, entrusting these matters to the monks for perpetual maintenance. The one who initiated this undertaking was the fifth generation.
Sun Dazhi was the primary founder who managed the enterprise; it was named Xingyun (Prosperity and Transport). Upon the completion of the work, he passed away through the process of transformation.
His disciple Faqin traveled no great distance to enter Fujian and requested that his deeds be recorded to illuminate future generations. I, Pei, was born late;

moreover, as many prior events have been lost to history, there is no way to conduct a thorough investigation. I shall therefore simply set forth what I previously heard from my former teacher and from our Grand Patriarch at that time.
Regarding the karmic connection between the Master and his elder [the Sixth Patriarch], he refined it through the Dharma and aimed for realization through wisdom.

The profound accord between teacher and disciple was such that even axes and hatchets could not sever it; this is truly not something that can be compared on the same day with [the lineages of] Mount Tai or Shaolin.

All descendants of later generations should look up to the traces of the former Dharma and aspire to emulate the conduct of the ancients, lest they fall into the ranks of those who merely follow contemporary trends.
This is to avoid staining the ancestral tradition and to ensure that the single thread of the lineage from above does not fall into ruin; this would be a great blessing for our school.
This serves as the record.
Record of the Rebuilding of the Mahāvīra Hall at Kaiyuan Temple.

The district of Jishi has long been renowned as a land of Buddhism. Ten great monasteries of the Chan school are distributed across its four suburbs, yet Kaiyuan Temple to the south of the city is the most eminent;
it commands the finest scenery of the streams and mountains and preserves the source of both Chan and Vinaya.

According to the local gazetteers, it was founded during the Yonglong era of the Jin dynasty under the name Linquan Lusi (Forest and Spring Vinaya Monastery). Its site originally belonged to Lord Lü Meng, the Marquis of Chancheng of the Wu state.
He donated his former residence to establish a temple; for generations it was inhabited by those of the Vinaya school. During the Li Tang (Tang) dynasty, its name was changed to its present title.

Reaching the middle period of the Song dynasty, it was first converted to the Chan school, and from it emerged Master Ying. His discourse upon ascending the hall said: "There is a mirror that hangs everywhere;
neither ordinary nor sage beings come before it—so who is above and who is below? He then took up his staff and said, "This is the staff."
"The staff. Which one is the mirror? After a long silence, he said: "The moon in the empty expanse over the azure depths of ten thousand ages;

only after repeated searching and grasping will you begin to know it. From that time, the flourishing of the school's style can be imagined. Subsequently, the lineage records were lost, leaving no means for verification.
As for the rise and fall of its halls and buildings through successive dynasties, they are not uniform; the present Great Hero Treasure Hall (Daxiong Baodian) dates from the Ming dynasty.
It was constructed during the Zhengtong era by the two masters Shun and Cong. It took thirteen years in total before it was finally completed. Now, more than two hundred years have passed;

the roof structure has become misaligned and the beams and pillars are decayed and rotten. Although small pieces of wood are used here and there to prop it up, its condition can no longer be sustained.
In the year Renzi, the eleventh year of the Kangxi reign... (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "二", indicating the sentence is incomplete.)
On the first day of the month, I was to receive offerings within the temple. As the assembly of monks struck the bell and came out to welcome me, we entered the hall to pay homage to the Buddha.
Raising my head to look upward, I beheld the structure towering so precariously that I feared it might collapse at any moment; I could not help but feel a sudden sense of trepidation.
