Thereupon, the venerable elders Shangjiejun Song, Yuandong, Xingche, and others prostrated themselves and requested, saying: "This hall is utterly decayed and dilapidated. Should it ever suddenly topple over..."
"In that case, the sacred images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would all be reduced to dust.
Could you not, Reverend, provide even a single blade of grass as the catalyst for the restoration of this hall? I was moved by these words and gave my assent. I reflected privately upon this temple;
its scenic beauty, with its streams and mountains, is renowned throughout the province. Ancient cypress trees stand tall and majestic before the hall, having endured through the ages.
Since the Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, Sui, Tang, and Song dynasties, more than a thousand years have passed.
During this time, eminent masters of Chan and Vinaya have appeared in succession. Yet, by the present day, the halls and buildings are dilapidated and the beams and pillars are collapsing.

Is it not possible that gold may once again be spread and the azure-roofed temple be restored to its former glory? Thereupon, the monastic community unanimously resolved to cultivate the aspiration for enlightenment, each contributing their robes.
Bao later again led a campaign for donations from all quarters. He sought large timbers at the foot of Mount Chen and hewed foundation stones from the source north of the river.
He stored provisions and fired bricks and tiles. Construction began on the eighteenth day of the first month of the following year, Gui-chou, and was completed on the eighth day of the twelfth month.
In total, over two thousand five hundred units of gold and grain were expended.
Both [projects] sought contributions from donors; as all conditions converged, they were successfully completed in a single year.

This was entirely due to the grace of our Buddha’s compassionate protection and the supportive power of the dragon deities and heavenly beings. Freed from all obstructing conditions, everything was accomplished in an instant. Later, he further re-enshrined sacred images and adorned the temple halls with colors;
auspicious light shone forth, and the gold and green glowed together, as if the realms of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Nāgas had been solemnly transplanted here.

In this human world, which is the palace of heaven, whenever one gives rise to a single thought of right faith, ascends this hall, and pays homage to this Buddha, one plants the true seed of Bodhi upon the site of enlightenment and causes the *utpala* flower to bloom within the ocean of nature. This is precisely what is meant.
The assembly on Vulture Peak remains as if it had never dispersed; how could this be empty talk? Furthermore, eight years later, in the autumn of the Gengshen year—
In the eighth month, the Hall of the Heavenly Kings was rebuilt once again. All that was dilapidated and decayed was completely removed and renewed.
The monastics of the temple each contributed their own possessions and further solicited donations from all quarters; before long, it was completed, just as the Great Hall had been.
Thereupon, I have compiled the essential points from beginning to end and engraved them upon jade tablets to endure for all eternity.
May those who come after see the worthy and strive to emulate them, succeeding one another in an unbroken lineage so as not to let the legacy of former masters fall into ruin.

As for those who managed the affairs of the temple until the project was successfully completed: the bhikṣu Zhengliang and the upāsakas Xi Dacai and Li Taiyong were responsible for the management of the Tianwang Hall.
The calligrapher was the monk Yuanzong Zhenjue; this record was inscribed by them together.
Record of the Re-establishment of Baofu Chan Temple:
Baofu is an ancient monastery located in Donghe. It lies to the east of the district seat, at a distance of more than twenty li from the city walls.

According to the local gazetteers, the temple was founded during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. In the first year of the Yonglong reign, Chan Master Bifeng took up residence there, and it became quite a flourishing monastery.
However, as many years have passed, the records and genealogical documents have been lost; thus, the successive periods of its decline and prosperity cannot be verified.

In the fortieth year of the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty, the mountain abbot Qingbi rebuilt the halls and sanctuaries, solemnizing the sacred images and establishing fields to provide for the incense and lamps;
he truly rendered great service to this mountain. In the seventh year of the Tianqi era, the main hall fell into decay, and the monks renovated it once again.
However, the site remained like a beehive or an anthill, with each person making it their own private home, despite being ordained bhikṣus.
Its outward form remained, yet the reality of its cultivation was utterly obscure. In the autumn of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era, it was ravaged by fire;
in a single night, it was reduced to ashes with nothing remaining. For eight cycles of winter and summer, it lay as a desolate ruin of tiles and rubble.
With three or four elderly monks and two or three thatched huts, the drums and bells fell silent and the incense offerings grew dim. Unable to abandon it, they continued to dwell there.
The resident monks, in their efforts to promote the welfare of the Sangha, felt a deep sense of regret in their hearts. At that time, I was residing at Jinghu Lake in Qingyuan.
I led my dharma-relatives, Tahe and Xingbao, to personally carry incense and offerings into the mountains to make a formal request.
Moved by their sincerity, I traveled to the site in person and observed the topography of the streams and mountains; it was well-suited as a place for a practitioner to dwell in seclusion. Therefore—

I accepted his request. It was the second month of winter in the year of Renzi. Subsequently, as I returned to Fusha to construct a stupa and temple, I traveled back and forth to oversee the assembly and protect the Dharma;
the gentry and scholars sent letters and gifts, inviting me on eight separate occasions. It was not until the third month of spring in the year of Jiwu that I finally managed to enter the mountain.
Thereupon, I consulted with the assembly to quarry stone and select timber, and the construction work flourished. [The text here indicates a change in the era name.]
On the site of the main temple, a precious hall for the Subduer (the Buddha) was constructed. It was flanked on both sides by guest halls.
Behind the hall was the Chao-yin Hall, consisting of seven bays. In front was the Maitreya Hall, consisting of five bays; the eastern and western corridors stood like wings.
To the left were the administrative offices, the Kitchen (Gandha-kuṭī), and the Chan-yue Hall. To the right were the Dharma-treasury Chamber, the Nāga Chamber, and...

The Liuyun Chamber (Retained Clouds Hall) was established; furthermore, to the left was the Brahma-conduct Quarters (Fanxing Liao), which served as a high pavilion, and to the right were the storehouse and the bathhouse.

At this point, the overall layout was roughly complete. Within the main hall, images of the Buddhas of the Three Ages and an image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara were solemnly installed.
The ancestral masters of the monastery reside here; in the front hall are statues of Wei Tian and Maitreya, their golden light shimmering and radiating throughout the groves.

Disciples from the four quarters who aspire to the Way gradually gather, often numbering more than a thousand. Morning and evening they engage in meditation and recitation, while the morning and evening bells and drums resound;
the clear and resonant sound of the Dharma fills one’s ears and eyes. It may truly be called a place of genuine *āraṇya* for the cultivation of the right practice.

Regarding the expenses for the practice grounds: every single coin and grain consumed originates from the gates of generosity, being established through the collective contributions of the resident monks and faithful patrons who have each renounced their own possessions.
The permanent endowment for the incense and lamps of this temple amounts to twenty-five *shí* and some oddities.

Furthermore, the bamboo huts of the branch cloisters totaled two *shi* and eight *dou* (plus a fraction), all of which were assigned to the permanent endowment (*changzhu*) of the four quarters to provide for the Three Jewels and the various "noble elephants" (*longxiang*).
This was established as a perpetual endowment for the monastic community (*conglin*) for a thousand years.

In the winter of the Guihai year, the carving of the commentaries and treatises on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was completed; after the assembly of Mount Gu invited me repeatedly, I shall depart to respond to their call next spring.
At that time, the Dharma-heir, Chanhui Ācārya, entered the mountains to visit his preceptor.

The monastic community of the entire temple, along with the local magistrate Yao Gong, lay patrons, and officials, earnestly entreated him to succeed to the seat and guide the region. Unable to decline, Chanhui accepted with a simple "yes.
The assembly was filled with joy. Thereupon, I have carefully recorded these events from beginning to end, carving them into stone to manifest for all to see.

May those who come hereafter—those who dwell here, partake of its provisions, and engage in ascetic practice within these walls—internally strengthen their resolve to seek the Way and externally propagate the spirit of non-contention.
May they cultivate their persons with precepts and govern their minds with wisdom, regarding one another with eyes of compassion.

May we illuminate one another with a compassionate heart and dwell together in the Dharma, thereby repaying the Buddha’s kindness in gratitude and ensuring that we do not fail the intention behind my establishment of the Triple Gem, nor the virtue of the donors’ pure offerings.
I pray that future generations will each strive diligently in this regard. This is the record.
Record of the Hall of Great Compassion at Wuzu Mountain:
The Thousand Hands and Eyes of Avalokiteśvara represent the manifestation of function from the essence. It begins with hearing, reflecting, and cultivating.

When birth and death have reached their ultimate end and are extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before one, then the seven calamities-averting powers, the two types of seeking, the thirty-two marks of response, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivable qualities—all immeasurable merits—manifest perfectly and completely; how much more so the thousand hands and eyes?

The Dharma-realm is its true body, and the myriad phenomena are all its hands and eyes. To speak merely of "a thousand hands and eyes" is simply to describe what is perceived according to the capacities of beings.
These hands and these eyes are inherently possessed by everyone; their wondrous functioning is ever-present.
Yet, due to lack of faith and understanding, they remain unrecognized in daily life, as if they did not exist at all. Try observing this present six-foot physical frame as it dwells here.

Between heaven and earth, how could it be merely like a single leaf among a thousand forests? Yet from morning until evening, and from youth to old age, the thoughts that arise moment by moment are each distinct;

one does not know their number—perhaps many thousands, tens of millions, or billions. When they manifest, they function through the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, each with its own specific utility.
In every single thought and every single hand or eye, everything is perfectly complete and fully endowed, without any deficiency.
There is no remainder. Yet, what is the distinction between sentient beings and Bodhisattvas? The mental thoughts of sentient beings arise from ignorance (*avidyā*);
the hands and eyes of Bodhisattvas arise from the mind of great wisdom and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*).

Therefore, Bodhisattvas are renowned for their great compassion, whereas sentient beings employ ignorance in their affairs. Thus, the ordinary and the sage are vastly different, and delusion and awakening are utterly separated. If...

If one can realize that ignorance is fundamentally empty and true nature is fundamentally present, then the differentiated mind of sentient beings in their daily activities is, in its entirety, the manifestation of the wisdom, compassion, hands, and eyes of a Bodhisattva; what difference could there be?
This is something only the wise can discern for themselves. Fusha Nanshan Suan Tan Gong received the precepts from Elder Zhangshi in his early years.
Having tasted the flavor of the Dharma in anticipation for over forty years, he encountered a period of upheaval as the world was convulsed by the turmoil of war.

He then led his disciples and grand-disciples, including Wuguan and Zhou Dai, to a secluded place at Longdu known as Wuzu Mountain. There, he cleared the wilderness and constructed a hermitage in which to dwell.
The hermitage consisted of five bays: the central bay served as the main hall, while those to the left and right served as meditation quarters. After some time, he further expanded it.
He established the foundation and expanded the palace halls. The golden image stood majestically, its radiance illuminating the mountains and valleys.
Behind the hall was a lofty pavilion where the sacred image of Mahākaruṇika (Avalokiteśvara) was enshrined; it was dignified and exquisitely beautiful, manifesting both compassion and majesty.

With forty-two arms, each holding a different implement, all of which had symbolic significance, there was no one who beheld it who did not transform their mundane mind, giving rise to reverence and faith. [End of] Chapter One.
The assembly gathered in harmonious and reverent order; the sounds of the sutras and the chanting of the Buddha’s name continued without interruption from dawn until dusk.
This place was truly an *āraṇya* (hermitage) in one direction. As for the gold and grain consumed, all of it was provided by the offering of their own robes and alms bowls;

they did not trouble the donors’ households. I observe that those who act as monks in this world are submerged in the dust of worldly toil; from youth until old age, they are unable to [practice] in the Buddha’s [Dharma].
Among those who give rise to even a single thought of right faith within the Dharma, such people are as numerous as the flowing waters.
It is like sitting in a well while suffering from thirst, or entering a mountain of jewels and returning empty-handed; is this not truly and deeply lamentable?

Now, Master An and his disciples and grand-disciples dwell in mountain forests far from the city; they find sweetness in solitude and delight in austerity, daily attending to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Adorned with the profound cultivation of merit and wisdom, An Gong first established the foundation, while Wu Guan, Zhou Dai, and others expanded upon it thereafter.
From these, a continuous stream has emerged, showing no sign of exhaustion.
Are they not truly the descendants of Ikṣvāku and the genuine lineage of the Bhikṣus? Otherwise, how could they surpass their contemporaries to such an extent?
This pavilion was completed on the seventh day of the seventh month of the Wuma year of the Kangxi era.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, the Great Compassionate Holy Image ascended its throne. Zhou Dai provided the stone and requested a record so that it might endure imperishably.

Whenever I reflect upon how my ancestors and descendants have tirelessly and diligently promoted the Three Jewels, I did not dare decline on account of my old age and infirmity; thus, I have specially composed this for them.
The hand-eye of the Great Being issues forth one by one from the heart of great compassion;

yet sentient beings, in their very presence, possess this perfect clarity in every thought-moment, requiring no external seeking. A single thought that turns back toward the source is identical to original attainment.

I pray that those who come after will deeply embody this meaning, skillfully continuing and transmitting it so as not to let the legacy of former practitioners fall into ruin, thereby not failing the One Who Acts for the Void.
The King’s Disciple: This is the record of Master Dao’an’s Dharma-heir.
A Praise for the World-Honored One Attaining Perfect Enlightenment beneath the Bodhi Tree.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, the Way of Enlightenment was first realized; grasping the moon in water, being wide awake within a dream.
Had Yunmen not seen through this long ago, his grievance would remain unredressed to this day. Hehe! Acquaintances fill the world, but how many can truly know one’s heart?
The World-Honored One puts on his robes and takes up his bowl, praising the Buddha as an old bhikṣu of Western Heaven. Clad in robes and holding his bowl, he displays his refined elegance;
through long streets and winding alleys, he wanders about, appearing in the world for the sake of all sentient beings.
Praise for the Sacred Trace of the World-Honored One’s Thousand-Spoked Wheel Mark on His Feet:
Our World-Honored One, possessing the four immeasurable minds, approached the threshold of nirvana and stepped upon this stone; thus remains the sacred trace of his wheel-marked feet.

The seal characters were vividly manifest; this auspicious omen was preserved to bring blessings and protection to humans and devas. Though it was destroyed eight times in succession, it remained unimpaired and undiminished.

When the water was cut and the light was blown away, there was not a single seam or gap to be found. Thus one knows that the Dharmakāya pervades the atoms of all lands, yet dwells neither in sound nor form.

The entire essence is manifest as the True; a rare encounter in ten thousand kalpas. Once again, this inscription upon the profound stone shall forever suspend the Sun of Wisdom within the Sahā world.
In praise of the World-Honored One’s auspicious sandalwood image:
The true form of the Tathāgata is originally formless; how could a skillful artisan ever carve it into being? It was simply that King Udayana could not bear not seeing him.
The Buddha, with his physical marks and signs, consoles the common mind;
the thirty-two marks are all carved out, yet only the Brahma-voice has not been carved forth. His broad and long tongue covers the three thousandfold world-system;
the sound of the mountain stream preaches the Dharma like the roll of thunder.
The Buddha is remembered within one's own mind and appears as a manifestation of one's own mind; it is neither self nor other, and possesses no front or back.
When Maudgalyāyana summoned his master to the celestial court, he carved out ten parts, yet still could not see him.

The auspicious sandalwood image arrived in China; the words from the Golden Mouth were recorded then without error. Only when all sentient beings have been delivered will the vow finally be fulfilled;
one knows not on what day it shall return to the Flowing Sands.

Eulogies for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara (Eight Poems) A single heart of compassionate concern, Manifesting forms throughout the ten realms of existence. Truly, who is this person? Who has attained such sovereign freedom!
Originally there are no names and no family; it is only because of the debts owed in Jambudvīpa.

One wears Amitābha upon the crown of the head and deeply contemplates Avalokiteśvara. The five aggregates are fundamentally empty, entirely free from obstruction. Responding to conditions as they arise, one accords with the needs of beings.
It is like the moon reflected in water; if one can turn back and observe, it is perfect and without deficiency. Like drawing blood with a golden blade, it gushes forth upon the tongue;
the entire body is it—there is no need to seek it elsewhere.
Bearing Amitābha upon the crown of the head, one walks with palms joined; the sound flows equally through the nine realms, reaching everywhere.
If within this one encounters a true connoisseur, peace will be established without the movement of weapons.
They cheaply sell their compassion and refuse to rest; whether ordinary or holy, they all follow the current.
It is only because they owe a debt to sentient beings that they force themselves to emerge from the perilous and evil paths.
Avalokiteśvara alone is the Great Compassionate Mother. She nurtures all living beings as if protecting her own infant. When moved by devotion, she responds;
when called upon, she comes—like the moon reflected in water, or like a plantain tree hearing the thunder. I exhort you, O sons of the Buddha: you should give rise to right faith.
The Great Being and I share the same true nature; by invoking His name and paying homage, He manifests His entire body before me.
May all vows be fulfilled, and may merit and wisdom flow forth continuously. (At the request of Layman Xie Shigong) Who indeed was Wu Daozi?
With the tip of his brush, he was able to conjure the complete spirit of the Great Being—His wondrous marks and compassionate countenance.

Majestic and sovereign, he manifests diverse forms in every place throughout the nine realms. Like the sun that universally brings warmth and the moon that universally brings coolness, he seeks out voices to save those in suffering, appearing in response without fixed direction.
Are the Son of the Way (Dàozi) and Guanyin one or two? Are Guanyin and the Son of the Way one or two?
What is that? What is this? A Eulogy on Avalokiteśvara Spontaneously Appearing (Composed for Layman Zai of Huang’ao).
The Great Being’s true compassion is seen within the very stone; his marks and signs are naturally perfected, manifesting universally through the Gate of Universal Access.
In praise of the image of Guanyin Emerging from the Mountains painted by Vinaya Master Jiyue:

Her form is slender as withered firewood; her clarity is like still water; her mind is as if an extinguished lamp; her compassion is like that of an old mother. Upon seeing the moon, one forgets the finger that pointed to it.
To attain the meaning and forget the image—this is the true Avalokiteśvara. He is worthy of our offerings.

Born in the world where no Buddha was present, he received a great and tall body. Following the Buddhas of the past, he spread the teachings and turned the Wheel of the True Dharma. His true body remains forever. *Praise for the Tooth Relic of the Pratyekabuddha at Kaiyuan Temple in Jianzhou* Produced in the world devoid of Buddhas, he assumed a massive form. Following the Buddhas of former times, he propagated the teachings and turned the Wheel of the True Dharma. His true body abides eternally.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, contemplate this mark of the tooth: it remains indestructible throughout kalpas.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma praised it as he crossed the vast deep seas to come to China; Lord Xiao knew his face but did not know his heart, yet he broke a reed and secretly crossed the river.
Depart! For a thousand ages, the pure wind stirs at Shaolin.
The two Great Beings, Han and Shi, praised each other as bitter enemies; together they entered Tiantai to sweep the stones, reviling all people until no one remained.
Awakened! Singing to myself and laughing to myself, I have forgotten my sorrows. Hehe! Since returning to these cold crags, the bright moon now shines upon Danqiu.
Xie Shigong, a man of talent, transcribed the sutras and fashioned Buddha images; the calligraphy of his characters was as fine as a hair.
The exquisite mind and wondrous hand are inconceivable. I respectfully compose this eulogy, viewing the Buddha through the Sūtra;
thus, he is the Master of Dharma. Viewing the Sūtra through the Buddha; thus, he is the Teacher of all Buddhas. He is neither one nor different.
The teacher is the disciple; this is expressed by the tip of your brush. Where there is a scripture, there is a Buddha; yet as for that which wields the brush, what exactly is it?
If you can turn back and contemplate your own physical form, it is likewise so—there is no difference between them.
Eulogy for the Most Sage Confucius (With Preface) I have read the eulogies for Confucius by various masters;
each captures but one partial aspect, and I have not yet seen a complete portrait. I privately desired to compose a comprehensive eulogy for Confucius, yet I was unable to do so.
One day, reading the *Zhongyong*, I came to the passage where it says that Zhongni (Confucius) "inherited and recounted [the past]..."
Chapter One. I have now realized that Zisi had already praised him; by pairing Confucius with Heaven and Earth and designating him the "Supreme Sage," what more could possibly be added?
The Song dynasty scholars failed to understand this, dividing it into two chapters and thereby severing the continuity of the text’s logic, which has led later students into confusion.
I have therefore specially transcribed this single chapter and sent it to Mr. Pan Shige.
Brother in the Way, I do not know whether my humble views are appropriate or not.
Confucius followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and took Wen and Wu as his model; above, he conformed to the timing of Heaven, and below, he followed the patterns of earth and water.
He was like Heaven and Earth, which sustain all things and cover all things; he was like the four seasons, which proceed in their alternating cycles, like the sun...
The moon takes turns with the sun to provide illumination. All things grow together without harming one another; the Way proceeds in parallel without conflict. Lesser virtues flow like rivers;
greater virtue brings about transformation through its thickness and stability. This is why Heaven and Earth are considered great.

Only the most sagely person in the world is capable of being intelligent, perceptive, and wise enough to preside over others; they are broad-minded, generous, gentle, and mild enough to be inclusive of all.
He is resolute, strong, firm, and courageous, sufficient for upholding principles. He is dignified, solemn, impartial, and correct, sufficient for inspiring reverence.

His patterns and principles are subtle and discerning, sufficient for making distinctions. Vast, expansive, deep, and springing forth, he brings them out in due season. As vast and expansive as heaven.
His depth was like that of a deep spring. When people saw him, there were none who did not revere him; when he spoke, there were none who did not believe him;
when he acted, there were none who were not pleased. Consequently, his fame spread throughout the Middle Kingdom and extended even to the lands of the Man and the Mo.

Wherever ships and carriages reached, wherever human effort extended, wherever heaven covers and earth bears, wherever the sun and moon shine, and wherever frost and dew fall—to all these places [his influence reached].
All who possess vital breath revere and love him; thus it is said he is "a match for Heaven.
In the *Eulogy on the Three Laughs*:
three gates and one room, three persons and one mind—suddenly they meet, and their laughter shatters past and present. Try looking at Tiger Creek.
The azure pines and the bright moon; the sound of the three smiles has not ceased even to this day.

Lord Guan, Prince Yunchang, you who upheld the great righteousness of the Spring and Autumn Annals solely to support the Han dynasty, you who caused the hearts and gallbladders of treacherous ministers to tremble—your single heart of sincerity pierces through the present.
In antiquity, why was it necessary to hold a candle to see the light?

When Han Yu, the Duke of Mawan, visited Chan Master Dadian to offer his memorial regarding the Buddha’s relics, he traveled ten thousand *li* to Chaozhou; yet upon seeing Dadian for the first time, he knew at once that rice is made from grain.
Eulogy for Vice Minister Bai’s Visit to Chan Master Niaoke:
To cease evil and practice good—infants know this well; yet for an octogenarian, its practice is all the more slow.
Eulogy for Real Man Lü’s Visit to Chan Master Huanglong.
Having not yet encountered the True Dharma, he practiced with diligent austerity; upon meeting Huanglong, the difference between gold and brass was instantly discerned.

When General Guan visited Master Zhizhe of Yuyuan, his spirit appeared before him at Yuyuan, where he personally received the full precepts. The image of General Guan striking the transformation-body remains to this day, a testament for a thousand ages.
Governor Sun Luyuan’s Eulogy:
This body is like a floating bubble; even one's name is established in vain. If both body and name are not real, how much more so the rank of "Two Thousand Shi"?
The affairs of birth, death, coming, and going are like seeking the tracks of a bird in the void. There is only the person of original nature, noble and peerless;
manifesting in full majesty before one’s face, neither sages nor ordinary people can recognize it.

Master Zhang Gengru inherited the spiritual refinement of Zhong Huanghua and grasped the quintessence of Mount Wuyi. He attained the civil service examinations as easily as picking up a blade of grass, and he cared for the common people as if tending an infant.
Though he faced peril and was prepared to sacrifice his life, he remained loyal in his sentiments. His lineage continues in an unbroken stream.
The tradition has not yet ceased. From this arose the family reputation of the Yanmei (Yan and Mei) clan. Mr.

Pan Tingming praised the son of Master Qushu as one who did not yield in the face of peril; his loyalty and filial piety were rooted in his heart like the bright sun, representing the orthodox lineage of our culture.
The Fu-sha clan is of noble lineage; their descendants flourish in great numbers. They stand in solemn array like jade, with celestial forms and sagely countenances, as upright as pines and bamboos.
Approaching them, they inspire awe; their pure fragrance may be gathered in one's hands.
Eulogy for Master Xie Xiange:

The Eastern Mountain excels in its refined excellence; from the Guilin branch, the family lineage has transmitted both farming and study. His longevity flourishes to reach the age of one hundred, and his son has already surpassed him in talent.

Sun Yu was precocious from his youth; his person was at ease and his mind leisurely, his nature tranquil and his spirit serene. He was a guest in the Imperial Academy, a model for the world in this degenerate age.
Alas! Such a man as this—I have nothing further by which to praise him.
Layman Xie Chunyi praised the conduct of Master Xingru:

"He employs the Buddha-mind while practicing the way of the Confucian scholar; he roams the ocean of the Dharma-realm and enters the groves of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra; he consults with friends across a hundred cities."
With a single path he dwells his spirit; with myriad practices he brings them forth in abundance.

Like withered wood that blooms in eternal spring, Layman Pan Shige’s prose is vast and expansive, his bearing dignified and composed. He has grasped the marrow of Confucianism and penetrated the essence of Buddhism; he sustains the world through virtue.
This family has transmitted its legacy through literature. At Mount Hua by the waters of Qin, spiritual brilliance mingles in dense clouds.

Layman Zhang Zifa possesses the refined character of a noble youth and the mind of a monk; tireless in serving as a bridge for others, his vows and practices are profoundly deep. He sits there, majestic and upright in the lotus posture.
Upon the meditation cushion, he neither speaks nor utters a word, yet smiles radiantly.
Layman Zhang Qisheng praises Master Wei:

His ancestors secured the protection of the entire city through their profound benevolence; the Master has gathered that legacy within his own person, upholding his ancestors' great virtue. Both his literary talent and his conduct are now manifest.
The worthy and virtuous take this as their standard; they integrate it with the Heart-Essence (cixin), so that the light of wisdom shines ever more brilliantly.

The layman Xie Jiansheng composed this eulogy while residing in a village of immortals. His moral nature was innate; he understood both Confucianism and Buddhism, possessing both words and deeds. His ocean of learning was profound and vast.
The array of his brushstrokes was unrestrained and sweeping; he served as a master at the Three Academies.
He held the scales of authority for this Way.

When Layman Su of Wei dreamed that "Su-hu" had departed, "Wei-hu" arrived in his place. Like-minded spirits resonating with one another, his eyes opened within the dream. Alas! I do not know [what came next].
Whether it was Su dreaming of Wei or Wei dreaming of Su, it is like Zhuang Zhou as a butterfly who has not yet awakened. The "Wei and Su" koan remains beyond the reach of conjecture.
Layman Ningshi of Wu sits beneath a bamboo grove; the bright moon hangs in the sky, and a zither is set before him.
To the left, he appears light and carefree, with an air of self-attainment. The eulogy says:
"Familiarity fills the world, yet only this gentleman understands my heart. A gentle breeze strikes it with a subtle resonance; its pure whistling is more than one can bear to hear."
Whether rising or sitting, he was always with me. A gentleman can endure separation from his flock. I entrust my zither-heart to the bright moon; sounds and colors are but a vain commotion.
Wu Zilin commissioned a portrait of me to be hung in the same frame as that of Prefect Shen, requesting a eulogy.

Prefect Shen supplemented the inscription: "When he first came to govern Fusha, he rescued the chaotic and supported the endangered; his administrative affairs were as numerous as hemp seeds. Once, he passed by Zhishan."
Knocking at the gate to inquire of the Way, his breast was vast and serene; how could he have known the clamor of the world? Beneath the ancient pines, a pure breeze drifts slowly;
sitting cross-legged in silent contemplation, his voice resounds like thunder. Wu Zilin was recognized by the Master and captured this moment in a single painting.
The bird’s tracks in the sky;
white clouds enshrouding the Chan Master’s visage.
Cold in countenance yet fervent at heart; gentle in spirit yet firm in bone. He grasped the authentic seal of Caodong and shook the banner of the religious teachings.
The collapsing social order was restored; he erected the banner of the Dharma across the six realms and spread his virtuous reputation to all quarters.

It is beyond what brush and ink can portray, and how could it ever be measured by mere hearing or sight? Amidst the shadows of white clouds, the colors of the green mountains remain—let the world forever look up to this radiant glory.

The Eulogy for Chan Master Baoshangu Chu states that he emerged from the Gate of Gushan and succeeded to the position of Baoshan; he was able to carry forward his predecessor’s legacy, ensuring the family’s reputation did not decline, as he sat to preside over this mountain.

For fourteen years, his compassionate virtue was widely diffused, and both the monastic and lay communities looked up to him with reverence. For over a month, he manifested illness, yet remained serene and untroubled.

He spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly and then passed away while sitting upright, his departure as tranquil and detached as the wind. Only these few instances are far beyond the ordinary; observe his posthumous image once more.
A Bridge for the Final Age.
Self-Appraisal (Six Verses).
The Vairocana’s vow-power pervades the Dharma-realm; This old man’s humble heart is likewise so. As a single rain universally nourishes the three types of grass, [so do these vows reach all beings].
Moistening. Wherever spring returns, the hundred flowers flourish;
the myriad phenomena of the universe display their vital spirit. How could a clever artisan ever paint them with true fidelity? A single stroke of ink and color would only defile them.
Before the courtyard gate, the withered tree naturally brings forth its own spring.
Entering the mountains and leaving them again; building halls and erecting pagodas. To seek out affairs when there are none to attend to—this truly makes people laugh to death.
Do not laugh to death! Master Zhigong was no ordinary monk; Xueling was originally no true Siddhārtha.
(At the invitation of Fusha Kaiyuan: This old bhikṣu—*ā-ā-lá-lá*. Looking at his appearance, he did not differ from others, yet his mind was remarkably expansive and open.
It is because he wishes to gather all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm into a single mote of dust and thereby manifest the fundamental wheel of Dharma;
and furthermore, because he wishes to draw in all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm into the tip of a hair and have them sit within the Jewel-King Land.
Moreover, his resolve does not seek results in the present life, but rather awaits the arising of the Buddha of Birth.

The realms are empty, yet only now do you bring them to a conclusion. The vast void may perish, but this mind cannot be obstructed. All that has been submitted above is entirely according to the truth;
it does not fail to cause others to harbor doubts.
I have come by chance beneath the pine trees; Strolling along, I loosen my robe. Looking up and down within heaven and earth— Who here is a true connoisseur?
The great void is ever vast and open; Sun and moon rise and set of their own accord. Only those who have forgotten artifice Can truly seek me out.
Within the great round mirror, there is not a single trace to be found. This very thing suddenly emerges like a thunderclap in a clear sky;
whether saint or ordinary person, it is neither different nor one. Only Śūnyatā (the Void) truly knows him.
Epitaph for the Stupa of Master Boshan Hanchen.
The mind of this Master was the mind of Boshan; the conduct of this Master was the conduct of Boshan. He cultivated himself and instructed his disciples.
In all matters of eating, resting, rising, and sitting, he followed the orthodox commands of Mount Bo-shan in every way.

He realized the profound essence within his own mind and transmitted the Vinaya to his descendants. Reaching the age of seventy, he remained vigorous; then, with serene composure, he suddenly entered the Nāga-samādhi.
The mountain colors of Huanglong are as ancient today as they were of old; the towering white stupa remains forever to guard this site.

Amidst the autumn evening of the ancestral temple, where white clouds conceal the stele inscription of the Chan Master, who shall revitalize the collapsing order? It is our Master Yin, a preeminent general of the Dharma, who spreads the Way of Dongshan.

The pulse of the Dharma flows through Longtang; this ancient monastery of the sixth stage flourishes ever more. Fundamentally, there is neither going nor staying—how could it be subject to existence or extinction?
Its roots lie in the veneration of the Buddha; now that the sun has set behind the western ridge, the towering stupa enshrines his jade bones. May these exemplary teachings be perpetuated forever.
The eternal radiance of ten thousand ages.
The inscription for the stupa of Chan Master Baoshan Guchu:
the sound of the Stone Drum does not fall within the registers of *gong* and *shang*; the waves of the Teao River—how could they ever reach such vast expanses? Master Chu followed in their footsteps.
His transformation flourished ever more greatly for fourteen years. Dew descended in profusion; those who were drowning found salvation, and those in obscurity were illuminated.

His influence spread like the wind and his power was as fierce as thunder; the resonance of the Way vibrated with clarity. When his transformative authority had been fully withdrawn, he took leave of the multitude and passed away while seated. He returned to the root, the ground of reality.
The sun has hidden behind the western ridges; towering stands the stūpa on the southern slope of Wu-keng. To all who come, I declare: follow this noble example and do not forget it.
Upon the auspicious mountain, we return as one to the stūpa.
In the clear sky, pure eyes behold flowers falling in profusion; their arising and ceasing have no source—whether you perceive them or not, such is the adamantine essence.
Refined a hundred times yet ever new; fundamentally there is not a single thing—how could there be even a speck of dust? This is the ground where yin and yang do not reach, the sproutless grass.
The fragrant elephant hides deep within, occasionally baring its tusks and claws. One body becomes many bodies, and many bodies become one body; all return together to this stupa.
Withered trees flourish through eternal spring;
white clouds honor the Bell Inscription of Chongfan Chan Monastery.

This ancient monastery of Chongfan is the meditation barrier of the patriarchs. Rolled forth from the red furnace, it shall forever stabilize this mountain. May the faculty of hearing of every person [be purified].
Possessing the threefold reality, it manifests through every strike; it is tranquil yet distinct. Addressed to you, O Son of the Buddha: immediately cease all doubt.
It is naturally true and wondrous, requiring no cultivation or effort.
The Inscription for the Bell of Kaiyuan Temple:
Kaiyuan of the Tang is the Linquan of the Jin. Here, dragons and elephants tread one another; Chan and Vinaya follow one after the other. One cultivates the self through the precepts.

To clarify the mind, one relies on Chan; to abandon these two [extremes], one knows not where to turn to heaven. Now that the great bell has been cast and the precious hall completed, this profound principle is inscribed to manifest it clearly for future sages.
Inscription on the Bell of Yongan Wanshou Chan Monastery:
Where the deep resonance vibrates, the Buddhist sanctuary is eternally secure; may the sovereign and his heirs enjoy ten thousand years of longevity, while the four seas rise in exultation.
Inscription on the Bell of the Many-Jeweled Buddha Stūpa:
The remaining copper from the stupa’s pinnacle was cast into this great bell, which shall eternally guard the precious stupa as it towers high toward the vault of heaven.
Unaffected by the three calamities, it shall long enjoy the five blessings; all who see or hear it shall attain Buddhahood.

Verses on the Six Similes from the Diamond Sutra (Six Poems): Dream All phenomena are like a dream; They have no fixed nature. If one can awaken to this truth, One will transcend birth and death. All phenomena are like a dream; They are empty and without self. If one can realize this principle, One will not fall into the three realms. All phenomena are like a dream; They arise from deluded thoughts. If one can sever these delusions, One will attain liberation. All phenomena are like a dream; They are illusory and deceptive. If one can see through their falsehood, One will reach the state of nirvana. All phenomena are like a dream; They are devoid of substance. If one can understand this lack of reality, One will be free from all attachments. All phenomena are like a dream; They are merely mental projections. If one can remain unmoved by them, One will achieve the ultimate fruit.

Long I have slept within the chamber of ignorance; my spirit wanders through a world of dreamy confusion. The single body is originally unmoving, yet ten thousand objects appear of their own accord as empty phantoms.

From what is not-dharma, dharma arises again; where there was no person, suddenly a person appears. I look back with longing upon the Great Awakened One: when the dream is shattered, one beholds the true nature of heaven.

The great illusionist, the *ālayavijñāna*, conjures all illusions through its mental artifice. Once the distinction between ordinary beings and sages has arisen, likes and dislikes naturally fall into disorder.
Mountains and rivers compete to flow and stand; palaces likewise come into being. Yet these illusions are fundamentally quiescent; they are neither real nor false.
The ocean of the fundamental source is clear and still; when delusion stirs, floating bubbles arise. They are born in an instant and perish in an instant; what is established, and what is destroyed?

Wandering through the six realms of existence, they sink and drift within the square inch of the heart-mind. Seeking the current, one suddenly discovers the source; in the ultimate sense, nothing exists apart from the water.
The shadow obscures the true form; life after life, one merely dandles with shadows. One falsely discriminates between the ugly and the beautiful, and in vain, hatred and love run wild.

Like a deluded monkey reaching for the moon in the water, or like an old man suffering from illness who suspects a snake in his cup—when light is turned back to shine alone, both mind and objects vanish together.
Dew upon the morning flowers: each drop is as round as a pearl. It provides moisture for no more than a moment, yet its solidity cannot be preserved for even an instant.
Life and the world are just like this; the same is true from antiquity to the present. Why wait for the sun to rise, only then to realize it has vanished?
Observing the mind like lightning, a crimson light shoots through the constellations. It dispels the darkness of the long night and illuminates ten thousand layers of mountains.
Brightness and darkness are fundamentally without interval; who can grasp its coming and going? Try to observe the place where it arises and ceases—the azure sky is naturally serene and secluded.
Verses on Encouraging the Recitation of the Buddha’s Name by Master Shandao (Eight Stanzas) Gradually the skin becomes like that of a rooster and the hair like that of a crane;
time passes, pressing in upon us in secret. Seeing the pitiable state of old age in others, one fails to observe it within oneself.
One must know that this body is not a true body, resembling nothing more than foam gathered upon a rushing torrent. I universally exhort you to act while there is still time.
Recite the Buddha’s name. Do not wait until your breath fails and your strength is gone;
look at how your steps have become faltering, and even a distance of ten paces feels like a thousand miles, making communication difficult.

Reflecting on your physical vigor in years past, you have needlessly stumbled through the dust of the world. Without ever having trodden upon the ground of reality, how could you understand the need for self-reflection? I exhort everyone: act with urgency.
Recite the Buddha’s name. This swift descent down the slope is difficult to encounter again.
Even if one fills the halls with gold and jade, calculating and deliberating day and night, once the two hands are suddenly flung open, everything will fall under the control of others.
One has obscured one's own precious treasury while greedily rushing after others' rubble. I universally exhort you all to bestow it all.
Recite the Buddha’s name. The West is indeed the Land of Treasures.

One cannot escape decline, aging, and illness. Who in this world can truly believe? Relying solely on the strength of one's vital energy and blood, one fails to consider that old age and sickness follow closely behind.
Once one is bedridden and entangled in suffering, the eight kinds of affliction burn together, impossible to endure. I urge you: take advantage of your current health.
Recite the Buddha’s name. You shall enter directly into a lotus womb to take conception;

though you may enjoy a thousand forms of pleasure, how could you know that such joy is the cause of suffering? Your entire being is composed of sinful karma, and for eternal kalpas you shall not escape sinking into the depths.
In the dark realm of the spirits, there are registers of good and evil deeds, upon which every single name is recorded. I universally exhort you to focus your mind with single-minded devotion.
Recite the Buddha’s name. The light of wisdom shall pierce through and dispel deluded attachments.
Impermanence will inevitably arrive; all things will be cast aside in a single moment. One vainly occupies a patch of green mountains, yet in the end, one's bleached bones are buried deep.
Not a single thing belongs to me; how could there be even a hair’s breadth to take back? I universally exhort you to prepare in advance.
Recite the Buddha’s name. The lotus root has been cultivated deeply by itself;

there is only the path of direct practice, where a single day surpasses a thousand lifetimes. It values only the vows and aspirations of the practitioner, while also relying upon the Buddha’s radiant light.
Samādhi is accomplished at every moment, and the defilements of sin are purified like melting ice with every thought. I universally exhort those with faith.
Recite the Buddha’s name. Your name shall be inscribed in the highest grade upon the lotus pedestal.

Simply recite Amitābha Buddha; there is no need to seek other dharma-gates. In this very moment, you shall transform from an ordinary person into a sage, just like the transformation of the giant fish *kūṃ* in the Northern Ocean.
Let every phrase be linked like pearls without interruption; let every character reflect like a mirror without dimming. See the Buddha as you recite His name.
It is seen immediately. Let us set aside for now the discussion of the Pure Land of Sahā.

The Verse on the Great Luminous Treasury of Perfect Enlightenment states that the enlightened nature is perfectly bright, neither internal nor external. The Bhagavān spoke of "entering" to reveal the profound ford; it is one and the same throughout past and present, with no time between them.

A Pause. The ordinary and the sage share the same source; who then is host and who guest? The numinous trees cast deep shadows, untouched by spring; the solitary peak stands bare, perpetually shrouded in mist.
Within this, a realm of golden light is conjured by illusion; father and son sit together in a circle, their conversation ever new.
At the end of the twelfth month of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era, I arrived at Mount He to pay homage to the traces left by my late Master, the Preceptor.
Since the Master planted his staff upon this mountain peak, forty years have suddenly passed since our parting. Whenever I draw water, I think of rushing over the steep ridges;
when gathering lotuses, I recall treading through the deep fields. Human life has undergone such vast changes as these; how could I dare to look upon my own face, now but a decaying bubble?
Self-Commiseration I wish to inquire of my Master about the ultimate meaning; The pines and bamboos before the gate remain evergreen.
Spending the Year at Huangmei Hermitage (With Preface).
On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era, at Baiyun, written by Yue Xie Feiqing Huangaozai.
The fellow practitioners Fan Shige and Wei Mengsu traveled to various renowned temples along the East Creek.
On that very day, they paid their respects at the remains of the former master at Heshan. The following day, they passed through Wanshan Monastery to visit Master Wu;
Shige took his leave and returned home. On the next day, they reached Huangmei, where Feiqing also returned. I, along with Ao Zai and Mengsu, then continued on our way.
During the year at Huangmei, the presiding master was as diligent in his courtesy as Zhizhe; host and guest were in harmonious accord.
On New Year’s Eve and the first day of the new year, they each composed poems to record these events.
It is said that this floating life is but a transient inn; who would have known that wherever one goes, it is home and mountain?
Gathering around the hearth to brew tea and speak of past events, host and guest alike forget themselves in a moment of laughter.
Of a hundred-year span, more than half has already passed; one year is subtracted from another year.
Even if one were to exhaust the kalpas of the mustard-seed city, the courtyard cypress remains ever-green, undaunted by the snow.
The Phoenix Calendar first opens as the year renews; gazing afar across the eight directions, purple clouds gather thick. Last night a rain fell, sufficient for the thousand forests;
plants and trees all rejoice, turning their faces toward spring.

The empty mountains are silent and vast, utterly without sound; Bells and chimes mingle with the purity of the *brahman* chants. With a single incense stick of *candana*, I pray for the longevity of Yao;
Together we behold the joy of peace throughout the four seas.

I traveled to Longtou Mountain to visit my old friend Zhiguang at his eminent monastery on Jianxi, which commands the splendor of Dragon Mountain. Having returned after twenty years, I knocked upon the bamboo gate; we met with mutual affection and inquired after one another’s travels.
Amidst the green mists, we burned incense and brewed tea.
Loftily it rises, towering over all the peaks; gazing down upon the mountains ahead, how many layers of emerald green? The pine path winds its way, allowing travelers to reach its end;
treading upon the mossy ground, the moonlight shines bright beneath one's feet.
In praise of Layman Huang Ao-zai:

In his old age he studies the Way, his resolve more sincere than ever. Having renounced both meat and wine, his realization enters the divine. He receives the precepts of the mind-ground from within the mind-ground itself;
he shall ferry all living beings across the ford of delusion.
To Layman Chen Xuekui:
The humble alley of the youth Yan is no cause for sorrow; he has instead cast aside his cares and finds joy in freedom.
Having realized the place of true happiness within himself, he views fortune and misfortune as but floating bubbles upon the same water.
To Layman Wei Mengsu:
Suzhou Dongpo’s wisdom-karma once covered the world, yet it was buried beneath the sounds of the stream and the hues of the mountains.
Now, at the moment he awakens from his own deluded dream, the mountains and rivers turn upside down and enter his thatched cottage.
Inscribed on the Wall at Samgungsa Temple in Sunyeong (Four Poems) Three Peaks surge from the southern land of Ao-yang;
In the early Song dynasty, the palace of Śakra and Brahmā was first opened. The lamp of the Buddha’s teachings has been passed down, never extinguished;
The Dharma-sound thunders forth whenever the bell is heard. Before the gate, the ancient path retains the new moon; At the valley mouth, the sparse forest swallows the sound.
The Evening Breeze Today I have come to inquire of the past; Deep in the night, a pure dream reveals hidden traces. The seventy-year-old monk opens his birthday feast;
From the south, the warm breeze sweeps across the stone terrace. Tea is offered like mist surging forth, as of Zhaozhou;

Delicacies are presented like clouds arriving from the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) Hall. With compassion, he transforms the violent and leaves the mountain valleys; With strength, he dismantles the bridge to ferry others across.
Beside the waters, ten thousand voices chant praises that constantly fill the way. This is the first time for one who has reached the age of seventy and beyond. (Right:

For the Abbot of Jōgo Myōji Temple) The spirit and bearing of this man are like those of a sovereign; he has cast off the worldly bridle and shines all the more brightly. On a single-leafed skiff he roams the illusory sea;
at the third watch, the solitary moon illuminates the empty corridor. Knowing that the ground of reality is originally luminous and wondrous, he sighs instead for the emptiness of this floating life.
How busy and hurried! All that once flourished before our eyes has become but a tale of old.
How few here can turn their light back within? Ancient pines and cedars stand arrayed at the three gates; winding stone steps lead along the path of awakening.

The jade halls are veiled by white clouds, and the golden countenance glows with the red sun. Profits and fame ever pursue those in high carriages; yet honor and disgrace do not touch the hundred-fold [sages].
Old Monk: A single scroll of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra just finished; atop the tower, I did not realize the bell had struck again.

Presented to Li Gong, the Prefect of Shouling—a refined immortal official with abundant leisure: With few lawsuits and harmonious people, you enjoy idle days all through the sun; a cup of wine and a hundred verses to repay your elegance.
How magnificent! Within this lies a world beyond the human realm;

heaven and earth are but a single pellet held between the fingers. Mount Ao Yang is but a tiny speck where ten thousand peaks cluster; though the great butcher’s blade was tested here, it was never for a small task.
Yet I am reminded of the man of Panxi, who once gripped his fishing rod.
I reside by Mirror Lake when the lay practitioner Wu Rugu visits; I respond in verse to present him with a gift.
