This is Ge Tianmin.
In the winter of the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era, he accompanied Master Xie Chunyi to Da Yun Monastery to construct a rear hall.

They transcribed the *Huayan shu lun zuanyao* (Essential Excerpts from the Commentary and Treatises on the Avatamsaka Sutra), and when both tasks were successfully completed, he composed this verse to record his joy.

The task of building halls and transcribing scriptures is but a trifle; let us instead look forward to passing through other mountains leaning on our staffs. The Buddha-lands of a mote of dust are not the result of human construction;
where could a single word of the Dharma-gate ever be deleted? Though the ink of the oceans may be soaked and exhausted, it is difficult to erect the towering, majestic halls of the Brahma-palace.
Once this new poem is written, you shall laugh long and loud, leaving it for your descendants to grasp and ascend.
The Layman Xiong Ziwěi has completed his transcription of the *Huayan jing shu lun zuanyao*. He writes this to present to you:

though the ocean’s ink could hardly record even a single gateway of letters, I rejoice that you have brought these subtle words to completion in three years; the radiance of your brush emits luster, forming golden script.
The axle turns; ink-waves and flying blossoms drench the Garden of Dharma. There is no need to strive for knowledge or seek to extinguish delusions;
simply cultivate merit and wisdom to nurture the roots from within. When shall we gather once more amidst the deep clouds, to once again examine and discuss these bequeathed volumes in detail?

On the occasion of the seventieth birthday of Master Li, the son of Shouqi, he sits with his fishing rod cast upon the White Dragon River; having fished through misty waves, his passion grows ever more grand. Having traversed the world, he knows not when his hair suddenly turned white;

yet he rejoices that his insight remains most lofty as he composes his writings. Before the courtyard, the purple cypress is nurtured and flourishing; beneath the hedge, the yellow chrysanthemums are planted.
It is already secure. I wish to offer my longevity to you, Master; how shall I bestow it? The sound of the tide drums through the cold waves day and night.
At the urging of the assembly of Mount Gu, I returned to the mountain, moved by a sense of resonance.
A single reed boat drifted lightly upstream, seeking the old monk to a desolate mound. We met with lingering affection; there was nothing else.
He spoke: "I only urge you to return to the mountains, as tears flow forth.
This useless dhūta is old and sick; though the home mountain is but a few inches away, it is like ascending to heaven.
Although there is an agreement to return once more, I still hesitate and cannot take another step forward."
In summer, I see off Mr. Xu Ruogu as he returns to Wulin;

the fragrant breeze has already reached the south. I bid you farewell as you return to your native land; I am utterly weary of the treacherous mountains of Min, and I deeply long for the vast waters of Zhejiang.
Repairing the fence to nourish the deer at will; finding the path, how could one lose the sheep? From here, proceeding to the West Lake, the lotus fragrance is at its peak.
On the twelfth day of the sixth month, I sent this letter to inquire after his well-being; on the eighth day of the seventh month, he passed away.
I compose this poem to offer my condolences.
I thought only that you, sir, shared the same heart with me; like wild geese flying south, you sent many messages. Before your calligraphy had even dried, you followed the Great Transformation;

your numinous light shines alone—what need is there to seek it? You composed books yourself as you traveled through the world; who will transmit your teachings on the patterns of reality to settle matters past and present?
The jade trees stand dense and now vie for brilliance; where the golden wind stirs, the autumn forest resounds.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the Guihai year of the Kangxi era, the carving and publication of the *Huayan jing shu lun zuanyao* (Essential Compendium of Commentaries and Treatises on the Avatamsaka Sutra) were completed;
I compose this verse to record my joy.

The ocean of the nature of the Avatamsaka is infinitely vast and boundless; The compassionate vessel of the commentaries and treatises carries all who come and go. The merit of compiling and carving these subtle words is now fulfilled.

The work is completed. My aspiration to propagate [the Dharma] throughout all eternity remains even firmer. The Buddha’s grace is vast and boundless, truly difficult to repay; the Dharma’s bounty is expansive and deep, indeed impossible to fully proclaim.
Do not say that the person for whom this teaching is intended cannot be seen; Sudhana still turns his steps toward the south as before.
The Four Daily Practices (with Preface).
The ancient masters had ten practices that could be performed. In my later years, my vigor has declined; beyond the necessities of sleep and food, I am only able to engage in four matters:
sitting in meditation, walking meditation, reading sutras, and reciting the Buddha’s name. Under each of these matters, I have appended a verse. Written by [Name].
Place it by your seat and observe it yourself from time to time.

When both person and dharma have vanished, one excels at sitting in meditation; ten thousand years are but a single thought, severing all distinctions between center and periphery. The various devas have no place to seek his traces;
he merely takes heavenly flowers and scatters them before his seat. (Sitting in Tranquil Meditation)
Walking upon the lapis lazuli ground, his movements are calm and slow, his steps light. The assembly of all noble beings gathers together, passing one another shoulder-to-shoulder in silence.
(While walking) in old age, with no affairs to occupy him, he passes the idle days;
daily unfolding the golden sutras, he examines them in detail. The deeds are as clear as a land deed.
Stable. Who would have known that the human world undergoes such vicissitudes? (Reading the scripture) Amitābha and I harbor a grievous enmity;
remembering him brings me ceaseless resentment. He has seized my Pure Land and returned it to this world of endurance;
where else shall I go to inquire about the Western Journey? (Reciting the Buddha’s name)
Avalokiteśvara and Sudhana Riding a Lion: Disciple Pan An requests a title for this.
Where can one seek Avalokiteśvara? One must traverse clouds and mountains until they vanish from sight. Suddenly, upon the Potalaka crag, he is seen;
a thousand peaks of blue, their emerald summits towering high.
The great lion and the little lion, father and son, ride forth together, playing with their claws and fangs;
they roam throughout the atoms of all lands but cannot descend, not yet knowing on what day they shall return home.
Preface for the Centennial Celebration of the Late Venerable Master of Gushan: I humbly submit this preface.
The Way of the Teacher has no fixed form; it remains indestructible throughout ten thousand kalpas. The grace of the Dharma endures; it shall persist until the end of all eternity.

There is no contradiction. A single thought-moment is ten thousand years; a single kṣaṇa is a hundred years. I respectfully present this according to the teachings of the Buddha, offering a small measure of ant-like sincerity.
I reverently contemplate the Dharma-name of the Honored Master Yuanxian, the thirty-second patriarch of the Caodong orthodox lineage and the founding teacher of the Drum Mountain Hall.
He manifested his birth on the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the Wuyin year of the Wanli era of the Ming Dynasty at the hour of Si. His manifestation has now ceased.
On the seventh day of the tenth month at the hour of the rat during the Qing Shunzhi Dingyou year, I reflect deeply upon my late Master, the patriarch of this ancestral temple.
He was a guiding bridge for the Dharma-ending age, the fundamental pillar distinguishing the orthodox from the heterodox, and the transmitter of the wondrous Way—whether it be passed on or not.
Occupying the seat of Xingsheng Monastery, his thunderous voice resounded throughout the heavens; propagating the lineage of Shouchang, the rain of Dharma moistened the entire earth.
Honored and revered by humans and devas, venerated and received with respect by spirits and ghosts, he entered *nirvāṇa* at the age of eighty, yet his legacy was celebrated on his hundredth birthday.

The true wind did not decline; the *dharma*-flower appeared once more at this time. His transformative radiance remains ever new, forever illuminating the dark alleys of ignorance throughout the infinite.
Thus, on his birthday, he established the "Water-Moon" Dharma-assembly (*mārga-kṣetra*) at his own hermitage for three days.
Throughout the entire day, I recited the three chapters of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—the "Brahmacarya," "Pure Conduct," and "Vows"—as well as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
I prostrated before the precious repentance liturgy of the names of the eighty-eight Buddhas and arranged pure offerings to express my sincerity, like gathering the *fán* herbs.
By chanting these secret verses, I looked up to rely upon the protection of the True Light. Having completed these rites...
Furthermore, we shall once again unfold the Golden Precepts to bestow Dharma-food upon the spirits in the netherworld and sprinkle sweet dew upon the burning house.

Regarding the meager causes we have accumulated to offer even a small recompense for such great virtue, we prostrate ourselves with the vow that you shall not arise from the Samādhi of Cessation, yet manifest clouds of bodies throughout the Dharma-realm without end.

Proclaiming the essential teachings to cure the chronic ailments of the monastic forests in this age of Dharma decline; continuing the life-force of the Tathāgata’s wisdom as it teeters on the brink of extinction;

rekindling the heart-lamp long extinguished within the ancestral chambers; may the rain of Dharma overflow throughout the human realm and the true wind of the Way sweep vast across this degenerate age.
Widely opening the eyes of wisdom for future students and eternally upholding the authentic regulations of the successive patriarchs, thereby repaying the four debts of gratitude.
Universally supporting those in the three realms of existence, I respectfully set forth my humble sincerity to trouble Your Sacred Compassion. This is the formal petition.
As I begin writing this commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I request Your empowerment and protection.
Within the centermost part of the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, amidst the Sea of Fragrant Waters of Boundless Sublime Flower Radiance... 普 (Pu) [The text continues].
In the thirteenth layer of the world-system of the Radiant and Blazing Jewel Light,
within as many worlds as there are atoms in thirteen buddha-fields, in the Sahā world, in one of the four continents among ten billion four-continents,
in the Great Qing State of Jambudvīpa, in Jian’an County of Jianning Prefecture, Fujian Province, at the Guangfu Hermitage, [the monk] Hongfa...
Written by the monk Daopai; the Mahāyāna and Uttara-yāna devotees and disciples, Xi Dacai and Pan Daojing;
and the disciples Wang Dachi and Xiong Shen, who together with sincere devotion, prostrate themselves a hundred times and address this submission:
We reverently contemplate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the foremost proclamation of the five periods of the Buddha’s teaching, the discourse that perfectly accords with the nature of reality. Sa...

This is the broad highway for the cultivation and realization of the six stages; it is the great path traversed by Sudhana alone. Herein, cause and effect penetrate one another, and phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated.
A single mote contains the Dharma-realm, and a single thought encompasses the three periods of time. This perfect and true exposition is inconceivable.

Since the holy master has already provided the commentary and treatise hereinbefore, I, an ordinary and ignorant person, have compiled this essential summary hereafter, endeavoring to ensure that it accords perfectly with the Buddha’s intent.
With a mind of skillful adaptability and wisdom, you have widely propagated the life-force of the Dharma and brought vast benefit to future generations.

On this auspicious day, the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month in the Wuma year of the Kangxi era, as I am about to begin the task of transcribing [the text], I reverently prepare offerings of incense and humbly set forth my petition.
I pray that the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Great Sage Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and...
May the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Sudhana, and all the sages and worthies throughout every land and every atom at the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
grant their witness and bestow their compassionate protection. May this cause the clouds of delusion for me, the bhikṣu Daopai, to be instantly dispersed,
so that the sun of wisdom may shine in full radiance, enabling me to open the sutra scrolls within a single mote of dust and penetrate the profound source of the ocean of Dharma.
May this merit be swiftly accomplished; may our vows not be in vain. May we forever be illumined by the Buddha’s light and eternally remain unassailed by demonic obstacles.

We further pray that the disciples, including Xie Dacai and others, may see their twilight years shine with brilliance, that the vast source of their ocean of blessings may increase, and that their wisdom-vocation may be renewed.

May they establish extraordinary achievements for the Dharma-gate, so that all may be universally bathed in the waves of grace and the entire dharma-realm may equally partake in the benefits of the Dharma.
Respectfully submitted.

This petition for rain at Baofu Temple earnestly reflects upon the fact that since the beginning of summer, incessant rains have fallen, thereby obstructing the completion of the temple’s construction. We therefore offer this sincere prayer.
Ancient Buddhas, if you would indeed grant your compassion, please bestow clear weather upon us. This would fulfill more than half the merit and intention of this excellent occasion.
However, as it has not rained for a full month, all things are withered and parched; the grain crops are beset by locusts and grasshoppers, and the common people are gripped by the fear of famine.
For this reason, we have reverently selected the thirteenth day of the seventh month to assemble the pure assembly and offer the purity of water plants and aquatic weeds.
I offer this service. Reciting the *Dhāraṇī of Great Compassion*, I venture to lay bare my heart and present this renewed earnest supplication.

I pray only that you will not forsake your great vow, but deign to respond to the common sentiment. May you spread the vast clouds of compassion and let fall a bountiful rain of sweetness, so that the crops may ripen and the villages may enjoy the blessings of abundance;
may pestilence be silently extinguished and people be free from the calamity of untimely death, so that all beings on this great earth may share in these benefits.
Your Virtuous Grace: Throughout the heavens, all share in the waves of your benevolence; everyone in their daily lives is entirely covered by your compassion.

I respectfully submit this memorial. Second, I reflect that during the three months of the dog days there has been no rain; the great earth is parched and withered, the fields have cracked open like tortoise shells, and the people are suffering the pangs of starvation.

With such anxieties, they called upon Heaven and struck the earth, praying to the Buddhas and beseeching the dragons; yet, though they might pour the nourishment of a cup of water, it was difficult to save them from the calamity of a wagon-load of firewood.
Therefore, this temple respectfully selected the seventh day of the seventh month to assemble the pure assembly and ascend to the precious hall.
We empower this Great Compassion Dharani and extol the sublime name of Prajñāpāramitā.

By virtue of these merits, we dedicate them exclusively to the Three Jewels—Eternal and Abiding throughout the ten directions—and to the eight classes of Dharma-protecting deities, dragons, and heavenly beings. We pray that you will grant us rain like that from a basin and bestow the blessings of a bountiful harvest.
May the heavens be fully saturated and the entire realm receive your grace; may every household enjoy the prosperity of abundance, and may no person suffer want.
With these ailments and maladies, I venture to trouble Your Majesty’s sacred compassion; I am overwhelmed by the utmost sincerity of my devotion.

In this memorial of thanks for the rain, I reflect deeply that the Way of Heaven favors life, bestowing both rain and sunshine with precise regularity, whereas the ordinary human mind is easily disturbed by even minor droughts or floods.
Moved by compassion, there was no way to appeal to Heaven or strike the earth; fearing to be late, we prayed to the Buddhas and recited the sutras.
The Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara did not disregard the hearts of sentient beings, and the Dragon King Sāgara was able to respond to the vows of the multitude.

Upon a single petition for rain, it fell in torrents like overturned basins. Both people and things were revived, and grasses and trees alike were satisfied. We respectfully present this *kaśyapa* offering.
This offering is made to look upward and repay your vast and boundless grace. We humbly pray that the dark clouds may disperse and the sun of wisdom may shine brilliantly.

May illnesses be secretly extinguished throughout the four quarters, and crops ripen across the entire land. May there be the joy of drumming the belly in the wilds, and no ill omens of "joyful lamentation" within households.
May all people give rise to hearts of kindness and compassion, and together enjoy the auspicious blessings of prosperity. This is respectfully submitted.

Second, one should contemplate that all the simple and common people are none other than the children of the August Heaven. One should also contemplate that the lush rows of grain and millet are all the refined essence of the Great Earth.
Reflecting upon the calamity wrought by the drought-demon *hantā*, which brings misfortune to the fields, one should offer fervent prayers everywhere.
With one heart in sincerity, this temple has accordingly established ritual altars and empowered divine mantras. As the various heavens revere Prajñā, we invoke its sublime name;
as divine dragons protect the land, we offer earnest prayers for the realm. Truly, we have received compassionate response and been granted vast blessings:
the scorching sun was withdrawn and clouds arose from the mountains and rivers; sweet rain poured down, reviving all that had withered.

All things flourish; the heavens are abundantly nourished, and the entire realm is moistened by grace. The world has no anxiety over years of famine, and the people enjoy the joy of bountiful harvests.

Though one might sacrifice body and life, the kindness of the Great Heaven could never be repaid. Yet, by advancing in virtue and cultivating one’s practice, one may slightly fulfill the sincerity of an ordinary person.
I respectfully present these meager offerings to briefly convey my gratitude. I pray that from this moment until—

In the future, may there forever be no anxiety regarding floods or droughts; may there always be timely rains and sunshine; may military conflict and disease be pacified, and the realm be peaceful and harmonious.
With utmost sincerity, I humbly offer these sentiments, looking up in hope for Your Sacred Inspection. Respectfully submitted.
Preface to the Ritual for the Great Compassion Repentance by Bao Shan:

I humbly reflect that the ocean of Dharma is vast and profound, universally nourishing all under heaven with its abundant moisture; the clouds of compassion cast a wide shade, pervading the great earth with their refreshing coolness.

With the sincere devotion of a sunflower, I reverently gaze upward toward the lotus-like sun. I earnestly consider the entire assembly gathered here: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the text.*
Having planted slight roots of goodness in former lives, I have been reborn among the ranks of humanity. Born within the land of Zhendan (China), I have encountered the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.

I have deeply understood the characteristics of transgression and merit, and further realized the source of cause and effect. One must cultivate both merit and wisdom to achieve perfection, and must surely benefit both oneself and others.
I have reverently heard that this Great Compassionate Divine Mantra has been widely propagated by all Buddhas, beginning with the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

I heard this from the Tathāgata Śatasahasraraśmivimalavihārin; tracing it back through successive transmissions to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in ninety-nine billion Ganges Rivers, its origins are so remote that they cannot be measured by the number of kalpas. Its wondrous marks are inconceivable—how could those of inferior station fathom them?
Upon hearing these dhāraṇī words but once, one suddenly transcends the eighth bhūmi at the very first thought; it is enough merely to make this vow.
It is said: To fully manifest the hand and eye within a single body, one unties the malignant disease that binds the person. Thus, the aspirational mind of seeking manifests;

it is like the reflection of a single moon in a thousand rivers, or like an empty valley echoing through ten thousand mouths. Responding immediately to every stimulus, there is no wish that is not fulfilled.
Its merit is boundless, and its praise can never be exhausted. Therefore, the Venerable One of Siming established this rite of repentance based on the sutras, and [he] took up...
Through contemplative cultivation and practice, this tradition has circulated through the ages, its spiritual efficacy unfailing.

Therefore, with deep reverence, we invite the faithful to assemble on a certain day to inaugurate, within these very precincts, a ritual arena for repentance and the invocation of blessings for the protection of the nation and the welfare of the people.
For one full cycle, we shall perform the Great Compassion Repentance Rite, solemnizing the altar protocols, arranging offerings, engaging in repentance and making vows, and burning incense.
Scattering flowers, he vowed to practice with diligent cultivation for twenty-one days, entering the Way with single-minded devotion.

His majestic deportment was uninterrupted as he appeared before all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Through his contemplative practice, he entered the subtle realm of the self-nature’s tranquil light.

Universally opening the gate of repentance for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, he accumulated the merit of devas and humans and established great vows of compassion to fulfill the path of Bodhi.

The primary cause for this [merit] is to offer our supreme prayers that the Sovereign alone may enjoy prosperity, that the four seas may be free from anxiety, that the miasma of war may be forever pacified throughout the eight directions, and that the Imperial Mean may abide in peace for ten thousand generations. May wind and rain be timely, and the harvests be abundant;
may all under heaven sing of the "What Have We" wind, and all within the realm rejoice in the transformation of non-action. Furthermore, we pray that those gathered here shall seek—

Those who seek fame and achievement shall have their aspirations fulfilled; those who engage in commerce and agriculture shall see their capital increase. Those seeking heirs shall soon obtain sons endowed with fortune and wisdom;

those seeking longevity shall ultimately ascend to the realm of benevolence and long life. Furthermore, for those who ward off calamities and resist afflictions, or who pray for blessings and peace, as well as those who cultivate pure karma to inscribe their names upon the highest grade, or who resolve to awaken the bodhicitta to achieve ultimate Buddhahood—may they all respond to my [invocation].
We seek [your] response through this invocation, looking upward to appeal to your unconditioned compassion.

As the year draws to a close, we reflect with deep earnestness that we, though claiming to be sons of the Buddha, have unworthily donned the robes of the fields; though we have cultivated the three studies, we have not achieved success, nor have we unified our single mind.
Though possessing [the teachings], one has not yet realized them. The burdens of body and speech have long accumulated; attachment to my Dharma remains ever firm.
Day after day, throughout three hundred and sixty days, there is nothing new; hour after hour, throughout the twelve periods of each day, things remain as they were before.

How much more so when engaged in construction, where felling trees and inflicting harm are especially frequent, or in planting and digging, where injury and killing are exceedingly abundant. Dwelling in a land of suffering, there is no activity that can be avoided.

I submit this petition. Having committed transgressions as dark as the color black, how could my sins be avoided? Moreover, at this time when the year draws to a close, I reflect in stillness upon the errors of the past year;

relying solely on the power of repentance, I hope to change my course toward self-renewal. Therefore, I have carefully selected this coming *lā* [the final day of the month] to assemble the pure assembly for Buddhist rites.
I humbly pray that the Buddha’s light may shine through and his spiritual power provide secret assistance, so that—
All you people gathered here today, your Way is renewed along with the sun. It is like the spring breeze bringing all things to life;
your obstructions have vanished entirely, like bright sunlight melting thin ice.

May the mountain gate be free from the sorrow of calamity, may the monastic community enjoy the joy of virtue and morality, may the donors’ households flourish with blessings, and may the world be peaceful and serene. May even the insects and ants attain transcendence.
May all living beings together ascend to liberation. We humbly pray that Your Great Compassion will deign to grant us clear discernment.
To the Kitchen God, Master of the Cauldron and Tripod (etc.). We respectfully venerate the Monitor of the Retreat, the Great Holy King of the Kiṃnaras, and the five...

To the Lord of the Office of Destiny: On this twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month, as the labors of the year have come to an end, we have reverently cleansed the kitchen and hearth and offered fragrant delicacies, while reciting and empowering sutras and mantras to look up in gratitude for your divine protection.

We pray that the monastic community may flourish and prosper, that the ocean of monks may remain peaceful and harmonious, and that the Hall of Fragrant Accumulation may always be abundant, providing inexhaustible offerings for the Buddhas and the Sangha. May the Dharma gate be blessed with joy, and may you protect us from fire and water.

One does not contemplate matters such as benefit, success, or failure; remaining peaceful, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.
If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind, the true Bodhimanda is established.
The Pure Land is called the Samādhi of One Practice. If a person possesses these two samādhis, it is like the earth having seeds, which can contain, nurture, and bring them to fruition.
The single mark and single practice are also like this. My current preaching of the Dharma is like seasonal rain that universally moistens the great earth;
your Buddha-nature is like the seed, and upon encountering this soaking moisture, it shall all attain [growth].
[Enlightenment] occurs. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi; those who rely on my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit. The Treatise says:
The Sixth Patriarch lived for eighty years as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Though he appeared to be illiterate, his realization of the school’s teachings was perfectly luminous.
These two kinds of samādhi are the swift path for practitioners to tread upon the profound way in their daily lives. Based on—
The Patriarch’s intent is as follows: "One mark" means to penetrate through to the true mark (*dharmatā*) within objects, rather than dwelling in illusory marks.

"One practice" means that the mind is always straightforward and abides in the true mark, not falling into a second thought. When both mind and objects are empty, one is in profound accord with principle;
this is called *samādhi*. The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-pāramitā-sūtra* asks: "What is called the 'one-practice *samādhi*'? The Buddha [replied]:...
It is said: "The Dharma-realm has a single characteristic. To bind one's conditions to the Dharma-realm is called the Samādhi of One Practice.
One who enters the Samādhi of One Practice fully knows that the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is characterized by non-differentiation.

Now, the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is itself the Samādhi of One Characteristic; binding one's conditions to the Dharma-realm is itself the Samādhi of One Practice. This is the distinction between principle and practice."
Thus, both the ancestral intent and the two [types of] practice proceed together; because they are darkly in accord with principle, they are ultimately non-dual. The adept understands this in detail.
This is from the *Song of Realizing the Way* by Chan Master Zhengjue of Yongjia.
Have you not seen? The idle man of the Way, who has severed study and attained non-action, does not eliminate delusive thoughts nor seek after truth.

The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. When the Dharma-body is fully awakened, there is not a single thing; it is the original source-nature, the celestial and true Buddha.
The five aggregates are like floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness; the three poisons are like bubbles on water, vainly appearing and disappearing. Thus one realizes...

The true mark (*dharmatā*) is devoid of persons or dharmas; it instantly extinguishes even the karma of Avīci hell. If one deceives sentient beings with false speech, one will personally incur the punishment of having one’s tongue plucked out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Upon sudden awakening, one realizes the Tathāgata-dhyāna: the essence of the six perfections and myriad practices is perfectly complete.
Within the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly clear; upon waking, all is empty, and not even a "great chiliocosm" exists. There is neither sin nor merit, neither loss nor gain—quiescence.
Within the nature of cessation, do not seek or inquire. For a long time, the mirror of dust has never been polished. Today, you must clearly analyze and discern:
who is without thought? Who is without birth? If it is truly neither born nor unborn, then go call upon the wooden mechanical man and ask him.

Seeking the Buddha’s grace, when will your merit be perfected? Let go of the four great elements; do not grasp at them. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with eating and drinking.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty; this is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. This is the definitive teaching that reveals the True Vehicle.
Some people are unwilling to accept this as it is, seeking instead through conceptualization. I do not seek out leaves or search for branches; I cut straight to the root, as sealed by the Buddhas.
The *maṇi* jewel, which people do not recognize, has been personally obtained within the *tathāgatagarbha*. Its six kinds of divine functions are both empty and not empty;
its single orb of light is neither color nor form. It purifies the five eyes and attains the five powers; only through realization can one know who is capable [of this].

Measuring: It is not difficult to see one’s form when looking in a mirror; how can one grasp the moon while clutching at its reflection in water? Always walking alone, always stepping forth by myself—those who have attained enlightenment travel together upon the path to Nirvana.
My tune is ancient and my spirit is pure, so the wind rises naturally high; my appearance is haggard and my bones are firm, yet people pay me no heed.
I am a destitute monk, claiming in speech that I am poor; in truth, it is my body that is poor, but the Way is not poor. Being poor, my body is constantly clad in [ragged robes].
Coarse cloth robes: the Way is the heart-treasury, a jewel of priceless value. This priceless jewel is inexhaustible in its use; it benefits all beings according to the time, never begrudging itself.
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within its essence; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of the mind-ground.

When a superior person makes a single resolution, everything is understood; those of middle or inferior capacity, though they hear much, mostly lack faith. Simply untie the soiled garment from within your own breast—who else could do this for you?
Outwardly boasting of one's diligence, one endures slander from others and tolerates their criticisms; to carry fire to burn the heavens is but to weary oneself in vain.

When I hear such things, it is like drinking nectar—melting away all barriers, I suddenly enter the inconceivable. To regard malicious words as merit, these become my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If one does not give rise to enmity or affection because of slander, how can this manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience? This is the essence.
Pervasive. My teaching is also pervasive; with concentration and wisdom perfectly clear and bright, I do not stagnate in emptiness. It is not that I alone have now attained realization;
the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical. With the lion’s roar, I preach fearlessly. When the hundred beasts hear it, their heads split open;

the fragrant elephants flee in haste, losing their majesty. The devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy. I have traveled across rivers and seas, traversed mountains and streams, seeking out teachers.
Seeking the Way is for the purpose of Zen meditation. Since I recognized the path of Caoxi, I have known that birth and death are not mutually involved.
Walking is Zen; sitting is Zen; whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, my essence remains at peace. Even if I encounter a sharp blade, I am ever composed;
even if I am given deadly poison, I remain indifferent. My Master beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; through many kalpas, he was once the Immortal of Forbearance.
How many times have I been born? How many times have I died? Birth and death drift on endlessly, without fixed end.

Since I suddenly awakened to the realization that there is no birth, what sorrow or joy can there be amidst all honors and insults? I entered the deep mountains to dwell in an araṇya, beneath long pines in a secluded and remote ravine.
Leisurely and at ease, sitting in quietude within the home of a wild monk; dwelling in profound stillness, truly serene and detached. Awakening is immediate, requiring no effort.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are different: practicing giving while clinging to signs may bring the merit of rebirth in heaven, yet it is like an arrow shot upward into the void;
when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, resulting in an unfavorable future life. How can this compare to the unconditioned reality-mark (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*)?
Gate. First is the direct entry into the stage of the Tathāgata. Simply attain the root; do not worry about the branches.

Like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon, once one can understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting oneself and others will never be exhausted. The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Throughout the eternal night and the clear evening, what is there to do?
The Buddha-nature is the precept-jewel, the seal of the mind-ground; mist, dew, clouds, and mists are its very substance.
The upper robe, the dragon-subduing bowl, and the tiger-releasing staff—two golden rings on the shafts jingle clearly. This is not for the sake of displaying outward form or empty ritual;
it is the personal trace of the Tathāgata’s precious staff. Do not seek the true, do not sever the delusory; understand that these two dharmas are empty and signless.
Signless, empty, yet not non-empty—this is the true mark of the Tathāgata. The mirror of the mind is bright, reflecting all.

Unobstructed, vast and transparently clear, it pervades the realms of sand; within this reflection of the myriad phenomena in their dense array, there is a single, perfectly luminous sphere, neither inside nor out.
To be expansively empty and to reject cause and effect leads to a vast, boundless state that invites calamity and misfortune.

To abandon attachment while clinging to emptiness is likewise a sickness—it is like avoiding drowning only to leap into fire. To discard the deluded mind and grasp at the True Principle—the very mind of grasping and discarding—[is itself the delusion].
One becomes skilled in artifice. When practitioners do not understand this, they continue to practice; truly, they mistake a thief for their own son.
The depletion of the wealth of Dharma and the destruction of merit—none of these arise except from this mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*).

Therefore, the Gate of Meditation (*dhyānamukha*) brings the mind to an end, allowing one to enter suddenly into the power of the vision of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*). A great man wields the sword of wisdom; the blade of Prajñā is like a diamond flame. Not only can it...

He crushes the hearts of the heterodox; long ago he already caused the demons and devas to lose their courage. He thunders the Dharma-thunder and beats the Dharma-drum; spreading clouds of compassion, he showers nectar.
As dragons and elephants trample through it, the moisture is boundless; those of the three vehicles and five natures are all awakened.
The fat and rich essence of the Snowy Mountains contains no impurities; I always receive this pure *sarpis* (clarified butter). One nature is perfectly penetrating all natures; one...
The Dharma universally encompasses all phenomena. As the single moon appears everywhere in all waters, yet every moon in the water is subsumed within that one moon;
so too do the Dharmakāyas of all Buddhas enter my own nature, and my nature in turn merges with that of the Tathāgata.

In a single stage, all stages are fully perfected—neither form nor mind, neither karma nor action. In the snap of a finger, the eighty-four thousand gates are perfectly accomplished; in a single instant, the three poisons are extinguished.
Throughout kalpas, all numerical and non-numerical categories—what connection do they have with my numinous awakening? It cannot be disparaged; it cannot be praised.
Its essence is like empty space, without boundaries or shores. Without leaving its present location, it is eternally serene.

If you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen. It cannot be grasped; it cannot be relinquished. Within this state of the unobtainable, there is simply obtaining as it is. Speaking in silence, speaking...
At that time, he remained silent. The Great Gate of Giving was opened without obstruction. When someone asked me what school of thought I understood, I replied:
"The power of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Whether this be right or wrong, people do not know; whether one acts contrary to the flow or with it, even the heavens cannot fathom it.
I have long practiced through many kalpas; this is no idle deception. I raise the Dharma banner and establish the fundamental tenets, making the Buddha’s wisdom clearly manifest.
The Imperial Edict states: Caoxi is the foremost; Kāśyapa first transmitted the lamp. Twenty-eight generations were recorded in the Western Heaven;
the Dharma flowed eastward and entered this land. Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch; the transmission of the robe through six generations became renowned throughout the world.

Those who subsequently attained the Way are beyond counting. Truth cannot be established; delusion is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside—not even an emptiness of emptiness. Twenty.

The Gate of Emptiness is fundamentally unattached; the single nature of the Tathāgata’s body is inherently identical. The mind is the root, and dharmas are the dust; these two are like stains upon a mirror.
When the stains are completely removed, the light finally appears. When both mind and dharmas are extinguished, the nature is itself the Truth. Alas for the final Dharma!
In this evil age, the merit of sentient beings is meager and difficult to regulate. Being far removed from the Sages, their false views are deep; demons...

The strong oppress the weak, and many harbor resentment and malice. Upon hearing the teachings of the Tathāgata’s sudden (sudden) vehicle, they harbor regret that it does not eliminate [their faults] and shatter them like tiles.

The karma is created in the mind, and the retribution falls upon the body. There is no need for resentment or complaint, nor should one lay further blame on others. If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, [you must practice accordingly].
Do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma. In the sandalwood forest, there are no mixed trees; dense and deep, it is where the lion dwells.
In the tranquil realm and amidst the secluded woods, he roams alone. The running beasts and flying birds all flee far away. Yet the lion cubs follow after him in a great multitude.
At three years of age, one can already let out a great roar. If a jackal were to pursue the Dharma King, it would be a hundred-year-old monster vainly opening its mouth.

The Perfect and Sudden Teaching does not accommodate human sentiments; if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, you must settle it directly. This is not for this mountain monk to flaunt his sense of self versus others.

I fear that if you do not practice correctly, you will fall into the pit of nihilism or eternalism. It is neither "not" nor "is"; it is neither "is" nor "is not. To err by a hair’s breadth is to lose a thousand miles.
Li. This is precisely why the dragon girl attained Buddhahood instantaneously, whereas Shanxing fell into ruin immediately upon birth.

Since my youth, I have accumulated learning and inquiry; I have also investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and treatises. I distinguished names and characteristics without knowing when to stop, entering the sea to count the sands only to weary myself in vain.
Consequently, the Tathāgata sternly rebuked me: "What benefit is there in calculating the treasures of others? From the beginning, I have been a mere wanderer...
Treading upon the void, you have wandered in vain for many years as a guest of the wind and dust. Your fundamental nature is perverse; your understanding is mistaken.

You do not comprehend the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching. The diligence of the Two Vehicles is no path to the Bodhi-mind; the cleverness of external paths lacks true wisdom. They are both deluded and utterly foolish.
With empty hands, they point toward the finger and conceive a real understanding; grasping the finger as the moon, they labor in vain. Root and object...
Within the Dharma, one falsely fabricates the bizarre; failing to see that not a single dharma exists is precisely what is called Avalokiteśvara.
When fully realized, karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty; if not yet realized, one must still repay past debts. Like one who encounters a royal feast while starving but cannot eat.
When the sick encounter the King of Physicians, how could they fail to recover? Through the power of insight and knowledge, one may practice dhyāna while remaining amidst desire;
a lotus born from fire can never be destroyed. Vīradatta committed a grave offense yet awakened to non-arising; he attained Buddhahood long ago and remains even now.

With the Lion’s Roar, he speaks fearlessly, deeply lamenting those who are muddled, dull-witted, and stubborn. They know only that committing a grave offense obstructs Bodhi, yet they do not see the Tathāgata opening [the way].
The Secret Instruction: Two bhikṣus committed the transgressions of lust and killing; Upāli’s accumulation of offenses was like a glowing ember.

The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispelled their doubts, just as the brilliant sun melts frost and snow. This inconceivable power of liberation has a wondrous function as boundless as the sands of the Ganges.

Even if one were to offer the four kinds of requisites without wearying, or offer ten thousand measures of gold, it would still be insufficient to repay his kindness. I would even grind my bones to powder to express my gratitude.
The body is not yet sufficient as recompense; a single phrase, clearly understood, transcends ten billion worlds. This King of Dharmas is most supreme;
Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have all together realized it. I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; those who receive it with faith will all be in accord.
Seeing clearly, there is not a single thing; there is no person, and there is no Buddha. The great trichiliocosm and its myriad realms are but bubbles upon the ocean. All holy ones—
Virtue is like a flash of lightning. Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one’s head, with concentration and wisdom perfectly clear and bright, one will never lose them.

The sun may grow cold; the moon may grow hot; no demons can destroy the True Teaching. When the great elephant-vehicle advances majestically along its path, who could see a cicada or a mantis capable of blocking its tracks?
A great elephant does not travel the narrow paths of a hare; a great awakening is not constrained by minor details. Do not...
To cast my narrow views as slander against the vast heavens—before I have fully realized this, I now offer you this parting word.
The Treatise says: The Chan Master Zhenjue of Yongjia left home at the age of eight and extensively explored the Tripiṭaka.

He mastered the perfect and subtle Dharma-gate of Tiantai and constantly practiced silent meditation and contemplation throughout the four modes of deportment. It was while reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* that he...
He attained great enlightenment and established the fundamental tenets at Caoxi.

Observing him as he shook his staff and circumambulated the Patriarch, and his several exchanges with the Patriarch, one sees that amidst the most ordinary social interactions, he directly transcended the mundane and penetrated the profound depths of the Dharma.
How could the Patriarch not have deeply approved of this? He stayed for only one night, and was thus called "One-Night Enlightenment" (*Yixiu Jue*);
this was no empty title. He then composed the "Song of Realizing the Way" (*Zhengdao Ge*) in one chapter to elucidate the path of the Chan school’s "separate transmission outside the teachings."
Having eliminated the maladies of expedient and shallow teachings, these [words] all flow forth from the mind of self-realization.

Their crushing of the heterodox and manifestation of the orthodox is like the brilliance of a Moheya sword drawn from its scabbard, its radiance illuminating the heavens; its power is inviolable. Since the beginning of the School of the Lineage (Zongmen), such a thing has been seen but once.
Reflecting upon this, I consider that those who have attained the Way throughout antiquity and the present are as numerous as the waters of the great ocean, yet an *asura*...
As for the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs, they drink as much as they desire, each filling its own measure.

If one were to say that Yongjia has overturned the great ocean until nothing remains, it would be no exaggeration; this is truly the pivotal essence of the Zen gate and the manifest secret of the separate transmission.
Its dissemination in the Western Heavens is universally praised as the *Sūtra on Realizing the Way*, and this is not false.
Chan Master Shitou Xiqian’s *Cantong Qi*:
"The mind of the Great Immortal of the Land of Chu has been secretly transmitted from east to west. Though human faculties may be sharp or dull, the Way has neither North nor South patriarchs."
The spiritual source is luminously pure; its branches and streams flow on in obscurity. To cling to phenomena is fundamentally delusion; to accord with principle is likewise not awakening.
In every gate, all objects are both interpenetrating and non-interpenetrating; they either mutually involve one another, or else they abide in their respective positions.

Form is fundamentally distinct in its essential nature; sound originally differs as pleasure or pain. Darkness accords with the words "superior" and "middling"; clarity corresponds to the phrases "pure" and "turbid.
The natures of the four great elements are self-reverting, like a child finding its mother: fire is heat, wind is movement, water is moisture, and earth is solidity.

The eye perceives form, the ear perceives sound; the nose perceives fragrance, and the tongue perceives saltiness and acidity. Yet, based upon each individual phenomenon, they are distributed according to their faculties and branches.

From beginning to end, one must return to the source. Use the language appropriate to the status of the vessel; one should clarify what is within while remaining aware of what lies in darkness, and not encounter darkness with darkness.
When there is darkness, there is brightness; do not seek to perceive brightness through its signs. Brightness and darkness face one another, like successive steps.

All things possess their own efficacy; one should speak of their function and their locus. In affairs, they exist as the meeting of lid and box; in principle, they correspond like the point of an arrow.

When receiving words, you must understand the fundamental source; do not establish your own rules and regulations. If you do not realize the Way upon meeting it with your eyes, how can you know the path as you take your steps?

Advancing forward is neither near nor far; delusion creates barriers as solid as mountains and rivers. I respectfully address those who study the profound mystery: do not let your time and energy be spent in vain.
The Treatise says: Master Shitou, upon reading the *Zhao Lun* (Treatise by Sengzhao), attained realization through the statement that "the myriad things are one's own self.

He thereby awakened to the fact that while the Sage has no self, there is nothing that is not his self. Furthermore, he dreamed that he and the Sixth Patriarch were riding together on numinous wisdom, wandering through the ocean of nature (*dharmatā*).
This was the origin of the composition of the *Cantong Qi* (Token of Accordance). Every sentence is the Dharma; it is intended for people to realize the truth by receiving these words.
The Essential Principle: To meet the Way at every glance; beyond this, there is not a single other dharma to bestow upon people.
This is the Dharma discourse of the Venerable Master Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou.
Students of the present day must first clarify their own authentic insight. If you attain your own insight, [you will realize that]...
Thus, one is not defiled by birth and death; going and staying are free and easy, requiring nothing from others, for all excellence is naturally possessed.
Now, you practitioners of the Way must simply not be obstructed by delusions. When you need to act, you act. If you cannot do so now, where does the illness lie?
The illness lies in a lack of self-confidence; because one’s own confidence is insufficient, one immediately becomes busily preoccupied with pursuing all external objects.
Great Virtue, if you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly runs in pursuit, you will be no different from the Patriarch. Do you wish to recognize the Patriarch?
He is none other than the one right before your eyes who is listening to the Dharma now. When a student lacks faith, they run outward in pursuit.
To "attain" is merely to study words; it is worlds apart from the Patriarchs. Do not err, O Great Virtue!

If you do not encounter this now, for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand births you will transmigrate through the three realms, pursuing objects of like and dislike, and end up inside the bellies of donkeys and oxen.
How are you different from the ancient sages today? What is lacking in you? It is the divine light of the six paths.
It has never ceased. If you can see in this way, you are a person who has nothing more to do for the rest of this life.
The light of purity in a single thought-moment is the Dharma-body Buddha within your own house; the light of non-discrimination in a single thought-moment is your Sambhogakāya Buddha;
the light of non-distinction in a single thought-moment is your Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. These three bodies are none other than those who are listening to the Dharma right before your eyes this very day.
People do not seek it outwardly. These three types of function, according to the teachings, are called the ultimate limit.
From the perspective of this mountain monk’s path, these three are merely names and words; thus it is said: "The body is established based on meaning, and the land is discussed based on essence.
The Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are clearly known to be but light and shadow. Great Virtue, you must first recognize the one who plays with the light.
The shadow-person is the source of all Buddhas; it is the dwelling place where all seekers of the Way return.
Venerable Sir, the body composed of the four great elements cannot understand preaching the Dharma or hearing the Dharma; empty space cannot understand preaching the Dharma or hearing the Dharma.

It is this vivid, solitary luminosity before your eyes—devoid of form or substance—that understands preaching the Dharma and hearing the Dharma. Therefore, I, this mountain monk, have said to you: the five aggregates...
Within the field of the body dwells the True Person of No-Station, manifest and majestic, without so much as a hair’s breadth of separation.
Why do you not recognize it? The mind-dharma is formless and penetrates the ten directions. In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing;
in the hand it grasps and seizes; in the foot it moves and runs. If the mind does not arise, one is liberated wherever one is. My way of seeing cuts off all such [conceptual] sitting.
The heads of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas are like those of hired laborers; the two levels of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment are like wearing shackles and chains;
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like dung and soil; Bodhi and Nirvana are like hitching posts for donkeys and horses. Why is this so?

It is because they have not realized that the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are empty, and thus these obstacles and barriers remain. If one belongs to the true stream of the Way, all [these things] are exhausted.
It is not so. Now, for the sake of you all, I shall briefly break through this matter with a general discourse. Examine for yourselves the distance and the nearness.
Time is precious; each of you must exert yourselves. Take care.

The Treatise states: Among the *Fayu* (Dharma Words) of the Old Man of Hutuo and the various *Guangyu* (Extensive Sayings) recorded in the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, only this single chapter has been preserved.
Because these are words of fundamental importance, they have been left as a shortcut for later generations to enter the Way.
If one’s realization is not authentic, one falls into what the ancients rebuked—namely, identifying with the conscious spirit—and the fault lies with the later practitioner.
This is not the fault of the teacher; it lies solely with the wise who possess the eye of the discernment of dharmas and are able to skillfully select for themselves.

This Dharma of the "Treasure Mirror Samādhi" (Pao-ching San-mei) of Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie was secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Now that you have obtained it, you should protect it well. It is like snow placed in a silver bowl.

The bright moon hides within the herons; though their kinds are not uniform, they know their place when mingled. The meaning does not reside in the words. When the opportune moment arrives, it is met;

yet once movement occurs, it becomes a mere trap. To hesitate or look back is to fall into error; both "contrary" and "touching" are non-existent. It is like a great mass of fire—there is only the manifestation of its brilliant patterns.
This immediately belongs to the defiled. At midnight it is perfectly luminous; at dawn it does not manifest. It serves as a model for all things and is used to uproot all suffering.
Although it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not without expression. It is like facing a precious mirror, where form and reflection behold one another. You are not that.

He is precisely you. Like an infant of the world, complete with the five marks, neither going nor coming, neither arising nor abiding, tranquil and harmonious, possessing both the phrase and the non-phrase, yet ultimately unable to grasp any object because his speech is not yet correct. This is like the six lines of the hexagram *Chongli* (Repetition of Separation).
The biased and the orthodox revolve and intermingle, layering into three; through transformation they become five. Like the taste of the *ch’i-tsao* herb, like a vajra scepter:

the orthodox center is subtly flanked by the biased. Striking and singing are raised together; penetrating the source and following the path, the biased carries the way. When these are interlaced, there is auspiciousness.
It must not be violated or opposed. It is innate and wondrous; it belongs neither to delusion nor to awakening. Through the conditions of time and season, it is serene yet manifest.

Subtly, it enters the infinitesimal; vast, it transcends all spatial dimensions. A deviation of even a hair’s breadth fails to accord with the musical scales. Thus, there are now the teachings of sudden and gradual.

Based on these conditions, the fundamental tenets are established; the tenets are thus divided. These are the very rules and standards. When the tenets are realized and the ultimate goal reached, the true and eternal flows forth.

While the exterior is tranquil, the interior wavers—like a tethered colt or a trapped rat. Out of compassion for this, the former sages bestowed the perfection of Dharma-giving (*dānapāramitā*) according to their various delusions.
To take black for white is to have perverted perceptions extinguished; with a sincere heart, one pledges oneself to follow the ancient path. Please observe the ancients:

when the Buddha’s Way was about to be perfected, he gazed at the tree for ten kalpas. He was like a tiger missing a claw or a horse with a white hind leg; because of these minor imperfections, he did not proceed.

Precious tables and rare treasures are met with astonishment; yet as for the dark-skinned slave or the white ox, even the skillful strength of Hou Yi could only shoot an arrow through a hundred paces.
When the tips of two arrows meet, what has skillful strength to do with it? A wooden man sings and a stone maiden dances; these are not reached by consciousness or cognition.
How could one permit the intrusion of discursive thought? A minister serves his sovereign; a son obeys his father. To be disobedient is not filial; to fail to serve is not to be an assistant.
Acting secretly and employing [the Way] in obscurity, appearing as if ignorant or dull-witted, yet being able to maintain continuity—this is called the Sovereign among Sovereigns.
The Commentary states: The Treasure Mirror Samādhi (*ratnādarśa-samādhi*) is the very source of the Caodong school.
Its opening statement says: "Such a Dharma as this has been secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; now that you have obtained it, you should protect it well.

It is evident that this teaching is addressed to those who possess realization, intended merely to ensure its diligent protection. If one does not protect it well, it will immediately become discordant with the Way.

This refers to the fact that even a deviation as slight as a hair’s breadth or a moment’s lapse fails to accord with the *lülü* (musical scales). Within this [teaching], the fundamental principle is established and the compass and square are set forth.

The absolute is precisely the absolute that is identical with the relative; the relative is the relative that is identical with the absolute. This is the pervasive integration of principle and phenomena, whether vertical or horizontal.

To speak of phenomena is to speak of phenomena alone; to speak of principle is to speak of principle alone. Thus, there is unimpeded freedom between the vertical and horizontal, and no trace remains of the distinction between the relative and the absolute. This is "flexibility."
